#### Consequences of Lemma 4.1.

We use the Gronwall lemma established above for the inequality (4.8).

#### Corollary 4.1.

For all $k\geq x$ and $\tau\in[X2^{-k-1},1]$ , we have the high frequency regime estimate:

$$ 2^{k}a_{k}(\tau)\mathbf{1}_{k,\tau}\lesssim A_{k}(\tau)+2^{-7k}\int_{\tau}^{1}\sum_{l=0}^{k-1}\frac{2^{5l}}{(\tau^{\prime})^{3}}\cdot A_{l}(\tau^{\prime})\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}d\tau^{\prime} $$

#### Proof.

We apply Lemma 4.1 for the inequality (4.8), where:

$$ u(k,\tau)=2^{k}a_{k}(\tau)\mathbf{1}_{k,\tau},\ b(k)=\frac{1}{10}\cdot 2^{-8k},\ c(k,\tau)=\tau^{-3}2^{6k}\mathbf{1}_{k,\tau}. $$

From (4.10) we obtain for $\tau\in[X2^{-k-1},1]$ :

$$ 2^{k}a_{k}(\tau)\mathbf{1}_{k,\tau}\leq A_{k}(\tau)+2^{-8k}\int_{\tau}^{1}\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}A_{l}(\tau^{\prime})\cdot\frac{1}{(\tau^{\prime})^{3}}2^{6l}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}\prod_{j=l+1}^{k-1}\bigg(1+\int_{\tau}^{\tau^{\prime}}b(j)c(j,\tau^{\prime\prime})d\tau^{\prime\prime}\bigg)d\tau^{\prime}. $$

In order to bound the above, we first note that:

$$ \int_{\tau}^{\tau^{\prime}}b(j)c(j,\tau^{\prime\prime})d\tau^{\prime\prime}=\frac{1}{10}\cdot 2^{-2j}\int_{\tau}^{\tau^{\prime}}\frac{\mathbf{1}_{j,\tau^{\prime\prime}}}{(\tau^{\prime\prime})^{3}}d\tau^{\prime\prime}\leq\min\big(X^{-2},2^{-2j}\tau^{-2}\big)\leq\min\big(1,2^{-2j}\tau^{-2}\big). $$

In this bound we used the good control of the constant in the definition of $b(k),$ obtained using the smallness of $\delta$ in (4.7). As a result, we obtain for all $\tau\in[X2^{-k-1},1]$ :

$$ \prod_{j=l+1}^{k-1}\bigg(1+\int_{\tau}^{\tau^{\prime}}b(j)c(j,\tau^{\prime\prime})d\tau^{\prime\prime}\bigg)\leq\prod_{j=l+1}^{k-1}\Big(\min\big(2,1+2^{-2j}\tau^{-2}\big)\Big)\lesssim 1+2^{-l}\tau^{-1}, $$

where we bounded the terms with $2^{-j}<\tau$ using the inequality $x+1\leq e^{x}.$ Finally, we conclude by noticing that:

$$ 2^{-8k}2^{6l}\cdot 2^{-l}\tau^{-1}\leq 2^{-7k}2^{5l}\cdot\frac{2^{-k}}{\tau}\leq 2^{-7k}2^{5l}\cdot\frac{2}{X}\leq 2^{-7k}2^{5l}. $$

∎

We use the definition of $A_{k}(\tau)$ to compute the new error terms obtained on the RHS of (4.11). For the data terms we compute:

$$ d_{k}+2^{-7k}\int_{\tau}^{1}\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}\frac{2^{5l}}{(\tau^{\prime})^{3}}d_{l}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim_{\delta}d_{k}+\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}2^{5(l-k)}d_{l}\lesssim_{\delta}d_{k}. $$

In this inequality, we used the fact that $\sum_{k}\sum_{l}2^{-5|k-l|}d_{l}\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II},$ so the term $\sum_{l}2^{-5|k-l|}d_{l}$ can be written schematically as $d_{k}.$ We will use similar bounds implicitly for the rest of the proof.

Additionally, we have the following bound for the discrete error terms $S_{k}:$

$$ S_{k}(\tau)+2^{-7k}\int_{\tau}^{1}\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}\frac{2^{5l}}{(\tau^{\prime})^{3}}S_{l}(\tau^{\prime})\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim S_{k}(\tau)+\delta X2^{-7k}\int_{\tau}^{1}\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}\frac{2^{-3l+6m}}{(\tau^{\prime})^{6}}a_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}d\tau^{\prime} $$

$$ \lesssim S_{k}(\tau)+\delta X2^{-7k}\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\tau<X2^{-m-1}\\
x\leq m\leq l\end{subarray}}\int_{X2^{-l-1}}^{X2^{-m-1}}\frac{2^{-3l+6m}}{(\tau^{\prime})^{6}}a_{m}(X2^{-m-1})d\tau^{\prime} $$

$$ \lesssim S_{k}(\tau)+\frac{\delta}{X^{4}}2^{-7k}\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\tau<X2^{-m-1}\\
x\leq m\leq l\end{subarray}}2^{2l+6m}a_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\lesssim\frac{\delta}{X^{2}}2^{-5k}\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{6m}a_{m}(X2^{-m-1}). $$

#### Discrete Gronwall inequality.

We deal with the sum of discrete error terms obtained in (4.11) using the discrete Gronwall inequality. We first write the estimate in a convenient form by defining:

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{S}_{k}(\tau) \displaystyle:=\frac{\delta}{X^{2}}2^{-5k}\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{6m}a_{m}(X2^{-m-1}), \displaystyle\widetilde{E}_{k}(\tau) \displaystyle:=E_{k}(\tau)+2^{-7k}\int_{\tau}^{1}\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}\frac{2^{5l}}{(\tau^{\prime})^{3}}E_{l}(\tau^{\prime})\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}d\tau^{\prime}, \displaystyle\widetilde{I}_{k}(\tau) \displaystyle:=I_{k}(\tau)+2^{-7k}\int_{\tau}^{1}\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}\frac{2^{5l}}{(\tau^{\prime})^{3}}I_{l}(\tau^{\prime})\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

Thus, (4.11) implies that for all $\tau\in[X2^{-k-1},1]$ :

$$ 2^{k}a_{k}(\tau)\mathbf{1}_{k,\tau}\lesssim C_{\delta}d_{k}+\widetilde{S}_{k}(\tau)+C_{\delta}\widetilde{E}_{k}(\tau)+C_{\delta}\widetilde{I}_{k}(\tau). $$

In particular, there exist constants $C^{\prime\prime\prime},C_{\delta}>0$ such that for any $k\geq x:$

$$ 2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1})\leq C_{\delta}d_{k}+C_{\delta}\widetilde{E}_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+C_{\delta}\widetilde{I}_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+C^{\prime\prime\prime}\frac{\delta}{X^{2}}2^{-5k}\sum_{m=x}^{k-1}2^{6m}a_{m}(X2^{-m-1}). $$

We fix the parameters $X,\delta>0$ satisfying (4.6), (4.7), and :

$$ C^{\prime\prime\prime}\frac{\delta}{X^{2}}<\frac{1}{10}. $$

We also introduce the notation:

$$ b_{k}=C_{\delta}d_{k}+C_{\delta}\widetilde{E}_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+C_{\delta}\widetilde{I}_{k}(X2^{-k-1}). $$

Using this notation, we have for any $k\geq x:$

$$ 2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1})\leq b_{k}+\frac{1}{10}2^{-5k}\sum_{m=x}^{k-1}2^{5m}\cdot 2^{m}a_{m}(X2^{-m-1}). $$

We apply the discrete Gronwall inequality according to [Jon64]:

$$ 2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1})\leq b_{k}+\frac{1}{10}2^{-5k}\sum_{m=x}^{k-1}\bigg(2^{5m}b_{m}\cdot\prod_{j=m+1}^{k-1}\big(1+1/10\cdot 2^{-5j}\cdot 2^{5j}\big)\bigg)\lesssim b_{k}+2^{-4k}\sum_{m=x}^{k-1}2^{4m}b_{m}. $$

As a consequence, we have the following bound for all $k\geq x$ :

$$ 2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1})\lesssim_{\delta}d_{k}+\widetilde{E}_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+\widetilde{I}_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+\sum_{m=x}^{k-1}2^{-4k+4m}\Big(\widetilde{E}_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+\widetilde{I}_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big). $$

Notation. We used the parameters $X>0$ and $\delta>0$ to apply Gronwall-like inequalities in the above proof. We now fixed these parameters (depending on $M,C_{0},C_{2}$ ), so we return to our usual notation convention that we write $A\lesssim B$ if there exists a constant $C>0$ depending only on the constants $M,C_{0},C_{2}$ such that $A\leq CB.$

#### Consequences of the discrete Gronwall inequality.

We use the estimate (4.14) in the high frequency regime estimate (4.12). From (4.14) we obtain for all $\tau\in[X2^{-k-1},1]$ :

$$ \widetilde{S}_{k}(\tau)\lesssim\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{-5k+5m}d_{m}+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{-4k+4m}\Big(\widetilde{E}_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+\widetilde{I}_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big) $$

$$ \lesssim\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{-5k+5m}d_{m}+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{-4k+4m}\Big(E_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+I_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big), $$

where the second bound follows by:

$$ \sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{-4k+4m}\cdot 2^{-7m}\sum_{l=x}^{m-1}\int_{X2^{-l-1}}^{1}\frac{2^{5l}}{(\tau^{\prime})^{3}}E_{l}(\tau^{\prime})d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim\sum_{\tau<X2^{-l-1}\leq 1}2^{-4k+4l}E_{l}(X2^{-l-1}), $$

and we have a similar inequality for the inhomogeneous terms $I_{l}.$ We also bound the remaining terms of (4.12):

$$ \widetilde{E}_{k}(\tau)=E_{k}(\tau)+2^{-7k}\int_{\tau}^{1}\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}\frac{2^{5l}}{(\tau^{\prime})^{3}}E_{l}(\tau^{\prime})\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim E_{k}(\tau)+2^{-2k}\tau^{-2}\sum_{l\geq x}\int_{\tau}^{1}e_{l}(\tau^{\prime})d\tau^{\prime} $$

$$ \lesssim E_{k}(\tau)+2^{-2k}\tau^{-2}\int_{\tau}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{3}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\Big)d\tau^{\prime}, $$

$$ \widetilde{I}_{k}(\tau)=I_{k}(\tau)+2^{-7k}\int_{\tau}^{1}\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}\frac{2^{5l}}{(\tau^{\prime})^{3}}I_{l}(\tau^{\prime})\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim I_{k}(\tau)+2^{-2k}\tau^{-2}\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

We combine these estimates and we obtain that (4.12) implies for all $\tau\in[X2^{-k-1},1]$ :

$$ 2^{k}a_{k}(\tau)\mathbf{1}_{k,\tau}\lesssim d_{k}+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{-5k+5m}d_{m}+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{-4k+4m}\Big(E_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+I_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big) $$

$$ +E_{k}(\tau)+I_{k}(\tau)+2^{-2k}\tau^{-2}\int_{\tau}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{3}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\Big)d\tau^{\prime}+2^{-2k}\tau^{-2}\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

#### Summing the high frequency estimates.

For each $\tau\in(0,1],$ we sum the above high frequency regime estimates for all $k\geq x$ such that $X2^{-k-1}\leq\tau:$

$$ \sum_{\tau\geq X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}a_{k}(\tau)\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\sum_{\tau\geq X2^{-k-1}}\Big(E_{k}(\tau)+I_{k}(\tau)\Big)+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}\Big(E_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+I_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big)+ $$

$$ +\int_{\tau}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{3}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\Big)d\tau^{\prime}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

Additionally, we have the estimates:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\tau\geq X2^{-k-1}}E_{k}(\tau)+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}E_{m}(X2^{-m-1}) \displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{k\geq x}\int_{\tau}^{1}e_{k}(\tau^{\prime})\lesssim\int_{\tau}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{3}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\Big)d\tau^{\prime}, \displaystyle\sum_{\tau\geq X2^{-k-1}}I_{k}(\tau)+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}I_{m}(X2^{-m-1}) \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

Therefore, we obtain the following high frequency regime estimate:

$$ \sum_{\tau\geq X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}a_{k}(\tau)\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\int_{\tau}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{3}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\Big)d\tau^{\prime}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

#### Proof of Proposition 4.6.

The final step in the proof of the optimal high frequency regime estimate (4.5) consists of bounding the second error term on the RHS of (4.15).

We first notice that we have the estimate for all $\tau\in(0,1]$ :

$$ \tau^{3}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\Big)\lesssim\tau^{3}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big)+\sum_{k\geq x}\tau^{3}2^{k}\Big(\big\|\nabla P_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\big\|P_{k}\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big) $$

$$ \lesssim\tau^{3}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big)+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-k-1}\leq 1}\tau^{3}2^{k}\Big(\big\|\nabla P_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\big\|P_{k}\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big)+\tau^{2}\sum_{\tau\geq X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}a_{k}(\tau) $$

$$ \lesssim\tau^{3}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big)+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-k-1}\leq 1}\tau^{2}\Big(\big\|\nabla P_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\big\|P_{k}\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big)+\tau^{2}\sum_{\tau\geq X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}a_{k}(\tau) $$

$$ \lesssim\tau^{2}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big)+\tau^{2}\sum_{\tau\geq X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}a_{k}(\tau). $$

We use the preliminary estimates in Proposition 4.2 and (4.15) to get:

$$ \tau^{3}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\Big)\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\int_{\tau}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{3}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\Big)d\tau^{\prime}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

Using Gronwall, we proved that for all $\tau\in(0,1]$ :

$$ \tau^{3}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\Big)\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

Finally, we use this estimate in (4.15) to obtain the optimal high frequency estimate (4.5).

### 4.6 The main estimate in Theorem 1.2

In this section, we prove the main estimate (1.13) in Theorem 1.2. For this, we first establish the following top order estimate for the singular component $\Phi_{0}:$

$$ \mathcal{E}^{0}_{II}(\tau)\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\sum_{m=0}^{M}\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{m}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}, $$

where we define the top order energy for the singular component:

$$ \mathcal{E}^{0}_{II}(\tau):=\tau\big\|\Phi_{0}\big\|_{H^{M+1/2}}^{2}+\tau^{2}\big\|\Phi_{0}\big\|_{H^{M+3/2}}^{2}+\tau^{2}\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\nabla^{M}\Phi_{0}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}+\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}\tau^{2}\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\nabla^{m}\Phi_{0}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|\Phi_{0}\big\|_{H^{M+1}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

Using Propositions 4.2, 4.4 and the estimate (4.5), we have the bound for all $\tau\in(0,1]$ :

$$ \tau^{2}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\Big)\lesssim\tau^{2}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big)+\sum_{k\geq x}\tau^{2}2^{k}\Big(\big\|\nabla P_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\big\|P_{k}\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big) $$

$$ \lesssim\tau^{2}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big)+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-k-1}\leq 1}\tau^{2}2^{k}\Big(\big\|\nabla P_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\big\|P_{k}\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big)+\tau\sum_{\tau\geq X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}a_{k}(\tau) $$

$$ \lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-k-1}\leq 1}2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1}). $$

We use the bound (4.14) for $2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1})$ to get:

$$ \sum_{\tau<X2^{-k-1}\leq 1}2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1})\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-k-1}\leq 1}\widetilde{E}_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-k-1}\leq 1}\widetilde{I}_{k}(X2^{-k-1}) $$

$$ \lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-k-1}\leq 1}E_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-k-1}\leq 1}I_{k}(X2^{-k-1})\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

We note that we used (4.16) in the last inequality. As a result, we proved that:

$$ \tau^{2}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\Big)\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

As usual, we also get for all $\tau\in(0,1]$ :

$$ \displaystyle\tau\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2} \displaystyle\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}\cdot\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\sqrt{\tau^{\prime}}\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}+\int_{\tau}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{3/2}\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime} \displaystyle\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\sqrt{\tau^{\prime}}\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

Applying Gronwall, we proved that:

$$ \tau^{2}\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+\tau^{2}\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}+\tau\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

We recall that $\xi=\nabla^{M}\Phi_{0}.$ Combining the above estimate with the preliminary estimates in Proposition 4.2, we proved (4.17).

#### Proof of (1.13).

We use the estimates for the regular quantities in Section 4.1 and the top order estimate for the singular quantities (4.17) to get:

$$ \mathcal{E}_{II}(\tau)\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\mathcal{F}_{II}(\tau)+\sum_{m=0}^{M}\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{m}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

We also recall our notation $F_{m}^{\prime}=\psi\sum_{i=1}^{I}\nabla^{m+1}\Phi_{i}+F_{m}^{0}.$ Using again the estimates for the regular quantities proved in Section 4.1, we conclude. ∎

### 4.7 Estimates for the asymptotic quantities

In this section we prove the estimates (1.14) and (1.15) for the asymptotic quantities $\mathcal{O}$ , $\mathfrak{h},$ and $\Phi_{i}^{0}$ with $1\leq i\leq I,$ in order to complete the proof of Theorem 1.2. We notice that the estimates for the regular quantities in Proposition 4.1 already imply the bound (1.26) for $\Phi_{i}^{0}$ with $1\leq i\leq I.$ As a result, we only need to prove the estimates (1.28) and (1.15) for $\mathcal{O}$ and $\mathfrak{h}$ .

#### Proposition 4.7.

The obstruction tensor $\mathcal{O}$ satisfies the estimate (1.28):

$$ \big\|\mathcal{O}\big\|_{H^{M+1}}^{2}\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\mathcal{F}_{II}(0). $$

#### Proof.

As a consequence of the preliminary estimates in Proposition 4.2, we obtain for all $0\leq m\leq M$ :

$$ \big\|\nabla^{m}\mathcal{O}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim\bigg(\big\|\Phi_{0}\big\|_{H^{m+3/2}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\Phi_{0}\big\|_{H^{m+1/2}}^{2}\bigg)\bigg|_{\tau=1}+\int_{0}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}\big\|F_{m}^{\prime}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\mathcal{F}_{II}(0), $$

so it remains to prove the above bound for $\big\|\nabla^{M+1}\mathcal{O}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}$ .

For any $k\geq x$ and $0\leq\tau<X2^{-k-1}\leq 1$ , the low frequency regime estimate in Proposition 4.4 implies:

$$ 2^{2k}\big\|\tau P_{k}\nabla_{\tau}\nabla^{M}\Phi_{0}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim 2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+2^{-k}\mathcal{D}_{II}+2^{k}\int_{\tau}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}\big\|P_{k}F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}+2^{-k}\int_{\tau}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

Using the expansion of $\nabla_{\tau}\nabla^{M}\Phi_{0}$ at $\mathcal{I}^{-}$ , we get that for all $k\geq x:$

$$ 2^{2k}\big\|P_{k}\nabla^{M}\mathcal{O}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim 2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+2^{-k}\mathcal{D}_{II}+2^{k}\int_{0}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}\big\|P_{k}F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}+2^{-k}\int_{0}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

Together with our previous estimate for $\|\mathcal{O}\|_{H^{M}},$ we obtain that:

$$ \big\|\nabla^{M}\mathcal{O}\big\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\mathcal{F}_{II}(0)+\sum_{k\geq x}2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1}). $$

We complete the proof since we already proved in Section 4.6:

$$ \sum_{k\geq x}2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1})\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\int_{0}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\mathcal{F}_{II}(0). $$

∎

In order to prove the estimate (1.15) for $\mathfrak{h}$ , we first prove that it can be reduced to the proof of (1.29). We recall the notation $\mathfrak{h}_{M}=\nabla^{M}h-2(\log\nabla)\nabla^{M}\mathcal{O},$ and notice that we have the bounds:

$$ \displaystyle\big\|\mathfrak{h}\big\|_{H^{M+1}}^{2} \displaystyle\lesssim\big\|\mathfrak{h}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\big\|\big[(\log\nabla),\nabla^{M}\big]\mathcal{O}\big\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla\mathfrak{h}_{M}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2} \displaystyle\lesssim\big\|\mathfrak{h}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+C\Big(\big\|\not{Riem}_{0}\big\|_{H^{M}}^{2}\Big)\big\|\mathcal{O}\big\|_{H^{M}}^{2}+\sum_{k\geq x}2^{2k}\big\|P_{k}\mathfrak{h}_{M}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\big\|\mathfrak{h}_{M}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2} \displaystyle\lesssim\big\|\mathfrak{h}\big\|_{H^{M}}^{2}+C\Big(\big\|\not{Riem}_{0}\big\|_{H^{M}}^{2}\Big)\big\|\mathcal{O}\big\|_{H^{M}}^{2}+\sum_{k\geq x}2^{2k}\big\|P_{k}\mathfrak{h}_{M}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}, $$

where we used the proof of Lemma 3.2 to bound the commutator term. Using the interpolation inequalities of [KR06] and the bound in Lemma 2.7, we obtain:

$$ \big\|\mathfrak{h}\big\|_{H^{M+1}}^{2}\lesssim\big\|h\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+C\Big(\big\|\not{Riem}_{0}\big\|_{H^{M}}^{2}\Big)\big\|\mathcal{O}\big\|_{H^{M}}^{2}+\sum_{k\geq x}2^{2k}\big\|P_{k}\mathfrak{h}_{M}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}. $$

Using the already established bound for $\mathcal{O},$ we showed that it suffices to prove (1.29):

$$ \sum_{k\geq x}2^{2k}\big\|P_{k}\mathfrak{h}_{M}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\mathcal{F}_{II}(0). $$

We recall our notation $\xi=\nabla^{M}\Phi_{0}$ and we consider the renormalized quantities for all $k\geq x$ :

$$ \overline{\xi}_{k}=P_{k}\xi-\tau\log(2^{k}\tau)P_{k}\nabla_{\tau}\xi. $$

Using the expansion for $\xi$ at $\mathcal{I}^{-},$ we get:

$$ \lim_{\tau\rightarrow 0}\overline{\xi}_{k}=\lim_{\tau\rightarrow 0}\Big(P_{k}\nabla^{M}\Phi_{0}-\tau\log(2^{k}\tau)P_{k}\nabla_{\tau}\nabla^{M}\Phi_{0}\Big)=P_{k}\nabla^{M}h-2\log(2^{k})P_{k}\nabla^{M}\mathcal{O}. $$

Recalling the definition of the operator $R_{k}$ in (2.29), we can write:

$$ P_{k}\nabla^{M}h-2\log(2^{k})P_{k}\nabla^{M}\mathcal{O}=P_{k}\mathfrak{h}_{M}+2P_{k}(\log\nabla)\nabla^{M}\mathcal{O}-2\log(2^{k})P_{k}\nabla^{M}\mathcal{O}=P_{k}\mathfrak{h}_{M}+R_{k}\nabla^{M}\mathcal{O}. $$

Thus, we obtain using (2.32):

$$ 2^{2k}\big\|P_{k}\mathfrak{h}_{M}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim 2^{2k}\lim_{\tau\rightarrow 0}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+2^{2k}\big\|R_{k}\nabla^{M}\mathcal{O}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim 2^{2k}\lim_{\tau\rightarrow 0}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\big\|\underline{P}_{k}\nabla^{M}\mathcal{O}\big\|_{H^{1}}^{2}. $$

Summing for all $k\geq x$ , we get that:

$$ \sum_{k\geq x}2^{2k}\big\|P_{k}\mathfrak{h}_{M}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim\big\|\mathcal{O}\big\|_{H^{M+1}}^{2}+\sum_{k\geq x}2^{2k}\lim_{\tau\rightarrow 0}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}. $$

According to the above estimate and (1.28), in order to prove (1.29) we need to establish the following result:

#### Proposition 4.8.

We have the following estimate:

$$ \sum_{k\geq x}2^{2k}\lim_{\tau\rightarrow 0}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\mathcal{F}_{II}(0). $$

As a result, (1.15) holds, completing the proof of Theorem 1.2.

#### Proof.

Using (4.4) as in the proof of Proposition 4.4, we get that $\overline{\xi}_{k}$ satisfies the equation on $\tau\in(0,X2^{-k-1}]$ :

$$ \nabla_{\tau}\overline{\xi}_{k}=[\nabla_{\tau},P_{k}]\xi-\log(2^{k}\tau)\nabla_{\tau}\big(\tau P_{k}\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big)= $$

$$ =\tau[\nabla_{4},P_{k}]\xi-\log(2^{k}\tau)\Big(4\tau\Delta P_{k}\xi+\tau P_{k}\big(\psi\nabla\xi\big)+\tau[\nabla_{4},P_{k}]\tau\nabla_{\tau}\xi+\tau P_{k}F_{M}^{\prime}\Big). $$

We contract by $\overline{\xi}_{k}$ to obtain the energy estimate:

$$ 2^{2k}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim\Big(2^{2k}\big\|P_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\big\|P_{k}\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big)\Big|_{\tau={X2^{-k-1}}}+\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}\cdot 2^{k}\tau^{\prime}\big\|[\nabla_{4},P_{k}]\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}+ $$

$$ +\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}\cdot|2^{k}\tau^{\prime}\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|\cdot\big\|\Delta P_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}+\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}\cdot|2^{k}\tau^{\prime}\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|\cdot\big\|P_{k}\big(\psi\nabla\xi\big)\big\|_{L^{2}}+ $$

$$ +\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}\cdot|2^{k}\tau^{\prime}\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|\cdot\big\|[\nabla_{4},P_{k}]\tau^{\prime}\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}+\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}\cdot|2^{k}\tau^{\prime}\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|\cdot\big\|P_{k}F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{L^{2}}. $$

We use Lemma 2.3, Gronwall, and the notation in Section 4.5 to obtain:

$$ \displaystyle 2^{2k}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim \displaystyle 2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}\big\|\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}|\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|^{2}\big\|\Delta P_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2} \displaystyle+\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{-k}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}|\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|^{2}\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}|\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|^{2}\big\|\nabla P_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2} \displaystyle+\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}|\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|^{2}\big\|\tau^{\prime}\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}|\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|^{2}\big\|P_{k}F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}. $$

We use the preliminary estimates in Proposition 4.2 to get:

$$ 2^{2k}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim 2^{-k}\mathcal{D}_{II}+2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+ $$

$$ +\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}|\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|^{2}\big\|\Delta P_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}+2^{-k}\int_{\tau}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|P_{k}F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

Using the finite band property of the LP projections for $P_{k}=\underline{P}_{k}^{2}$ , we have the bound:

$$ \int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}(\tau^{\prime})^{2}|\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|^{2}\big\|\Delta P_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{3k}(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})^{2}|\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|^{2}\big\|\underline{P}_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

Once we established the above estimate for $2^{k}\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\|_{L^{2}},$ the idea of the proof is to decompose the error term in (4.18) into its low frequency and high frequency regime parts, in order to use our previous estimates. For each $\tau^{\prime}\in[\tau,X2^{-k-1}]$ we have:

$$ \big\|\underline{P}_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}(\tau^{\prime})\lesssim\sum_{l<x}\big\|P_{l}^{2}\underline{P}_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}+\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}\big\|P_{l}^{2}\underline{P}_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l\geq k\\
\tau^{\prime}<X2^{-l-1}\end{subarray}}\big\|P_{l}^{2}\underline{P}_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}+\sum_{l\geq k}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}\big\|P_{l}^{2}\underline{P}_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}. $$

The first three terms in (4.19) are in the low frequency regime, and the last term is in the high frequency regime.

We bound the first term in (4.19) using the $L^{2}$ almost orthogonality of the LP projections:

$$ \sum_{l<x}\big\|P_{l}^{2}\underline{P}_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}(\tau^{\prime})\lesssim\sum_{l<x}2^{-5k+5l}\big\|P_{l}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}(\tau^{\prime})\lesssim 2^{-5k}\big\|\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}(\tau^{\prime}). $$

The corresponding term in (4.18) is bounded using Proposition 4.2:

$$ \int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{-6k}(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|^{2}\cdot\tau^{\prime}\big\|\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim 2^{-k}\mathcal{D}_{II}+2^{-k}\mathcal{F}_{II}(\tau). $$

For the second term in (4.19) we use Cauchy-Schwarz and we consider a projection operator with $\underline{P}_{k}=\underline{\widetilde{P}}_{k}^{2}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\bigg(\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}\big\|P_{l}^{2}\underline{\widetilde{P}}_{k}^{2}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}(\tau^{\prime})\bigg)^{2} \displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}2^{-5(k-l)}\big\|\underline{\widetilde{P}}_{k}P_{l}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}(\tau^{\prime})\lesssim\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}2^{-2k}2^{-5(k-l)}\big\|\nabla P_{l}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}(\tau^{\prime}) \displaystyle\lesssim\frac{1}{(\tau^{\prime})^{2}}\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}2^{-2k}2^{-5(k-l)}\big(2^{-2l}\cdot 2^{l}a_{l}(X2^{-l-1})+2^{-3l}\mathcal{D}_{II}+2^{-3l}\mathcal{F}_{II}(\tau^{\prime})\big), $$

where we used Proposition 4.4 in the second line. The corresponding term in (4.18) is bounded by:

$$ \int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}2^{k}|\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|^{2}2^{-3(k-l)}\bigg(2^{l}a_{l}(X2^{-l-1})+2^{-l}\mathcal{D}_{II}+2^{-l}\mathcal{F}_{II}(\tau^{\prime})\bigg)d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim $$

$$ \lesssim 2^{-k}\mathcal{D}_{II}+2^{-k}\mathcal{F}_{II}(\tau)+\sum_{l=x}^{k-1}2^{-3(k-l)}\cdot 2^{l}a_{l}(X2^{-l-1}). $$

For the third term in (4.19), we have similarly from Proposition 4.4:

$$ \bigg(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l\geq k\\
\tau^{\prime}<X2^{-l-1}\end{subarray}}\big\|P_{l}^{2}\underline{\widetilde{P}}_{k}^{2}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}(\tau^{\prime})\bigg)^{2}\lesssim\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l\geq k\\
\tau^{\prime}<X2^{-l-1}\end{subarray}}2^{-5(l-k)}\big\|\underline{\widetilde{P}}_{k}P_{l}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}(\tau^{\prime})\lesssim\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l\geq k\\
\tau^{\prime}<X2^{-l-1}\end{subarray}}2^{-2k}2^{-5(l-k)}\big\|\nabla P_{l}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}(\tau^{\prime}) $$

$$ \lesssim\frac{1}{(\tau^{\prime})^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l\geq k\\
\tau^{\prime}<X2^{-l-1}\end{subarray}}2^{-2k}2^{-5(l-k)}\big(2^{-2l}\cdot 2^{l}a_{l}(X2^{-l-1})+2^{-3l}\mathcal{D}_{II}+2^{-3l}\mathcal{F}_{II}(\tau^{\prime})\big). $$

As a result, the corresponding term in (4.18) is bounded using Proposition 4.4:

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l\geq k\\
\tau<X2^{-l-1}\end{subarray}}\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-l-1}}2^{k}|\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|^{2}2^{-7(l-k)}\big(2^{l}a_{l}(X2^{-l-1})+2^{-l}\mathcal{D}_{II}+2^{-l}\mathcal{F}_{II}(\tau^{\prime})\big)d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim $$

$$ \lesssim\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l\geq k\\
\tau<X2^{-l-1}\end{subarray}}\big(2^{l}a_{l}(X2^{-l-1})+2^{-l}\mathcal{D}_{II}+2^{-l}\mathcal{F}_{II}(\tau)\big)\cdot\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-l-1}}2^{k}|\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|^{2}2^{-7(l-k)}d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim $$

$$ \lesssim 2^{-k}\mathcal{D}_{II}+2^{-k}\mathcal{F}_{II}(\tau)+\sum_{l\geq k}2^{-7(l-k)}\cdot 2^{l}a_{l}(X2^{-l-1}). $$

For the high frequency regime fourth term in (4.19), we have using our notation in Section 4.5:

$$ \bigg(\sum_{l\geq k}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}\big\|P_{l}^{2}\underline{P}_{k}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}(\tau^{\prime})\bigg)^{2}\lesssim\sum_{l\geq k}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}2^{-5(l-k)}\big\|P_{l}\xi\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}(\tau^{\prime})\lesssim\tau^{\prime}\sum_{l\geq k}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}2^{-5(l-k)}a_{l}(\tau^{\prime}). $$

The corresponding term in (4.18) is bounded in Lemma 4.2 at the end of the section.

We combine the previous bounds and we get from (4.18) that for all $\tau\in(0,X2^{-k-1}]$ :

$$ 2^{2k}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim d_{k}+\tau^{6}2^{6k}\mathcal{D}_{II}+2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+\sum_{l\geq x}2^{-3|k-l|}\cdot 2^{l}a_{l}(X2^{-l-1}) $$

$$ +\big(2^{-k}+\tau^{6}2^{6k}\big)\mathcal{F}_{II}(\tau)+\sum_{l\geq k}2^{-6(l-k)}\int_{\tau}^{1}2^{l}\tau^{\prime}\big\|P_{l}F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}+\widetilde{E}_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+\widetilde{I}_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+ $$

$$ +\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{-4|k-m|}\Big(E_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+I_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big)+\sum_{l\geq k}2^{-6(l-k)}\int_{\tau}^{1}e_{l}(\tau^{\prime})d\tau^{\prime}. $$

We take the limit $\tau\rightarrow 0$ and sum for all $k\geq x:$

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k\geq x}\Big(2^{2k}\lim_{\tau\rightarrow 0}\big\|\overline{\xi}_{k}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big) \displaystyle\lesssim\mathcal{D}_{II}+\mathcal{F}_{II}(0)+\sum_{k\geq x}2^{k}a_{k}(X2^{-k-1}) \displaystyle+\sum_{k\geq x}\big(\widetilde{E}_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+\widetilde{I}_{k}(X2^{-k-1})\big)+\int_{0}^{1}(\tau^{\prime})^{3}\Big(\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\Big)d\tau^{\prime}. $$

For the last three terms, we use the estimates in Section 4.5 and we obtain the conclusion. ∎

We conclude the section by proving the additional estimate used in the previous proof:

#### Lemma 4.2.

We have the bound for all $\tau\in(0,X2^{-k-1}]$ :

$$ \int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})^{3}|\log(2^{k}\tau^{\prime})|^{2}\sum_{l\geq k}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}2^{-6(l-k)}\cdot 2^{l}a_{l}(\tau^{\prime})d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim $$

$$ \lesssim d_{k}+\tau^{6}2^{6k}\cdot\big(\mathcal{D}_{II}+\mathcal{F}_{II}(\tau)\big)+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{-4|k-m|}\Big(E_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+I_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big)+ $$

$$ +\widetilde{E}_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+\widetilde{I}_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+\sum_{l\geq k}2^{-6(l-k)}\bigg(\int_{\tau}^{1}e_{l}(\tau^{\prime})d\tau^{\prime}+\int_{\tau}^{1}2^{l}\tau^{\prime}\big\|P_{l}F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}\bigg)+2^{-k}\mathcal{F}_{II}(\tau). $$

#### Proof.

We use the estimate (4.12) as a starting point. We also use the bound on $\widetilde{S}_{l}$ in Section 4.5, and the definitions of $\widetilde{E}_{l}$ and $\widetilde{I}_{l}$ . Thus, we have for all $\tau\in[X2^{-l-1},1]$ :

$$ 2^{l}a_{l}(\tau)\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau}\lesssim d_{l}+\widetilde{S}_{l}(\tau)+\widetilde{E}_{l}(\tau)+\widetilde{I}_{l}(\tau) $$

$$ \lesssim d_{l}+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{-5l+5m}d_{m}+\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{-4l+4m}\Big(E_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+I_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big)+ $$

$$ +E_{l}(\tau)+I_{l}(\tau)+2^{-7l}\int_{\tau}^{1}\sum_{m=x}^{l-1}\frac{2^{5m}}{(\tau^{\prime})^{3}}\Big(E_{m}(\tau^{\prime})+I_{m}(\tau^{\prime})\Big)\mathbf{1}_{m,\tau^{\prime}}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

We use this bound to obtain a total of 8 error terms that control our main integral. We notice that the first two terms can be dealt with in a straightforward way. For the third and fourth terms we compute that:

$$ \int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\sum_{l\geq k}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}2^{-6(l-k)}2^{-4l+4m}\Big(E_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+I_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big)d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim $$

$$ \lesssim\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1}2^{-4|k-m|}\Big(E_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+I_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big), $$

where we used the fact that $l\geq m$ and $l\geq k$ in the first line. For the fifth and sixth terms we have:

$$ \int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\sum_{l\geq k}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}2^{-6(l-k)}\Big(E_{l}(\tau^{\prime})+I_{l}(\tau^{\prime})\Big)d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim $$

$$ \lesssim\sum_{l\geq k}2^{-6(l-k)}\bigg(\int_{\tau}^{1}e_{l}(\tau^{\prime})d\tau^{\prime}+\int_{\tau}^{1}2^{l}\tau^{\prime}\big\|P_{l}F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}\bigg)+2^{-k}\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}. $$

For the seventh and eight terms we can write:

$$ \int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\sum_{l\geq k}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}2^{-6(l-k)}\cdot\bigg(2^{-7l}\int_{\tau^{\prime}}^{1}\sum_{m=x}^{l-1}\frac{2^{5m}}{(\tau^{\prime\prime})^{3}}\Big(E_{m}(\tau^{\prime\prime})+I_{m}(\tau^{\prime\prime})\Big)\mathbf{1}_{m,\tau^{\prime\prime}}d\tau^{\prime\prime}\bigg)d\tau^{\prime}\lesssim I+II+III, $$

where we introduce the notation:

$$ \displaystyle I \displaystyle=\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\sum_{l\geq k}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}2^{-6(l-k)}\cdot 2^{-7l}\sum_{m=x}^{k-1}\bigg(\int_{\tau^{\prime}}^{1}\frac{2^{5m}}{(\tau^{\prime\prime})^{3}}\Big(E_{m}(\tau^{\prime\prime})+I_{m}(\tau^{\prime\prime})\Big)\mathbf{1}_{m,\tau^{\prime\prime}}d\tau^{\prime\prime}\bigg)d\tau^{\prime}, \displaystyle II \displaystyle=\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\sum_{l\geq k}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}2^{-6(l-k)}\cdot 2^{-7l}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1\\
k\leq m<l\end{subarray}}\bigg(\int_{\tau^{\prime}}^{1}\frac{2^{5m}}{(\tau^{\prime\prime})^{3}}\Big(E_{m}(\tau^{\prime\prime})+I_{m}(\tau^{\prime\prime})\Big)\mathbf{1}_{m,\tau^{\prime\prime}}d\tau^{\prime\prime}\bigg)d\tau^{\prime}, \displaystyle III \displaystyle=\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\sum_{l\geq k}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}2^{-6(l-k)}\cdot 2^{-7l}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\tau>X2^{-m-1}\\
m<l\end{subarray}}\bigg(\int_{\tau^{\prime}}^{1}\frac{2^{5m}}{(\tau^{\prime\prime})^{3}}\Big(E_{m}(\tau^{\prime\prime})+I_{m}(\tau^{\prime\prime})\Big)d\tau^{\prime\prime}\bigg)d\tau^{\prime}. $$

We first notice that in the inner integral of $I$ we have $\tau^{\prime\prime}\geq X2^{-m-1}>X2^{-k-1}.$ Thus, we have the bound:

$$ I\lesssim 2^{-7k}\sum_{m=x}^{k-1}\bigg(\int_{X2^{-k-1}}^{1}\frac{2^{5m}}{(\tau^{\prime\prime})^{3}}\Big(E_{m}(\tau^{\prime\prime})+I_{m}(\tau^{\prime\prime})\Big)\mathbf{1}_{m,\tau^{\prime\prime}}d\tau^{\prime\prime}\bigg)\lesssim\widetilde{E}_{k}(X2^{-k-1})+\widetilde{I}_{k}(X2^{-k-1}), $$

where in the second inequality we used the definitions of $\widetilde{E}_{k}$ and $\widetilde{I}_{k}.$ Next, we have the bound:

$$ \displaystyle II \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\sum_{l\geq k}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}2^{6k-13l}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1\\
k\leq m<l\end{subarray}}\bigg(\Big(E_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+I_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big)\int_{\tau^{\prime}}^{1}\frac{2^{5m}}{(\tau^{\prime\prime})^{3}}\mathbf{1}_{m,\tau^{\prime\prime}}d\tau^{\prime\prime}\bigg)d\tau^{\prime} \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\sum_{l\geq k}\mathbf{1}_{l,\tau^{\prime}}2^{6k-13l}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq 1\\
k\leq m<l\end{subarray}}2^{7m}\Big(E_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+I_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big)d\tau^{\prime} \displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq X2^{-k-1}}2^{7m}\Big(E_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+I_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big)\cdot\sum_{l>m}2^{6k-13l} \displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{\tau<X2^{-m-1}\leq X2^{-k-1}}2^{-6|m-k|}\Big(E_{m}(X2^{-m-1})+I_{m}(X2^{-m-1})\Big), $$

where we used again $\tau^{\prime\prime}\geq X2^{-m-1}$ to compute the inner integral in the first line.

Finally, we notice that the last error term $III$ must vanish as $\tau\rightarrow 0,$ since the inner sum would be empty. We prove a bound consistent with this expectation:

$$ \displaystyle III \displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{\tau>X2^{-m-1}}\bigg(\int_{\tau}^{1}\frac{2^{5m}}{(\tau^{\prime\prime})^{3}}\Big(E_{m}(\tau^{\prime\prime})+I_{m}(\tau^{\prime\prime})\Big)d\tau^{\prime\prime}\bigg)\cdot\int_{\tau}^{X2^{-k-1}}2^{k}\sum_{m<l}2^{-6(l-k)}\cdot 2^{-7l}d\tau^{\prime} \displaystyle\lesssim 2^{6k}\sum_{\tau>X2^{-m-1}}2^{-8m}\bigg(\int_{\tau}^{1}\frac{1}{(\tau^{\prime})^{3}}\Big(E_{m}(\tau^{\prime})+I_{m}(\tau^{\prime})\Big)d\tau^{\prime}\bigg) \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{\tau}^{1}\Big(\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}+(\tau^{\prime})^{3}\big\|\xi\big\|_{H^{3/2}}^{2}+(\tau^{\prime})^{3}\big\|\nabla_{\tau}\xi\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}\Big)d\tau^{\prime}\cdot\tau^{-2}2^{6k}\sum_{\tau>X2^{-m-1}}2^{-8m} \displaystyle\lesssim\tau^{6}2^{6k}\bigg(\mathcal{D}_{II}+\int_{\tau}^{1}\tau^{\prime}\big\|F_{M}^{\prime}\big\|_{H^{1/2}}^{2}d\tau^{\prime}\bigg)\lesssim\tau^{6}2^{6k}\big(\mathcal{D}_{II}+\mathcal{F}_{II}(\tau)\big). $$

Collecting all the bounds proved for the error terms, we conclude the proof. ∎

# Discretely self-similar exterior-naked singularities for the Einstein-scalar field system

**Authors:** Serban Cicortas ††thanks: cicortas@princeton.edu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Fine Hall, Washington Road, Princeton NJ 08544, United States of America Christoph Kehle ††thanks: kehle@mit.edu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Building 2, 77 Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge, MA 02139, United States of America

## Abstract

The problem of constructing naked singularities in general relativity can be naturally divided into two parts:

the construction of the region exterior to the past light cone of the singularity, extending all the way to (an incomplete) future null infinity and yielding the nakedness property (what we will call exterior-naked singularity regions)

attaching an interior fill-in that ensures that the singularity arises from regular initial data.

This problem has been resolved for the spherically symmetric Einstein-scalar field system by Christodoulou [Chr94], but his construction, based on a continuously self-similar ansatz, requires that both the exterior and the interior regions are mildly irregular on the past cone of the singularity. On the other hand, numerical works suggest that there exist naked singularity spacetimes with discrete self-similarity arising from smooth initial data. In this paper, we revisit part (i) of the problem and we construct exterior-naked singularity regions with discretely self-similar profiles which are smooth on the past cone of the singularity. We show that the scalar field remains uniformly bounded, but the singularity is characterized by the infinite oscillations of the scalar field and the mass aspect ratio. (Our examples require however that the mass aspect ratio is uniformly small, and thus the solutions are distinct from the exterior regions of the numerical examples.) It remains an open problem to smoothly attach interior fill-ins as in (ii) to our solutions, which would yield a new construction of naked singularity spacetimes, now arising from smooth initial data.

## 1 Introduction

The Einstein-scalar field system

$$ \begin{cases}Ric_{\mu\nu}=2\partial_{\mu}\phi\partial_{\nu}\phi\\
\square_{g}\phi=0\end{cases} $$

for a spherically symmetric spacetime $\big(M^{3+1},g\big)$ and a scalar field $\phi$ is a well-established model for studying the physics of gravitational collapse [Chr71]. The spacetime $\big(M^{3+1},g\big)$ admits double null coordinates $(u,v,\vartheta,\varphi)$ such that the metric takes the form

$$ g=-\Omega^{2}(u,v)dudv+r^{2}(u,v)d\sigma_{S^{2}}, $$

where $d\sigma_{S^{2}}\doteq d\vartheta^{2}+\sin^{2}\vartheta d\varphi^{2}$ is the standard metric on the sphere $S^{2}$ and the function $r(u,v)$ is the area radius of the orbits of the $SO(3)$ action.

For asymptotically flat spherically symmetric initial data for (1.1), solutions arising from small data disperse to Minkowski space, while there exist large-data solutions that contain a black hole region. A third class of solutions that play a special role are naked singularity spacetimes. Informally, these spacetimes contain a singularity that is visible to far away observers and not hidden behind the event horizon of a black hole. An alternative way to think about naked singularities is that they cause the incompleteness of future null infinity $\mathcal{I}^{+},$ which represents the set of idealized far away observers. It is well-known that such a singularity, denoted by $b_{\Gamma}$ , can only form at the center $\{r=0\}$ and the past lightcone $C_{0}^{-}$ of $b_{\Gamma}$ naturally divides a naked singularity spacetime into an exterior-naked singularity region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ and an interior fill-in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ , see Fig. 1. It is precisely the geometry of the exterior region that determines the nakedness of the singularity, while the interior fill-in ensures that the spacetime arises dynamically from regular collapse.

The incompleteness of $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ of naked singularity spacetimes constitutes a failure of global existence for far away observers and threatens the predictability of general relativity. The weak cosmic censorship conjecture, originally formulated by Penrose in [Pen69] for more general Einstein-matter systems, postulates that, generically, naked singularities do not form and $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ is complete [GH78, Chr99]. In the seminal work [Chr99a], Christodoulou proved the conjecture for (1.1) in spherical symmetry. We shall return to this work in Section 1.5.

*Figure 1: Penrose diagram of a spacetime with future incomplete $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ and a naked singularity at $b_{\Gamma}$ arising from data on $C_{0}^{+}$ . The past ingoing light cone of the singularity $b_{\Gamma}$ is denoted with $C_{0}^{-}$ and divides the spacetime into the exterior region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ and the interior fill-in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ .*

The genericity condition in formulating the weak cosmic censorship conjecture is indeed necessary because naked singularity spacetimes have been shown to form dynamically for (1.1) in spherical symmetry. We describe two kinds of naked singularities below, which can be classified as featuring continuous self-similarity and discrete self-similarity. The continuously self-similar solutions were rigorously constructed, while the discretely self-similar solutions have been obtained only numerically. We refer to Fig. 2 for an illustration highlighting the differences between continuous and discrete self-similarity.

*(a) Continuous self-similarity*

*(b) Discrete self-similarity*

*Figure 2: Penrose diagram and illustration of the naked singularities with continuous and discrete self-similarity. The self-similarity is only depicted in a bounded region as the data on $C_{0}^{+}$ have to be truncated in order to obtain an asymptotically flat $C_{0}^{+}$ .*

#### Continuous self-similarity.

In [Chr94], Christodoulou constructed naked singularities based on a continuous self-similar ansatz for the solution. The singular nature of the spacetimes is a result of the blow-up of the scalar field towards $b_{\Gamma}$ along the ingoing self-similar cone $C_{0}^{-}$ . The additional continuous symmetry reduces the PDE system (1.1) to an autonomous ODE system, which plays an essential role in the construction. The proof is divided into two parts:

- (i) the construction of the exterior-naked singularity region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$

- (ii) attaching an interior fill-in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ .

In each region, the solution is obtained from a suitable orbit of the autonomous ODE system. A key feature of Christodoulou’s examples is the limited regularity on the past cone of the singularity. In particular, the exterior-naked singularity region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ is already mildly irregular at $C_{0}^{-}$ . Thus, when viewed in the context of the Cauchy problem, the data have an initial mild singularity at $C_{0}^{-}\cap C_{0}^{+}$ . We refer to Section 1.4 for a more detailed discussion. These naked singularities have been generalized recently in [Sin24] to solutions with an asymptotically continuous self-similar profile. The strategy of dividing the problem into (i) and (ii) is also used in the recent groundbreaking work [RS23, Shl22] of Rodnianski and Shlapentokh-Rothman who constructed naked singularities for the Einstein vacuum equations, necessarily outside of spherical symmetry, for which the continuous self-similarity is generalized to a twisted self-similarity. We will discuss this work in more detail in Section 1.4.

#### Discrete self-similarity.

In the numerical study [Cho93] on critical gravitational collapse for (1.1), Choptuik first observed naked singularities with asymptotically discretely self-similar symmetry to occur on the black hole formation threshold—the interface in the moduli space of solutions between dispersion and collapse. In these spacetimes, the singularity is caused by bounded infinite oscillations of the scalar field along the past light cone $C_{0}^{-}$ of the singular point $b_{\Gamma}$ . Further numerical studies showed that all naked singularity solutions obtained using Choptuik’s procedure asymptote to a universal solution with exact discretely self-similar symmetry as the singularity $b_{\Gamma}$ is approached, see the review article [GM07]. We refer to this conjectured universal solution as the conjectured Choptuik solution. Note that in view of the exact discrete self-similarity, the conjectured Choptuik solution would not itself be asymptotically flat, although it would occur as the limit of asymptotically flat solutions as the singularity is approached.

### 1.1 The main theorem: construction of exterior-naked singularity regions

To date, no rigorous construction of discretely self-similar naked singularities has been achieved. As explained above, all examples to date have continuous self-similar symmetry and are of limited regularity. The difficulty arises from the fact that, unlike continuous self-similarity, imposing discrete self-similarity does not reduce the system to ODEs and one is still faced with a system of PDEs.

The main result of this paper is to address part (i) of the strategy outlined above and construct a class of exterior-naked singularity regions $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ with discretely self-similar profile along $C_{0}^{-}$ arising from initial data which are moreover smooth away from the singularity.

#### Theorem 1.

For any $\Delta>0$ , there exist spherically symmetric exterior-naked singularity solutions to (1.1) in the region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}\doteq\{-1\leq u<0,\ v\geq 0\}$ with a future incomplete $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ and a Penrose diagram as depicted in Fig. 3. In addition, the following hold.

- 1. The solutions are smooth in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ , in particular up to and including the ingoing cone $C^{-}_{0}:=[-1,0)\times\{0\}$ , i.e. they are smooth away from the singularity $b_{\Gamma}:=(0,0)$ .

- 2. Along the ingoing cone $C_{0}^{-}$ , the solutions satisfy the discrete self-similarity properties

$$ \phi\circ\theta_{\Delta}=\phi,\quad\mu\circ\theta_{\Delta}=\mu,\quad\frac{\partial_{v}\phi}{\partial_{v}r}\circ\theta_{\Delta}=e^{\Delta}\frac{\partial_{v}\phi}{\partial_{v}r}, $$

(1.3) where $\theta_{\Delta}(u,0)=(e^{-\Delta}u,0)$ and the gauge condition $r|_{C_{0}^{-}}=-u$ holds.

- 3. The scalar field $\phi$ and the mass aspect ratio $\mu=\frac{2m}{r}\doteq 1+4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{u}r\partial_{v}r$ remain small in amplitude

$$ \sup_{C_{0}^{-}}|\phi|\ll_{\Delta}1,\quad\sup_{C_{0}^{-}}|\mu|\ll_{\Delta}1 $$

(1.4) but undergo infinite oscillations along $C_{0}^{-}$ as the singularity $b_{\Gamma}$ is approached.

*Figure 3: Penrose diagram of an exterior-naked singularity region constructed in Theorem 1. Along the ingoing cone $C_{0}^{-}$ , the solution is discretely self-similar and satisfies (1.3). The singularity at $b_{\Gamma}$ is characterized by the infinite but uniformly bounded oscillations of the scalar field $\phi$ and the mass aspect ratio $\mu$ towards $b_{\Gamma}$ .*

#### Remark 1.1.

The solutions constructed in Theorem 1 have an exactly discretely self-similar profile only along the ingoing cone $C_{0}^{-}$ and are approximately discretely self-similar away from $C_{0}^{-}$ . We note that constructing spacetimes with asymptotically flat null infinity $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ requires the data on $C_{0}^{+}$ to be asymptotically flat, which is incompatible with global discrete self-similarity. However, one should be able to produce non-asymptotically flat spacetimes with exact discrete self-similarity using the extracting procedure of [RS18, Theorem 1.2]. These would still have the Penrose diagram of Fig. 3, but would not satisfy the usual notions of asymptotical flatness at $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ , as for instance the Bondi mass would diverge there.

### 1.2 Attaching an interior fill-in and constructing a naked singularity from smooth data

Our main result provides a construction of an exterior-naked singularity region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}},$ while it remains an open problem to construct an appropriate interior fill-in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ , in the past of $C_{0}^{-}$ .

#### Open problem.

Does any of the exterior-naked singularity regions constructed in Theorem 1 admit an interior fill-in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ which can be attached smoothly to obtain a naked singularity spacetime $\mathcal{R}_{\rm Int}\cup\mathcal{R}_{\rm Ext}$ as depicted in Fig. 1?

We stress that our exterior-naked singularity regions are fundamentally different from those numerically observed by Choptuik in [Cho93]. Specifically, the naked singularities in Choptuik’s simulations are incompatible with the smallness condition (1.4).

A natural way to construct an interior solution $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ is to make an exactly discrete self-similar ansatz in the interior region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ . Since the self-similar vector field (see already (1.14))

$$ S=u\partial_{u}+(1-\kappa)v\partial_{v} $$

is timelike in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ , this requires constructing periodic-in-time solutions to hyperbolic PDEs. On the other hand, in the region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ which is successfully constructed in Theorem 1, the vector field $S$ is spacelike, and we have to construct approximately periodic-in-space solutions. (For the construction in the exterior region there are robust techniques available, even outside spherical symmetry [RS23], to which we return in Section 1.4.)

An additional challenge in smoothly attaching an interior fill-in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ to the exterior-naked singularity regions of Theorem 1 follows from the extension principle of Christodoulou [Chr93, Theorem 5.1], applied to solutions that are at least $C^{2}$ regular. By the extension principle, for any such interior fill-in, the mass aspect ratio $\mu$ cannot satisfy the smallness bounds (1.4) globally on $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ , and there would have to be a region in $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Int}}$ where $\mu\sim 1$ .

### 1.3 The black hole formation threshold and the conjectured Choptuik solution

We recall that the numerical simulations in [Cho93] suggest that the black hole formation threshold consists of asymptotically discretely self-similar naked singularities which asymptote to a universal solution—the conjectured Choptuik solution. Based on these numerics we formulate the following open problem.

#### Open problem.

Does the black hole formation threshold consist of asymptotically discretely self-similar naked singularities? If so, do all such naked singularities asymptote to a universal discretely self-similar solution—the conjectured Choptuik solution—as the singularity is approached?

A natural first problem in addressing the above is constructing a possible candidate for the conjectured Choptuik solution. Indeed, based on the numerical simulations in [Cho93], the work [RT19] gives a computer-assisted construction of a smooth, discretely self-similar, spherically symmetric solution to (1.1), defined however only in an open neighborhood of the causal past of an ingoing cone $C_{0}^{-}$ with singular vertex. If it can be proved that one can smoothly attach an exterior discretely self-similar solution, the construction would correspond to a natural candidate for the conjectured Choptuik solution.11 1 By an easy truncation argument in the far region one could then produce asymptotically flat examples, and this would then show the formation of naked singularities from smooth asymptotically flat initial data.

### 1.4 Comparison with the $k$ -self-similar solutions and the vacuum case

We compare the solutions of Theorem 1 with the naked singularity spacetimes of Christodoulou [Chr94] and the examples of Rodnianski and Shlapentokh-Rothman [RS23, Shl22]. Since we construct only exterior-naked singularity regions in Theorem 1, we restrict our comparison to the exterior regions in [Chr94] and [RS23] and the behavior on the past light cone of the singularity.

As discussed before, the $k$ -self-similar spacetimes constructed in [Chr94] are continuously self-similar solutions of (1.1) and have naked singularities for a certain range of the parameter $k.$ Along the ingoing cone $C_{0}^{-}$ , the $k$ -self-similar solutions satisfy

$$ \phi=kt+O(1),\ \mu=\frac{k^{2}}{1+k^{2}}, $$

where $t\doteq-\log|u|$ denotes the self-similar time. Thus, the singularity is a consequence of the blow-up of the scalar field and the failure of the mass aspect ratio to converge to zero. This is in contrast to the solutions constructed in Theorem 1 for which the scalar field and mass aspect ratio are periodic (see (1.3)) along $C_{0}^{-}$ in terms of the self-similar variable $t$ and the singularity is a consequence of this infinite oscillation.

In the works [RS23, Shl22], the first examples of the dynamical formation of naked singularities for the Einstein vacuum equations were constructed. The solutions have a twisted self-similar symmetry along $C_{0}^{-}$ , which represents a novel continuously self-similar mechanism for singularity formation, see also [Shl23]. The construction of the exterior-naked singularity regions in [RS23] is similar to that in Theorem 1 in many aspects. In both spacetimes the singularity is caused by a self-similar profile on $C_{0}^{-},$ with the infinite twisting of the geometry in [RS23] being replaced by the infinite oscillation in Theorem 1. However, the exterior regions are not assumed to have an exact self-similar symmetry in the future of $C_{0}^{-}$ , and they turn out to be only asymptotically self-similar. For both constructions the strategy is to first prescribe characteristic initial data compatible with the self-similar symmetry on $C_{0}^{-}$ and then prove global existence of the solution. We note that the guideline of [RS23] is the natural approach to construct exterior-naked singularity regions, in the case where the system of equations does not reduce to ODEs as in [Chr94].

In terms of the regularity of the spacetimes, there is a stark contrast between the solutions of Theorem 1 and the examples of [Chr94] and [RS23, Shl22]. In agreement with the numerical heuristics for discretely self-similar spacetimes, the solutions of Theorem 1 are globally smooth, except for $\{u=0\}$ of course. In particular, the solutions are smooth at $C_{0}^{-}.$ On the other hand, for the $k$ -self-similar and twisted self-similar examples of naked singularities, the construction of the exterior region already restricts the regularity of the spacetime to $C_{v}^{1,\gamma}$ for some $\gamma>0$ at $C_{0}^{-}$ , while the solution is smooth away from $C_{0}^{-}$ .

The solutions of Theorem 1 arise from small data by construction. Even though the infinite oscillation of the mass aspect ratio $\mu$ on $C_{0}^{-}$ causes the singularity, we obtain that $\mu$ is everywhere small, which is essential in the proof of global existence. On the other hand, the solutions of [Chr94] do not have any restrictions on the smallness of data, and global existence is obtained by the study of an autonomous ODE system. Finally, the solutions of [RS23] are in a large data regime on $C_{0}^{-}$ . Global existence is achieved since the initial data on $C_{0}^{+}$ decays rapidly away from $C_{0}^{-}$ , but this is done at the cost of the aforementioned limited Hölder regularity along $C_{0}^{-}$ .

### 1.5 The instability of naked singularities

In [Chr99a], Christodoulou showed that all naked singularity solutions to (1.1) are unstable, thereby proving the weak cosmic censorship conjecture for the Einstein-scalar field system in spherical symmetry. The precise formulation of his result required a low regularity class of initial perturbations. The argument crucially relies on rough perturbations that trigger a blue-shift instability along the cone $C_{0}^{-},$ which inevitably leads to the formation of trapped surfaces. Moreover, we note that the continuously self-similar naked singularity solutions in [Chr94] belong to the low regularity class considered, so the genericity assumption in the formulation of weak cosmic censorship in the low regularity class is indeed necessary. In the smooth class, both the question of the formation of naked singularities and the question of their genericity remain open. In view of the recent linear analysis in [Sin24a], the latter appears to be a very subtle and intricate problem.

### 1.6 Outline of the proof of Theorem 1

In the following, we will outline the main ideas used in the proof of Theorem 1. We begin by writing down the system of equations (1.1) in spherical symmetry expressed in double null coordinates which reduces to the wave equations

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{u}\partial_{v}\log\Omega^{2} \displaystyle=-2\partial_{u}\phi\partial_{v}\phi+\frac{\Omega^{2}}{2r^{2}}+\frac{2\partial_{v}r\partial_{u}r}{r^{2}} \displaystyle\partial_{u}(r\partial_{v}r) \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{4}\Omega^{2} \displaystyle r\partial_{u}\partial_{v}\phi \displaystyle=-\partial_{v}\phi\partial_{u}r-\partial_{u}\phi\partial_{v}r $$

and the Raychaudhuri equations

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{u}(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{u}r) \displaystyle=-r\Omega^{-2}(\partial_{u}\phi)^{2} \displaystyle\partial_{v}(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r) \displaystyle=-r\Omega^{-2}(\partial_{v}\phi)^{2}. $$

Moreover, the Hawking mass

$$ m\doteq\frac{r}{2}(1+4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r\partial_{u}r) $$

satisfies

$$ \partial_{v}m=2r^{2}\Omega^{-2}(-\partial_{u}r)(\partial_{v}\phi)^{2}. $$

#### Discretely self-similar characteristic data (Section 2).

We will set up smooth characteristic initial data on the cones $C_{0}^{-}\cup_{p}C_{0}^{+}=\{-1\leq u<0\}\times\{v=0\}\cup\{u=-1\}\times\{v\geq 0\}$ , which intersect at the sphere located at $p=(-1,0)$ . Characteristic data for the system (1.1) consist of prescribing $r,\Omega,\phi$ which satisfy (1.8) on $C_{0}^{-}$ and (1.9) on $C_{0}^{+},$ together with suitable gauge conditions, see Section 2.1.

The starting point in our construction is to consider smooth, discretely self-similar functions $\phi:C_{0}^{-}\times\{0\}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ satisfying

$$ \kappa\Delta=\int_{-1}^{-e^{-\Delta}}(-u^{\prime})\big(\partial_{u}\phi\big)^{2}du^{\prime} $$

for some small constant $0<\kappa\ll 1$ as well as the additional pointwise bounds

$$ \phi(e^{-\Delta}u,0)=\phi(u,0),\ |\phi(u,0)|\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa},\ |\partial_{u}\phi(u,0)|\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa}/|u|. $$

The parameter $\kappa$ in (1.11) can be seen as the analog of $k^{2}$ in the $k$ -self-similar spacetimes in [Chr94].

The lapse function $\Omega^{2}$ is determined by $\phi$ on $C_{0}^{-}$ according to (1.8), and satisfies the scaling relation

$$ \Omega^{2}(e^{-\Delta n}u,0)=e^{-n\Delta\kappa}\Omega^{2}(u,0). $$

We remark that the scaling of $\Omega^{2}$ implies that the underlying vector field which determines the self-similar scaling (1.3) is given by

$$ S=u\partial_{u}+(1-\kappa)v\partial_{v}. $$

Enforcing the discrete self-similarity (1.3) along $C_{0}^{-}$ introduces rigidity conditions on the outgoing data on $C_{0}^{+}$ to first order at $p$ . In particular, from the discrete self-similarity property (1.3), equations (1.6) and (1.7), we obtain that the transverse derivatives $\partial_{v}r$ and $\partial_{v}\phi$ at $p$ are completely determined by the data on $C_{0}^{-}$ .22 2 We are only concerned with discrete self-similarity to first order at $C_{0}^{-}$ , but higher order versions of (1.3) would lead to higher order rigidity for the transverse derivatives at $p$ . An essential aspect of our discretely self-similar construction is that the rigidity condition give us the smallness properties

$$ \big|\partial_{v}\phi(p)\big|\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa},\quad\mu(p)\lesssim\kappa. $$

This is in contrast with the $k$ -self-similar spacetimes in [Chr94], where the outgoing data $\partial_{v}\phi(p)$ is of size $1/k,$ which is never small in the range of the parameter $k$ . At higher order on $C_{0}^{+}$ , we have the freedom to prescribe $\phi$ smoothly33 3 Our proof also works if $\phi$ is at least $C^{1,\gamma}_{v}\big([0,\infty)\big)$ regular, where $\gamma=2\kappa/(1-\kappa).$ This is the same regularity exponent as in [RS23]., provided that certain smallness properties and asymptotically flat conditions hold.

#### Construction of the exterior region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ (Section 3).

Once we set up the characteristic initial data, we prove that it leads to a global solution in the exterior region $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ . Our argument for global existence follows the strategy of [RS23] and relies only on the smallness of the initial data and bounds compatible with self-similarity, without requiring the solution to be exactly self-similar. In our proof, we decompose the spacetime into certain regions, and use bootstrap arguments to show suitable pointwise estimates for the solution in each region. In the last step, these bounds are then used to prove that $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ is incomplete, so the spacetime constructed represents indeed an exterior-naked singularity region.

We consider a small constant $\underline{v}$ such that $0<\kappa\ll\underline{v}\ll 1$ , and the regions depicted in Fig. 4

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{I} \displaystyle=\bigg\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}:v\in[0,\underline{v}^{1-\kappa}],\ \frac{v}{|u|^{1-\kappa}}\leq\underline{v}^{1-\kappa}\bigg\} \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{II} \displaystyle=\bigg\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}:v\in[0,\underline{v}^{-1+\kappa}],\ \underline{v}^{1-\kappa}\leq\frac{v}{|u|^{1-\kappa}}\leq\underline{v}^{-1+\kappa}\bigg\} \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{III} \displaystyle=\bigg\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}:v\in[0,1],\ \frac{v}{|u|^{1-\kappa}}\geq\underline{v}^{-1+\kappa}\bigg\} \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{IV} \displaystyle=\bigg\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}:v\in[1,\infty),\ \frac{v}{|u|^{1-\kappa}}\geq\underline{v}^{-1+\kappa}\bigg\}. $$

*Figure 4: The decomposition of $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{Ext}}$ into the regions $\mathcal{R}_{I}$ – $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$*

In region $\mathcal{R}_{I}$ , we propagate the pointwise bounds on the solution on the ingoing cone $C_{0}^{-},$ using the smallness of $\underline{v}.$ The estimates are straightforward for the quantities satisfying transport equations in the $\partial_{v}$ direction, such as $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r,\ \partial_{u}\phi,\ \partial_{u}r,$ and $\partial_{u}\log\Omega^{2}.$ On the other hand, in order to bound $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi$ we integrate the $\partial_{u}$ equation satisfied by $\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi(u,v)-\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}\phi(u,0).$

In regions $\mathcal{R}_{II}$ , $\mathcal{R}_{III}$ , and $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$ , we consider the regular change of coordinates $V=v^{\frac{1}{1-\kappa}}$ motivated by the scaling vector field $S$ in (1.14), and we denote the new lapse function by $\bar{\Omega}.$ We prove estimates in region $\mathcal{R}_{II}$ by conjugating the equations with $\exp\big(D\cdot V/u\big)$ , for some large constant $D.$ These estimates are analogous to applying a local-in-time energy estimate in the “time” variable $V/u$ , with data on the spacelike hypersurface $\big\{V=-\underline{v}u\big\}.$

In region $\mathcal{R}_{III}$ we prove pointwise estimates using the smallness of $\underline{v}$ for the quantities satisfying transport equations in the $\partial_{u}$ direction, such as $\bar{\Omega}^{-2}\partial_{u}r,\ \partial_{V}\phi,\ \partial_{V}r,$ and $\partial_{V}\log\bar{\Omega}^{2}.$ However, in order to bound $\partial_{u}\phi,$ we conjugate the equation for $r\partial_{u}\phi$ by $|u|^{p}/V^{p},$ for some small constant $p>0.$ In particular, we obtain that $\phi\in C_{u}^{1-p}$ , but we cannot conclude that $\partial_{u}\phi$ and $\bar{\Omega}$ extend continuously to $\{u=0\}.$ Nevertheless, the quantitative bounds obtained will suffice for our purposes.

We prove estimates in region $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$ using the a priori bound on the Hawking mass obtained from the initial data bound and the monotonicity properties. It is convenient to split region $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$ into two sub-regions: $\mathcal{R}_{IV}\cap\{v\leq\underline{v}^{-1+\kappa}\}$ with similar pointwise bounds to those of region $\mathcal{R}_{III}$ , and $[-1,0)\times[\underline{v}^{-1+\kappa},\infty)$ with bounds specific to an asymptotically flat region. Finally, we then use the estimates in region $\mathcal{R}_{IV}$ to show that $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ is incomplete.
