## 1 Introduction

One of the main open problems in general relativity is the weak cosmic censorship conjecture, proposed by Penrose in [41] for general Einstein-matter systems. The conjecture states that, for generic initial data, so-called "naked singularities" do not form. That is to say, singularities are generically hidden inside black holes and invisible to far away observers who exist for all time (more formally, null infinity $\mathcal{I}$ is future complete [27, 15]). The conjecture is motivated by the fact that the future incompleteness of $\mathcal{I}$ would threaten the predictability of general relativity as a physical theory.

While the weak cosmic censorship conjecture is completely open in its full generality, in the remarkable work [16], Christodoulou proved a suitable formulation of the conjecture for the model problem of the spherically symmetric Einstein-scalar field system in $3+1$ dimensions. The argument of [16] relies on a novel blueshift effect to show that, while explicit naked singularity spacetimes can be constructed [14, 10], all naked singularities are in fact unstable to black hole formation and the set of naked singularity spacetimes is indeed non-generic in a suitable sense. However, the instability mechanism in [16] required working in a topology defined by a low-regularity class of solutions. Thus, the question of weak cosmic censorship in a smoother topology remains open even in this setting. We discuss the work [16] in detail in Section 1.4.1.

In the present work, we initiate the mathematical study of gravitational collapse in $2+1$ dimensions for the circularly symmetric Einstein-scalar field system in the presence of a negative cosmological constant $\Lambda<0$ , and we prove a version of the weak cosmic censorship conjecture for this system. We note that the natural problem in this setting is solving an initial-boundary value problem with reflective boundary conditions at null infinity $\mathcal{I}$ (which is now in fact timelike). This model was first studied in the numerical relativity literature by Pretorius and Choptuik [42], and we will discuss its motivation in detail in Section 1.1. We also discuss the existence of examples of naked singularities for this model in Section 1.4.2. To prove weak cosmic censorship, we use the blueshift effect as the main instability mechanism, similarly to [16]. A key new feature in our setting is the presence of a mass gap, which states that no singularities form in the domain of dependence of a disk bounded by a circle with Hawking mass strictly less than 1. (In particular, this allows us to confirm a conjecture of [7]). Moreover, the different scaling in the present model allows us to activate the blueshift instability in the class of $C^{k}$ solutions, for any $k\geq 2$ . Thus, unlike [16], our formulation of weak cosmic censorship in the present setting does not rely on low-regularity perturbations and holds in a topology of arbitrary smoothness.

### 1.1 The Einstein-scalar field system in $2+1$ dimensions with $\Lambda<0$

We consider the Einstein-scalar field system of equations with a negative cosmological constant $\Lambda<0$ :

$$ \begin{cases}Ric_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}Rg_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=\nabla_{\mu}\phi\nabla_{\nu}\phi-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}|\nabla\phi|^{2},\\
\square_{g}\phi=0.\end{cases} $$

In $2+1$ dimensions, the system (1.1) has been studied extensively in the physics and numerical relativity literature [6, 9, 42, 26, 25, 33]. This represents perhaps the most elementary model for gravitational collapse in $2+1$ dimensions which allows for the dynamical formation of singularities [42, 33].

The simplest solution of (1.1) is given by Anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetime $\big(\mathbb{R}^{3},g_{AdS},\phi_{AdS}\big):$

$$ g_{AdS}=-\big(1+|\Lambda|r^{2}\big)dt^{2}+\big(1+|\Lambda|r^{2}\big)^{-1}dr^{2}+r^{2}d\sigma_{1}^{2},\ \phi_{AdS}=0, $$

where $d\sigma_{1}^{2}$ is the standard metric on $S^{1}.$ We note that AdS spacetime is circularly symmetric, does not contain any singularities, and is geodesically complete. Moreover, we can attach an asymptotic boundary at infinity, called null infinity $\mathcal{I}$ , which is timelike and complete.

In the present work, we initiate the rigorous mathematical study of the system (1.1). We consider the class of circularly symmetric solutions, which take the following form with respect to global double null coordinates $(u,v):$

$$ g(u,v)=-\Omega^{2}(u,v)dudv+r^{2}(u,v)d\sigma_{1}^{2},\ \phi=\phi(u,v). $$

The solutions of (1.1) studied in this paper will be the unique maximal developments of $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data sets, obtained by solving (1.1) as an initial-boundary value problem with reflective boundary conditions at null infinity $\mathcal{I}$ . Moreover, we only consider solutions arising in gravitational collapse, i.e. solutions with a regular center $\Gamma=\{r=0\}.$ In particular, AdS spacetime itself is contained in this class of solutions. We refer the reader to Section 2 for a detailed introduction to the circularly symmetric Einstein-scalar field system in $2+1$ dimensions.

An essential role in the study of (1.1) is played by the Bañados–Teitelboim–Zanelli (BTZ) spacetimes [6]. These are a $1$ -parameter family of circularly symmetric static solutions11 1 We change the notation convention from the physics literature and translate the mass parameter by 1. For us, AdS spacetime is given by $M=0,$ whereas in [6] AdS spacetime is given by $M=-1$ .,22 2 More generally, [6] constructs a $2$ -parameter family of axially symmetric stationary solutions $g_{M,J}$ . The rotating BTZ solutions with $J\neq 0$ are not circularly symmetric and they do not play a role for the rest of the paper. of (1.1) defined for $M\geq 0$ with respect to static coordinates $(t,r):$

$$ g_{M}=-\Big(1-M+|\Lambda|r^{2}\Big)dt^{2}+\Big(1-M+|\Lambda|r^{2}\Big)^{-1}dr^{2}+r^{2}d\sigma_{1}^{2},\ \phi_{M}=0. $$

We briefly explain some properties of the BTZ solutions and we refer the reader to the survey [9]. For $M=0,$ the solution coincides with AdS spacetime. In the case $M\in(0,1)$ the metric (1.3) has a conical singularity at $r=0,$ while for $M=1$ the metric (1.3) has a cusp singularity at $r=0$ . Finally, for $M>1,$ the spacetime has no center but it can be extended to a two-ended black hole spacetime. In view of our restriction in the previous paragraph to the class of spacetimes arising in gravitational collapse, the only member of the BTZ family that lies in our class of solutions is AdS spacetime. Nonetheless, the entire BTZ family will play an important role in the asymptotic behavior of the solutions in our class at $\mathcal{I}.$

### 1.2 The main result

In order to state the main result in detail, we consider the moduli space $\mathfrak{M}$ of $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data posed on an outgoing null cone $C_{0}^{+}$ which extends from the center $\Gamma$ to null infinity $\mathcal{I}$ . The moduli space $\mathfrak{M}$ is endowed with the structure of a metric space (see already Definition 2.9). To each element $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}$ , we associate the unique (up to isometry) maximal development of the initial data $\mathfrak{D}.$

We briefly define certain subsets of the moduli space $\mathfrak{M}$ , and we refer the reader to Section 2.4 for the precise definitions. These subsets are defined based on the global properties of the maximal development of the initial data. First, we denote by $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}\subset\mathfrak{M}$ the set of initial data that evolve to black hole spacetimes, i.e. spacetimes such that $J^{-}(\mathcal{I})$ has a nontrivial complement. We classify black hole spacetimes depending on the nature of the singularity inside the black hole region. We denote by $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}\subset\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}$ the set of initial data that evolve to black hole spacetimes with a spacelike-only singularity, as depicted in Figure 1a). Then, we denote by $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{loc.naked}}\subset\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}$ the set of initial data that evolve to black hole spacetimes with the property that their Penrose diagram is that in Figure 1b) (the superscript stands for locally naked, which we define below). We prove in Section 2 that we have the disjoint union:

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}=\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{loc.naked}}. $$

Next, we denote by $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\subset\mathfrak{M}$ the set of initial data that evolve to non-collapsing spacetimes, defined by the property that their Penrose diagram is that in Figure 1c) (for example AdS spacetime). Furthermore, we denote by $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}\subset\mathfrak{M}$ the set of initial data that evolve to naked singularity spacetimes, defined33 3 One can show that any solution with future incomplete $\mathcal{I}$ is the development of initial data in $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}.$ We note that in our definition, $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}$ will also include initial data that evolve to spacetimes with complete $\mathcal{I}$ , see Remark 2.3. by the property that their Penrose diagram is that in Figure 1d). Finally, we denote by $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}\subset\mathfrak{M}$ the set of initial data that evolve to locally naked singularity spacetimes, defined by the property that their causal boundary contains a null component $\mathcal{B}_{0}$ arising out of the first singularity at the center $b_{\Gamma}$ . Equivalently, locally naked singularities do not contain trapped surfaces in a neighborhood of $b_{\Gamma}$ . We prove in Section 2 that we have the disjoint union:

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}=\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{loc.naked}}. $$

The classification of the general structure of the causal boundary of spacetimes leads to a decomposition of the moduli space $\mathfrak{M}$ . Adapting the work of [36, 30] to the $(2+1)$ -dimensional setting, we prove in Section 2 that the moduli space $\mathfrak{M}$ can be written as the disjoint union:

$$ \mathfrak{M}=\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{loc.naked}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}. $$

For a discussion of the non-emptiness of the various subsets of $\mathfrak{M},$ see Section 2.4.

Using these definitions, we state the main result of our paper:

#### Theorem 1.1 (Weak cosmic censorship for circularly symmetric solutions of (1.1)).

For any $k\geq 2$ , the maximal development of generic $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data does not contain naked singularities. More precisely, we have that:

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{generic}}:=\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}\sqcup\mathrm{int}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\big)\text{ is open and dense in }\mathfrak{M}, $$

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}\subset\mathrm{cl}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}\big)\backslash\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}\subset\mathfrak{M}\backslash\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{generic}}, $$

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}\subset\mathrm{cl}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}\big)\backslash\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}. $$

In particular, naked singularity spacetimes are non-generic and are unstable to black hole formation. Additionally, locally naked singularities are unstable to the formation of spacelike-only singularities.

#### Remark 1.1.

For reasons to be explained later, see already Section 1.4.1, we choose a more elementary notion of genericity than [16]. Thus, we prove that $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}$ is contained in the complement of an open and dense subset of $\mathfrak{M}$ , rather than proving that $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}$ has positive codimension in $\mathfrak{M}$ .

### 1.3 Idea of the proof

We briefly outline the main ideas of the proof, then we flesh out our discussion with more details in Sections 1.3.1-1.3.5. The overall strategy of the proof goes back to the work of Christodoulou [16]. In the present section we explain our argument, then we describe in detail in Section 1.4.1 the similarities and differences to [16]. We refer the reader to Section 2 for the precise notation and definitions used in this section.

The main step in the proof of Theorem 1.1 is establishing (1.9). To show that locally naked singularities are unstable to the formation of spacelike-only singularities, it suffices to prove that locally naked singularities can be perturbed to form trapped surfaces arbitrarily close to $b_{\Gamma}$ .

The proof relies on two fundamental results about circularly symmetric solutions of (1.1). Firstly, in Section 1.3.1 we state Theorem 1.2, which establishes the presence of a mass gap, showing that no singularities form in the domain of dependence of a disk bounded by a circle with Hawking mass strictly less than 1. We also state some notable consequences of Theorem 1.2. Secondly, in Section 1.3.2 we state Theorem 1.3, which provides a quantitative criterion for the formation of trapped surfaces.

We explain in Section 1.3.3 how Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 are used to prove a quantitative description of locally naked singularity spacetimes. In particular, we note that any first singularity at the center must have unbounded blueshift. In Section 1.3.4, we explain why locally naked singularities can be perturbed to form trapped surfaces arbitrarily close to $b_{\Gamma}$ . The idea is to consider perturbations that leave the causal past of $b_{\Gamma}$ unchanged and activate the blueshift instability. The blueshift effect will then amplify the initial data perturbation and allow us to apply Theorem 1.3 to conclude the existence of trapped surfaces arbitrarily close to $b_{\Gamma}$ . Finally, we explain in Section 1.3.5 how to complete the proof of Theorem 1.1.

#### 1.3.1 The mass gap

The first essential ingredient of our proof is the presence of a mass gap for circularly symmetric solutions of (1.1). We define44 4 Similarly to the BTZ family (1.3), we change the notation convention from the physics literature and translate the Hawking mass by 1. the Hawking mass by:

$$ m=-g(\nabla r,\nabla r)-\Lambda r^{2}+1. $$

We note that the Hawking mass is non-negative for solutions arising in gravitational collapse. Moreover, a solution is exactly AdS spacetime in the domain of dependence of a disk bounded by a circle if and only if the Hawking mass of the circle is zero.

For asymptotically AdS characteristic data $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M},$ we define the Bondi mass $M=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}m|_{C_{0}^{+}}(r).$ We note that the reflective boundary conditions at $\mathcal{I}$ imply that $m|_{\mathcal{I}}$ is constant, so $M=m|_{\mathcal{I}}.$

The numerical relativity work [7] conjectures that initial data must have Bondi mass at least 1 to form singularities in evolution, and provides some evidence in the case of very small Bondi mass. In Section 3, we prove the following local version of this conjecture in terms of the Hawking mass:

#### Theorem 1.2.

For any $k\geq 2$ , let $\big(\mathcal{M},g,\phi\big)$ be the maximal globally hyperbolic development of $C^{k}$ characteristic data on the outgoing null cone $C_{0}^{+}=\{u=u_{0},\ v_{\Gamma}\leq v\leq\tilde{v}\}$ with $r(u_{0},v_{\Gamma})=0,\ r(u_{0},\tilde{v})<\infty.$ If $m(u_{0},v_{0})=1-\delta<1$ for some $v_{\Gamma}<v_{0}<\tilde{v},$ then $\big(\mathcal{M},g,\phi\big)$ is regular in the domain of dependence of $C_{0}^{+}\cap\{v\leq v_{0}\}.$

We briefly explain the idea of the proof of Theorem 1.2. We note that in Section 3 it is convenient to work in Bondi coordinates $(u,r).$ First, we show that the bound on $m$ implies quantitative control of the geometry of the spacetime. We then prove a non-concentration estimate for the scalar field, which in particular implies that the scalar field cannot blow up at a faster than self-similar rate, so $r\partial_{r}\phi$ is bounded. We further improve this estimate by a small power of $r,$ showing in particular that $r^{1-\rho}\partial_{r}\phi$ is bounded, where $\rho>0$ is sufficiently small. The preliminary bounds for the geometry of the spacetime and the scalar field allow us to propagate from initial data boundedness for the local well-posedness norm, concluding that no singularities form in evolution.

The main use of Theorem 1.2 for the purposes of this paper is the following description of first singularities at the center:

#### Corollary 1.1.

Let $b_{\Gamma}=(u_{*},v_{*})$ be a first singularity at the center $\Gamma.$ Then $m(u,v_{*})\rightarrow 1^{+}$ as $u\rightarrow u_{*}^{-}.$

As a corollary of Theorem 1.2, we also obtain the mass gap result in terms of the Bondi mass, thus proving the conjecture of [7]:

#### Corollary 1.2.

Solutions with Bondi mass less than 1 do not form singularities. More precisely, if $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}$ has $M<1,$ then $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathrm{int}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\big).$ In particular, small perturbations of AdS spacetime are non-collapsing.

This result marks a sharp contrast between AdS spacetime in $2+1$ dimensions and AdS spacetime in $3+1$ dimensions, since the latter is unstable to black hole formation [21, 8, 39, 40]. In view of the numerical study of [7], it is expected that AdS spacetime in $2+1$ dimensions is dynamically unstable and perturbations of it exhibit weak turbulence. Finally, we refer the reader to [21], which conjectures that the Eguchi-Hanson solitons in $4+1$ dimensions are unstable to naked singularity formation.

#### 1.3.2 Formation of trapped surfaces criterion

The second essential ingredient in our argument is a quantitative criterion for trapped surface formation, inspired by the work of Christodoulou [12]. Intuitively, this result states that if the mass within an annular region bounded by two circles on the outgoing null cone $C_{0}^{+}$ is large compared to the size of the region, then a trapped surface will form in evolution. We prove the following result in Section 4:

#### Theorem 1.3.

For any $k\geq 2$ , let $\big(\mathcal{M},g,\phi\big)$ be the maximal globally hyperbolic development of $C^{k}$ characteristic data on the outgoing null cone $C_{0}^{+}=\{u=u_{0},\ v_{\Gamma}\leq v\leq\tilde{v}\}$ with $r(u_{0},v_{\Gamma})=0,\ r(u_{0},\tilde{v})<\infty,$ and $\partial_{v}r(u_{0},v)>0$ for $v\in[v_{\Gamma},\tilde{v}].$ Assume that there exists an ingoing cone $C_{1}=\{u_{0}\leq u<0,\ v=v_{1}\}$ satisfying $r(u,v_{1})\rightarrow 0$ as $u\rightarrow 0^{-}$ and $m(u,v_{1})\geq 1$ for all $u\in[u_{0},0)$ . We consider any ingoing cone $C_{2}=\{u\geq u_{0},\ v=v_{2}\}$ such that $v_{1}<v_{2}<\tilde{v},$ and we denote:

$$ \delta_{0}=\frac{r(u_{0},v_{2})}{r(u_{0},v_{1})}-1,\ \eta_{0}=\frac{m(u_{0},v_{2})-m(u_{0},v_{1})}{|\Lambda|r^{2}(u_{0},v_{2})}. $$

If $\delta_{0}>0$ is small enough and $\eta_{0}>\delta_{0}$ , then a marginally trapped surface $(u_{\mathcal{A}},v_{2})$ forms on $C_{2}$ with:

$$ r(u_{\mathcal{A}},v_{2})\geq\frac{5\delta_{0}/4}{1+\delta_{0}}r(u_{0},v_{2}). $$

To prove Theorem 1.3, we adapt the proof of [12] to the $(2+1)$ -dimensional setting. The main idea is to use the monotonicity properties of the system (1.1) in circular symmetry and derive a differential inequality for the quantity $\eta(u,v_{2})=|\Lambda|^{-1}r^{-2}(u,v_{2})\cdot\big(m(u,v_{2})-m(u,v_{1})\big).$

#### Remark 1.2.

In analogy with [12], one might naively expect on dimensional grounds that $\eta_{0}$ should be defined as $m(u_{0},v_{2})-m(u_{0},v_{1}).$ However, since the cosmological constant $\Lambda$ scales like inverse length squared, the quantity $|\Lambda|r^{2}$ is dimensionless. Thus, the definition of $\eta_{0}$ in (1.11) is dimensionally consistent.

#### 1.3.3 Locally naked singularity spacetimes

As a foundation for the instability argument, in Section 5 we establish a detailed description of locally naked singularity spacetimes in a suitable neighborhood of $b_{\Gamma}.$

We introduce the set-up of Section 5, which will be used in the present section and in Section 1.3.4. We consider $\big(\mathcal{M},g,\phi\big)$ to be the maximal globally hyperbolic development of a $C^{k}$ characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}},$ posed on the outgoing null cone $C_{0}^{+}.$ We assume that the ingoing null cone $C_{0}^{-}$ passing through $b_{\Gamma}$ intersects $C_{0}^{+}$ , and we choose double null coordinates $(u,v)$ such that:

$$ b_{\Gamma}=(0,0),\ C_{0}^{-}=\big\{v=0,\ 2r=-u\big\},\ C_{0}^{+}=\big\{u=u_{0},\ 2r=v-u_{0}\big\}. $$

We define the renormalized lapse and renormalized outgoing derivative of the scalar field by:

$$ \gamma=\frac{\Omega^{2}}{\partial_{v}r},\ \theta=\sqrt{r}\frac{\partial_{v}\phi}{\partial_{v}r}. $$

The quantity $\theta$ satisfies the following propagation equation:

$$ \partial_{u}\theta=-\frac{\Lambda}{2}r\gamma\theta-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{r}}\partial_{u}\phi. $$

We define the blueshift as the integrating factor for (1.13):

$$ \mathbf{b}(u,v)=\int_{u_{0}}^{u}\frac{|\Lambda|}{2}r\gamma(u^{\prime},v)du^{\prime},\ \mathbf{b}(u)=\mathbf{b}(u,0). $$

The main implication of the mass gap property in Theorem 1.2 is that first singularities at the center have infinite blueshift. More precisely, in Proposition 5.1 we show that $\mathbf{b}$ is unbounded on $C_{0}^{-}$ and satisfies the following lower bound for any $u\in[u_{0},0):$

$$ \mathbf{b}(u)\geq 2\log\frac{u_{0}}{u}. $$

*Figure 2: Schematic representation of the region $\mathcal{P}\subset\mathcal{M}$ .*

In Proposition 5.2 we prove quantitative estimates for the solution in a suitable region $\mathcal{P},$ represented schematically in Figure 2, whose definition depends on the strength of the blueshift, as made precise in Section 5. The remarkable aspect is that the absence of trapped surfaces in a neighborhood of $b_{\Gamma}$ implies by the contrapositive of Theorem 1.3 bounds for the energy of the scalar field. More precisely, for any $(u,v)\in\mathcal{P}:$

$$ \int_{0}^{v}\theta^{2}(u,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}\lesssim v|u|\gamma(u,0). $$

Additionally, in the region $\mathcal{P}$ we also prove that $\gamma(u,v)\sim\gamma(u,0),\ e^{\mathbf{b}(u,v)}\sim e^{\mathbf{b}(u)},\ \partial_{v}r(u,v)\sim e^{-\mathbf{b}(u)}$ .

#### 1.3.4 The blueshift instability

In Section 6, we prove that locally naked singularities can be perturbed to form trapped surfaces arbitrarily close to $b_{\Gamma}.$ We explain the main steps of the argument and highlight the key role of the blueshift instability.

We consider perturbations of the initial data on $C_{0}^{+}$ , which are supported on $\{u=u_{0},\ v\geq 0\},$ so they leave the causal past of $b_{\Gamma}$ unchanged. By domain of dependence, it suffices to restrict to $v\leq v_{0}^{\prime},$ for some $v_{0}^{\prime}>0$ sufficiently small. For any integer $n>k+1$ and any $\lambda\neq 0,$ we define the characteristic data $r_{\lambda}=r,\ \phi_{\lambda}=\phi$ on $\{u=u_{0},\ v\in[u_{0},0]\},$ and $r_{\lambda}=r,\ \theta_{\lambda}=\theta+\lambda v^{n}$ on $\{u=u_{0},\ v\in[0,v_{0}^{\prime}]\},$ which determine a $C^{k}$ characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}.$ We denote by $\big(\mathcal{M}_{\lambda},g_{\lambda},\phi_{\lambda}\big)$ the maximal development of $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}.$

In Proposition 6.1, we prove that $\big(\mathcal{M}_{\lambda},g_{\lambda}\big)$ contains a sequence of trapped surfaces converging to $b_{\Gamma}.$ The first step consists of establishing existence and quantitative estimates in a suitable region $\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}\subset\mathcal{P},$ represented schematically in Figure 3, which depends on $\lambda,\ n,$ and the strength of the blueshift on $C_{0}^{-}.$ In the region $\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}$ , we show that $\gamma_{\lambda}(u,v)\sim\gamma(u,0),\ e^{\mathbf{b}_{\lambda}(u,v)}\sim e^{\mathbf{b}(u)},$ and $\partial_{v}r_{\lambda}(u,v)\sim e^{-\mathbf{b}(u)}$ . The main role of the blueshift instability is to amplify the initial data perturbation. To illustrate this, we use (1.13) for $\theta_{\lambda}$ and $\theta$ to derive the equation:

$$ \partial_{u}\big(\theta_{\lambda}-\theta)=-\frac{\Lambda}{2}r_{\lambda}\gamma_{\lambda}\big(\theta_{\lambda}-\theta)+Err, $$

where the term $Err$ is defined exactly in Section 6.1.3. The main contribution in $\theta_{\lambda}-\theta$ comes from the integrating factor (i.e. the blueshift) acting on the initial data perturbation $\theta_{\lambda}(u_{0},v)-\theta(u_{0},v)=\lambda v^{n}$ , while the contribution of the term $Err$ is proved to be of lower order. This behavior is captured by the following key estimate in Section 6.1:

$$ \int_{0}^{v}\Big|\big(\theta_{\lambda}-\theta\big)(u,v^{\prime})-e^{\mathbf{b}_{\lambda}(u,v^{\prime})}\big(\theta_{\lambda}-\theta\big)(u_{0},v^{\prime})\Big|^{2}dv^{\prime}\leq\lambda^{2}v^{2n+\frac{4}{3}}e^{2\mathbf{b}(u)}\ll\lambda^{2}v^{2n+1}e^{2\mathbf{b}(u)}. $$

*Figure 3: Schematic representation of the region $\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}\subset\mathcal{M}_{\lambda}$ , the curve $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda},$ and $S_{\lambda}\in\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}.$*

The second step in the proof of Proposition 6.1 consists of showing that the blueshift instability causes the amplification of $\theta_{\lambda}$ sufficiently close to $b_{\Gamma},$ and allows us to apply Theorem 1.3 to obtain a sequence of trapped surfaces converging to $b_{\Gamma}.$ In Section 6.2, we define a suitable curve $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda},$ parametrized by $\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)$ for $u\in[u_{0},0),$ which converges to $b_{\Gamma}$ and is contained in the region $\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}$ sufficiently close to $b_{\Gamma}$ , as illustrated schematically in Figure 3. The curve $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}$ is chosen such that (1.16) and (1.18) imply the following lower bound for all $|u|$ sufficiently small:

$$ \int_{0}^{v_{\sharp}(u)}\big|\theta_{\lambda}(u,v^{\prime})\big|^{2}dv^{\prime}\gtrsim\lambda^{2}\big[v_{\sharp}(u)\big]^{2n+1}e^{2\mathbf{b}(u)}. $$

We consider any $S_{\lambda}=\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)\in\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}$ sufficiently close to $b_{\Gamma},$ as in Figure 3. In Section 6.2, we show that the lower bound (1.19) implies:

$$ \eta_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)=\frac{m_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)-m_{\lambda}(u,0)}{|\Lambda|r_{\lambda}^{2}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)}>\delta_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)=\frac{r_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)}{r_{\lambda}(u,0)}-1. $$

Thus, (1.20) allows us to apply Theorem 1.3 and show that the future ingoing null cone passing through $S_{\lambda}$ contains a trapped surface. As a result, we conclude that the spacetime $\big(\mathcal{M}_{\lambda},g_{\lambda}\big)$ contains a sequence of trapped surfaces converging to $b_{\Gamma}$ .

#### 1.3.5 The proof of Theorem 1.1

We explain briefly how we complete the proof of (1.9) and Theorem 1.1 in Section 7. In order to prove (1.9), we show that any $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}$ can be perturbed to some $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}.$ We notice that it is not always the case that for the maximal development of $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}$ we have $C_{0}^{-}\cap C_{0}^{+}\neq\emptyset,$ as can be seen for example in Figure 1b) and 1d). However, we can reduce the proof to the case $C_{0}^{-}\cap C_{0}^{+}\neq\emptyset$ by Cauchy stability, so we can use the results outlined in Sections 1.3.3-1.3.4. We note that the argument described in Section 1.3.4 constructs $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}$ only in a compact subset of $C_{0}^{+}.$ For $\lambda$ sufficiently small, we use the results in Appendix A to extend $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}$ to an asymptotically AdS characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ as a perturbation of $\mathfrak{D}$ . We note this is a nontrivial step that is necessary due to the presence of a timelike asymptotic boundary at $\mathcal{I}.$ The results outlined in Section 1.3.4 show that the maximal development of $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}$ contains trapped surfaces arbitrarily close to $b_{\Gamma}$ , which implies that $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}},$ completing the proof of (1.9). Having established (1.9), the remaining statements in Theorem 1.1 follow from (1.6), the fact that $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}\subset\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}$ , and the fact that $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}$ is open.

### 1.4 Previous results

We present some previous results relevant for the weak cosmic censorship conjecture. In Section 1.4.1, we discuss [16] in detail and mention additional works regarding the instability of naked singularities. In Section 1.4.2, we discuss some previous results on the construction of examples of naked singularity spacetimes. We refer the reader to the recent survey [45] for an extended literature review.

#### 1.4.1 Instability of naked singularities

In the remarkable work [16], Christodoulou proved a version of the weak cosmic censorship conjecture for the spherically symmetric Einstein-scalar field system in $3+1$ dimensions. We state the main result of [16] following the formulations in [16, 15, 45]:

#### Theorem 1.4 ([16]).

We parametrize initial data for the $(3+1)$ -dimensional spherically symmetric Einstein-scalar field system of equations by a choice of $\vartheta=r\partial_{v}\phi$ along an initial outgoing null cone $C_{0}^{+},$ normalized such that $\partial_{v}r=1/2.$ We consider as the space of initial data the space $AC$ of all absolutely continuous functions $\vartheta$ of finite total variation on the half-line. We denote by $\mathcal{E}\subset AC$ the subset consisting of initial data whose maximal development is a locally naked singularity spacetime. Then $\mathcal{E}$ has positive codimension in $AC.$

The present paper is inspired by the strategy of [16], so we explain in more detail the common features and key differences of the two works. We begin with some comments regarding the differences in the statements of Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.4. Firstly, the space of initial data in Theorem 1.4 has a low-regularity topology, namely $AC$ , which is necessary in order to activate the blueshift instability. On the other hand, Theorem 1.1 holds in a topology of arbitrary smoothness, as the different scaling in our setting and the quantitative lower bound (1.15) allow us to use the blueshift instability in the class of $C^{k}$ solutions, for any $k\geq 2.$ Secondly, Theorem 1.4 uses a stronger notion of genericity than Theorem 1.1, showing that $\mathcal{E}$ has positive codimension in $AC.$ The argument outlined in Section 1.3.4 is consistent with this stronger notion of genericity, but the need to extend the initial data perturbations globally and satisfy the boundary conditions at $\mathcal{I}$ forces us to settle for the notion of genericity in Theorem 1.1. For similar reasons, Theorem 1.1 only proves the non-genericity of naked singularities, rather than locally naked singularities.

We make some further comments regarding the proofs of Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.4. Firstly, we follow the strategy of [16] and use the formation of trapped surfaces criterion in two different ways: we use Theorem 1.3 directly in Section 6, but we also use the contrapositive of Theorem 1.3 in Section 5 to get a priori control of the scalar field for any locally naked singularity spacetime. Secondly, both Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.4 rely on the fundamental fact that locally naked singularity spacetimes have unbounded blueshift. In our case, this follows as a consequence of the presence of a mass gap in Theorem 1.2, as explained in Section 1.3.3. (Unfortunately, there is no published account of this part of the proof in the case of Theorem 1.4. Strictly speaking, from the published versions in [16, 15], one can only infer that Theorem 1.4 applies for $\mathcal{E}\subset AC$ consisting of initial data whose maximal development is a locally naked singularity spacetime and has unbounded blueshift along the past lightcone of the singularity $b_{\Gamma}$ , see also [45]). Thirdly, we follow the idea of [16] and use the blueshift effect to prove the instability of locally naked singularities. We explain how the two approaches are somewhat different. [16] derives refined necessary conditions for a spacetime to be a locally naked singularity, in the form of compatibility conditions between the initial data on $C_{0}^{+}$ and the solution on $C_{0}^{-},$ which are then violated by suitable perturbations of the initial data. On the other hand, we start with the perturbation in Section 1.3.4 and we carry out most of the argument at the level of the perturbed spacetime, providing a detailed description of how the solution enters the regime where Theorem 1.3 applies.

We mention some further results regarding the instability of naked singularities for the Einstein-scalar field system in $3+1$ dimensions. The work [38] revisits the proof of [16], while [37] considers non-spherically symmetric perturbations of spherically symmetric naked singularity spacetimes. Finally, in the recent work [1], An uses anisotropic perturbations to construct finitely many unstable directions for the examples of [14].

#### 1.4.2 Previous examples of naked singularities and upcoming work

Constructing examples of naked singularities plays a fundamental role in understanding their general properties and their instability. Moreover, the existence of such examples justifies the need to include genericity conditions in any formulation of the weak cosmic censorship conjecture. We outline some of the previous results on the construction of examples of naked singularities, and we refer the reader to [45, 18] for further discussion. We also discuss the upcoming work [19].

For the spherically symmetric Einstein-scalar field system in $3+1$ dimensions, [14] constructed examples of naked singularities, which were recently revisited55 5 The recent works [47, 49, 46] study the stability properties of the examples of [14]. In particular, Singh and Zheng show that the naked singularity spacetimes of [14] are stable to smooth perturbations. We refer the reader to [49] for the sharp result established. by [48] and [47, 49, 46]. Notably, the examples of [14] arise from low regularity initial data (more precisely, in the notation of Theorem 1.4, $\vartheta$ is only Hölder continuous). However, based on numerical relativity works on critical collapse [10, 28], it is conjectured that there exist naked singularities arising from smooth data on $\partial\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}\cap\partial\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}},$ which represents the moduli space threshold between black hole formation and non-collapse. Outside of spherical symmetry, the groundbreaking work [43, 44] constructed examples of naked singularities for the Einstein vacuum equations in $3+1$ dimensions, which also arise from low regularity initial data.

In the case of certain matter models, there are more elementary examples of naked singularities arising from smooth initial data. The first known examples of naked singularities arising in gravitational collapse are due to Christodoulou [11] for the spherically symmetric Einstein-dust system in $3+1$ dimensions. Remarkably, [11] constructs examples of stable naked singularities, so weak cosmic censorship is false for this model. More recently, the remarkable work [29] constructed examples of naked singularities for the spherically symmetric Einstein–Euler system in $3+1$ dimensions. Since these models are prone to singularity formation even in the absence of gravity, it is not clear however what is the physical significance of these results for the issue of weak cosmic censorship.

In $2+1$ dimensions, to date, no rigorous examples of naked singularities for (1.1) have been constructed. Similarly to our discussion in the previous paragraph, the numerical relativity works on critical collapse [42, 33] suggest that there exist such examples arising from smooth data on $\partial\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}\cap\partial\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}.$ In the upcoming work [19], we prove a local version of this result and we provide the first rigorous construction of locally naked singularities arising in (local) critical collapse. More precisely, on the finite outgoing cone $C_{0}^{+}=\{u=u_{0},\ 0\leq r<r_{0}\},$ we construct a 2-parameter family of $C^{3}$ characteristic data $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}^{q}$ , for any integer $q\geq 4$ and $\lambda\in(-\epsilon,\epsilon),$ which satisfies the following properties:

- • For $\lambda<0,$ the development of $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}^{q}$ does not form singularities.

- • For $\lambda=0,$ the development of $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}^{q}$ is a locally naked singularity spacetime and contains no trapped surfaces. Moreover, the case $(\lambda,q)=(0,4)$ corresponds to the numerical examples of [42, 33].

- • For $\lambda>0,$ the development of $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}^{q}$ contains trapped surfaces.

In the above, it is then the $\lambda=0$ solutions which represent examples of locally naked singularities arising in (local) critical collapse. An interesting quantitative aspect of the examples of [19] is that for $\lambda=0,$ the blueshift defined in (1.14) satisfies the following rate as $u\rightarrow 0^{-}:$

$$ \mathbf{b}(u)=\bigg(3-\frac{1}{2q}\bigg)\log\frac{u_{0}}{u}+o(1), $$

which should be compared to the general lower bound (1.15) for first singularities at the center.

In the context of the moduli space $\mathfrak{M}$ of the present paper, an immediate consequence of the results in [19] is that $\mathfrak{D}_{0}^{q}$ can be extended to asymptotically AdS data $\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{0}^{q}$ such that $\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{0}^{q}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}.$ In particular, it follows that $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}\neq\emptyset.$ It would be an interesting problem to prove that the family $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}^{q}$ can be extended to a family $\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{\lambda}^{q}$ of asymptotically AdS data, such that in fact $\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{0}^{q}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}$ and $\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{0}^{q}\in\partial\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}\cap\partial\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}.$

### 1.5 Outline of the paper

We outline the rest of the paper. In Section 2, we introduce general properties of the Einstein-scalar field system (1.1) in circular symmetry. In Section 3, we prove the mass gap result in Theorem 1.2. In Section 4, we prove the formation of trapped surface criterion in Theorem 1.3. In Section 5, we provide a detailed description of locally naked singularity spacetimes. In Section 6, we prove the instability of locally naked singularity spacetimes to trapped surface formation. In Section 7, we prove the main result in Theorem 1.1. Finally, in Appendix A we construct asymptotically AdS characteristic data perturbations.

## 2 The Einstein-scalar field system in circular symmetry

The goal of this section is to introduce the general properties of circularly symmetric solutions of the Einstein-scalar field system (1.1). In Section 2.1, we rewrite the system (1.1) using double null coordinates. In Section 2.2 we define the notion of asymptotically AdS characteristic data sets. In Section 2.3, we introduce the local well-posedness theory for asymptotically AdS spacetimes. In Section 2.4, we state additional important properties of circularly symmetric solutions of (1.1), including a description of the general structure of maximal globally hyperbolic developments arising in gravitational collapse.

### 2.1 Equations in double null coordinates

In this section, we introduce global systems of double null coordinates for circularly symmetric spacetimes, which allow us to represent certain causal properties of spacetimes using Penrose diagrams. We also rewrite the Einstein-scalar field system of equations (1.1) in double null coordinates.

We first make precise the notion of circular symmetry:

#### Definition 2.1.

We say that $\big(\mathcal{M},g,\phi\big)$ is circularly symmetric if the group $U(1)$ acts by isometry on $\mathcal{M}$ and preserves the scalar field $\phi.$ Moreover, we require that:

$$ \mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{M}/U(1) $$

inherits the structure of a $1+1$ dimensional Lorentzian manifold with boundary. Denoting by $\overline{g}$ the metric induced on $\mathcal{Q},$ we also require that the metric $g$ on $\mathcal{M}$ takes the form:

$$ g=\overline{g}+r^{2}d\sigma_{1}^{2}, $$

where $d\sigma_{1}^{2}$ is the standard metric on $S^{1}.$ Moreover, $r$ and $\phi$ are functions on $\mathcal{Q},$ and $r$ is nonnegative.

As a $1+1$ dimensional Lorentzian manifold, $\mathcal{Q}$ can be globally covered by double null coordinates $(u,v)$ . In these coordinates, the induced metric $\overline{g}$ takes the form:

$$ \overline{g}=-\Omega^{2}dudv. $$

Thus, the spacetime $(\mathcal{M},g)$ can be covered globally by the double null coordinates $(u,v,\theta):$

$$ g=-\Omega^{2}dudv+r^{2}d\theta^{2}. $$

Since the metric on $\mathcal{Q}$ is conformal to that of the $1+1$ dimensional Minkowski space, we can represent $\mathcal{Q}$ as a submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^{1+1}$ using Penrose diagrams. This approach offers a canonical way of attaching a boundary to the quotient $\mathcal{Q}$ . We point out that we use the topology and causality of the ambient $\mathbb{R}^{1+1}$ .

Next, we define two components of the boundary of $\mathcal{Q}$ : the center $\Gamma$ and null infinity $\mathcal{I}.$ We denote by $\Gamma$ the portion of the boundary of $\mathcal{Q}$ corresponding to the set of fixed points of the action of $U(1)$ , and note that $r=0$ on $\Gamma$ . We also define the set $\mathcal{U}=\big\{u:\sup_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{Q}}r(u,v)=\infty\big\},$ which is nonempty according to Section 2.3. We notice that for any $u\in\mathcal{U},$ there exists a unique $v_{\mathcal{I}}(u)$ such that $\big(u,v_{\mathcal{I}}(u)\big)\in\overline{\mathcal{Q}}\backslash\mathcal{Q}.$

#### Definition 2.2.

We define null infinity as the set:

$$ \mathcal{I}=\bigcup_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\big(u,v_{\mathcal{I}}(u)\big). $$

According to Section 2.3, null infinity $\mathcal{I}$ is a timelike curve. We denote by $i^{+}$ the future limit point of $\mathcal{I}$ .

We rewrite the Einstein-scalar field system with respect to double null coordinates. The system of equations (1.1) is equivalent to:

$$ \displaystyle 2r\partial_{u}\partial_{v}\phi \displaystyle=-\partial_{u}r\partial_{v}\phi-\partial_{v}r\partial_{u}\phi, \displaystyle 2\partial_{u}\partial_{v}r \displaystyle=\Lambda\Omega^{2}r, \displaystyle 2\partial_{u}\partial_{v}\log\Omega^{2} \displaystyle=-2\partial_{u}\phi\partial_{v}\phi+\Lambda\Omega^{2}, \displaystyle\partial_{u}\big(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{u}r\big) \displaystyle=-\Omega^{-2}r(\partial_{u}\phi)^{2}, \displaystyle\partial_{v}\big(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r\big) \displaystyle=-\Omega^{-2}r(\partial_{v}\phi)^{2}. $$

In double null coordinates, the Hawking mass defined in (1.10) takes the form:

$$ m(u,v)=4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{u}r\partial_{v}r-\Lambda r^{2}+1. $$

We impose the boundary condition at the center $m|_{\Gamma}=0$ , necessary for the regularity of $(\mathcal{M},g)$ .

We derive the following propagation equations for the mass:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{v}m \displaystyle=-4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{u}r\cdot r(\partial_{v}\phi)^{2}, \displaystyle\partial_{u}m \displaystyle=-4\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r\cdot r(\partial_{u}\phi)^{2}. $$

We define the renormalized outgoing derivative of the scalar field by:

$$ \theta=\sqrt{r}\frac{\partial_{v}\phi}{\partial_{v}r}. $$

Finally, we define the quantity $\gamma,$ which plays a key role in our analysis:

$$ \gamma=\frac{\Omega^{2}}{\partial_{v}r}. $$

Using this notation, the Raychaudhuri equation (2.6) is equivalent to:

$$ \partial_{v}\log\gamma=\frac{r(\partial_{v}\phi)^{2}}{\partial_{v}r}=\theta^{2}\partial_{v}r. $$

### 2.2 Asymptotically AdS characteristic data

It is essential to have a local well-posedness theory for circularly symmetric solutions of (1.1). In compact regions of spacetime, such results are standard in the literature, see for example [13, 23, 36]. The main difficulty lies in dealing with the boundary at infinity, as $\mathcal{I}$ represents a timelike asymptotic boundary of spacetime. Our strategy is to adapt the $(3+1)$ -dimensional theory of [30] to our $(2+1)$ -dimensional setting. The main goal of this section is to define a suitable notion of asymptotically AdS characteristic data and the moduli space of initial data.

Since we want to prove a well-posedness theory which accounts for the boundary at infinity, the discussion only applies to the $J^{-}(\mathcal{I})$ region of spacetime, i.e. the causal past of $\mathcal{I}.$ In particular, in the case of black hole spacetimes, our discussion only applies to the exterior region as defined in Section 2.4. To emphasize the distinction from the Sections 2.1 and 2.4, in Sections 2.2 and 2.3 we use the notation $(U,V)$ for systems of double null coordinates that are adapted to the region $J^{-}(\mathcal{I})$ .

The first goal is to define asymptotically AdS spacetimes. In particular, the definition must apply to the BTZ spacetimes (1.3). For the metric (1.3), we consider double null coordinates $(U,V)$ which are Eddington-Finkelstein normalized as follows:

$$ \frac{\partial_{V}r}{1-M+|\Lambda|r^{2}}=\frac{1}{2},\ \frac{\partial_{U}r}{1-M+|\Lambda|r^{2}}=-\frac{1}{2},\ \text{and }U=V\text{ on }\mathcal{I}. $$

To achieve this, we define $U=t-r_{*},\ V=t+r_{*},$ where $r_{*}$ satisfies:

$$ dr_{*}=\frac{dr}{1-M+|\Lambda|r^{2}},\ \lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}r_{*}(r)=0. $$

With respect to the Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates $(U,V),$ the BTZ metric (1.3) becomes:

$$ g_{M}=-\Big(1-M+|\Lambda|r^{2}\Big)dUdV+r^{2}d\theta^{2}. $$

We remark that the leading behavior of the lapse at $\mathcal{I}$ in (2.13) is dictated by the cosmological constant and is independent of the dimension. We adapt the definition of asymptotically AdS spacetimes in [30, Section 2.4] to our setting:

#### Definition 2.3.

We say that a circularly symmetric spacetime $\big(\mathcal{M},g\big)$ is asymptotically AdS if for every $p\in\mathcal{I}$ there exists a coordinate system $(U,V)$ and a neighborhood of $p$ in $\mathcal{M}$ :

$$ \Big\{V\geq U_{0},\ U\in(V,U_{0}+\delta]\Big\}, $$

such that $U=V$ on $\mathcal{I},$ $\partial_{U}r<0,\ \partial_{V}r>0$ and the metric satisfies the asymptotic behavior for some $M\geq 0$ :

$$ g=-\Big(1+O\big(r^{-3}\big)\Big)\Big(1-M+|\Lambda|r^{2}\Big)dUdV+r^{2}d\theta^{2}, $$

$$ T(\Omega^{2})=O\big(r^{-1}\big),\ R_{*}(\Omega^{2})=O\big(r^{3}\big),\ T(r)=O\big(r^{-1}\big),\ R_{*}(r)=1-M+|\Lambda|r^{2}+O\big(r^{-1}\big), $$

$$ T(\partial_{U}r)=O\big(r^{-1}\big),\ R_{*}(\partial_{U}r)=O\big(r^{3}\big),\ T(\partial_{V}r)=O\big(r^{-1}\big),\ R_{*}(\partial_{V}r)=O\big(r^{3}\big), $$

where $T=\partial_{U}+\partial_{V},\ R_{*}=\partial_{V}-\partial_{U}.$

Our next goal is to define characteristic initial data. We first define the notion of an asymptotically Eddington-Finkelstein coordinate, similarly to [30, Proposition 3.1]:

#### Definition 2.4.

We consider the interval $[0,\infty)$ parametrized by $r.$ Let $V:[0,\infty)\rightarrow I=\big[V_{\Gamma},V_{\mathcal{I}}\big)$ be a coordinate function such that $V(0)=V_{\Gamma},$ and $\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}V(r)=V_{\mathcal{I}}.$ We say that the coordinate $V$ on $I$ is asymptotically Eddington-Finkelstein if there exists $M\geq 0$ such that as $V\rightarrow V_{\mathcal{I}}$ :

$$ \partial_{V}r=\frac{1}{2}\big(1-M+|\Lambda|r^{2}\big)+o\big(r^{-1}\big),\ \partial_{V}\bigg(\frac{\partial_{V}r}{1-M+|\Lambda|r^{2}}\bigg)=o(r^{-2}). $$

We introduce the weighted spaces used in the definition of initial data:

#### Definition 2.5.

We define the weighted Sobolev norm $H^{n}\big([0,\infty)\big)$ for any $n\geq 0:$

$$ \big\|f\big\|_{H^{n}([0,\infty))}^{2}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\bigg[\big(1+r^{2}\big)^{n}\Big(\partial_{r}^{n}f\Big)^{2}+\ldots+\big(1+r^{2}\big)\Big(\partial_{r}f\Big)^{2}+f^{2}\bigg]rdr. $$

With respect to an asymptotically Eddington-Finkelstein coordinate $V$ on $I=\big[V_{\Gamma},V_{\mathcal{I}}\big)$ , we define:

$$ \big\|f\big\|_{H^{n}(I)}^{2}=\int_{V_{\Gamma}}^{V_{\mathcal{I}}}\bigg[\big(1+r^{2}\big)^{n}\bigg[\bigg(\frac{\partial_{V}}{\partial_{V}r}\bigg)^{n}f\bigg]^{2}+\ldots+\big(1+r^{2}\big)\bigg(\frac{\partial_{V}f}{\partial_{V}r}\bigg)^{2}+f^{2}\bigg]r(V)\partial_{V}rdV. $$

We define asymptotically AdS characteristic data sets, similarly to [30, Definition 3.3]:

#### Definition 2.6 (Asymptotically AdS characteristic data).

For any $k\geq 2,$ we say that the tuple:

$$ \mathfrak{D}=\big(r,\ldots,\partial_{U}^{k+1}r,\Omega,\ldots,\partial_{U}^{k}\Omega,m,\ldots,\partial_{U}^{k}m,\phi,\ldots,\partial_{U}^{k}\phi,\mathcal{T}\phi,\ldots,\mathcal{T}^{k}\phi\big) $$

represents a $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data set if there exists $M\geq 0$ and an asymptotically Eddington-Finkelstein coordinate $V$ on $I=\big[V_{\Gamma},V_{\mathcal{I}}\big)$ satisfying (2.14), such that the following hold:

- 1. Regularity conditions:

$$ \partial_{U}^{i}r\in C^{k+1-i}(I),i=\overline{0,k+1},\ \partial_{U}^{j}\Omega,\partial_{U}^{j}m\in C^{k-j}(I),j=\overline{0,k}, $$

(2.17)

$$ \phi\in H^{k+1}(I),\mathcal{T}\phi\in H^{k}(I),\ldots,\mathcal{T}^{k}\phi\in H^{1}(I), $$

(2.18)

$$ \partial_{U}^{i}\phi\in C^{k-1-i}(I),i=\overline{0,k-1},\ \sqrt{r}\partial_{V}^{k-j}\partial_{U}^{j}\phi\in C^{0}(I),j=\overline{0,k}. $$

(2.19)

- 2. Compatibility conditions: the elements of $\mathfrak{D}$ satisfy the compatibility conditions obtained by differentiating equations (2.2)-(2.9) and taking the Kodama vector field $\mathcal{T}$ to be given by:

$$ \mathcal{T}=\Omega^{-2}\partial_{V}r\partial_{U}-\Omega^{-2}\partial_{U}r\partial_{V}. $$

(2.20)

- 3. No trapped or anti-trapped surfaces: $\partial_{V}r>0,\ \partial_{U}r<0$ on $I.$

- 4. Boundary conditions at $\Gamma:$ for any $0\leq i\leq k+1,\ 0\leq j\leq k,$ and $0\leq l\leq k-2,$ we have that $\mathcal{T}^{i}r(V_{\Gamma})=0,\ \mathcal{T}^{j}m(V_{\Gamma})=0,$ $\mathcal{T}^{l}(\Omega^{-2}\partial_{V}r\partial_{U}\phi+\Omega^{-2}\partial_{U}r\partial_{V}\phi)(V_{\Gamma})=0.$

- 5. Boundary conditions at $\mathcal{I}:$ $\lim_{V\rightarrow V_{\mathcal{I}}}m(V)=M.$

- 6. Asymptotic behavior as $V\rightarrow V_{\mathcal{I}}$ : • $r$ satisfies (2.14) and for $0\leq i\leq k+1:$

$$ \partial_{V}^{i}r=O\big(r^{i+1}\big). $$

(2.21) • $\partial_{U}r$ satisfies the asymptotics for $0\leq i\leq k+1:$

$$ \partial_{U}r=-\frac{1}{2}\big(1-M+|\Lambda|r^{2}\big)+O\big(r^{-1}\big),\ \partial_{V}^{i}\partial_{U}r=O\big(r^{i+2}\big). $$

(2.22) • $\Omega$ satisfies the asymptotics for $0\leq i\leq k:$

$$ \Omega^{2}=1-M+|\Lambda|r^{2}+O\big(r^{-1}\big),\ \partial_{V}^{i}\Omega^{2}=O\big(r^{i+2}\big). $$

(2.23) • The scalar field satisfies the asymptotics for $0\leq i+j\leq k$ :

$$ \partial_{V}^{i}\partial_{U}^{j}\phi=O\big(r^{i+j-\frac{3}{2}}\big). $$

(2.24)

#### Remark 2.1.

In Definition 2.6 we adapted [30, Definition 3.3] from the $(3+1)$ -dimensional case to the $(2+1)$ -dimensional case, so we highlight some of the differences:

- 1. The initial data in our case models the setting of gravitational collapse, so it extends from $\Gamma$ to $\mathcal{I},$ whereas the definition of [30] is localized to a neighborhood of $\mathcal{I}.$ Thus, we also prescribe regularity conditions at $\Gamma.$ Moreover, in view of the analysis of (2.2) near $\Gamma$ in $(2+1)$ -dimensions, for the scalar field it is convenient to assume Sobolev regularity at top order as in (2.18), which can be propagated by energy estimates, instead of only assuming the pointwise regularity conditions in (2.19).

- 2. The initial data in Definition 2.6 is prescribed on an outgoing null cone, whereas [30] prescribes initial data on an ingoing null cone. Therefore, unlike [30], we cannot enforce the conditions in (2.18)-(2.19) by simply requiring suitable decay rates for $\phi,$ so we need to impose quantitative conditions on $\mathcal{T}\phi,\ldots,\mathcal{T}^{k}\phi$ . A similar approach is taken by [31] in the setting of spacelike initial data, see [31, Remark 5.1].

- 3. The notion of a characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}$ is over-determined, subject to the compatibility conditions and boundary conditions at the center. Alternatively, one could attempt to prescribe only the function $\phi$ as initial data (referred to as seed data), similarly to [30]. However, since in our setting the initial data is prescribed on an outgoing null cone, (2.18) imposes nonlinear and non-local constraints on $\phi$ , see already Remark A.3, so the initial data conditions are stated more naturally for $\mathfrak{D}$ .

- 4. We make assumptions on the asymptotic rates up to order $k\geq 2$ , whereas [30] only requires asymptotic rates up to order $2.$

#### Remark 2.2.

Equation (2.18) represents the main quantitative condition in the definition of asymptotically AdS characteristic data sets and motivates our definition of a distance function below. In particular, (2.18) implies (2.19) by Sobolev embedding. Moreover, (2.18) implies that $\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}m(r)$ exists and that $\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}\mathcal{T}m(r)=0,$ which are consistent with the reflective boundary conditions at infinity $m_{\mathcal{I}}=M.$

The aim for the rest of the section is to define the moduli space of initial data. We define the following quantity measuring the size of asymptotically AdS characteristic data sets, which is independent of the choice of $(U,V)$ coordinates:

#### Definition 2.7.

We consider a $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}$ . We define:

$$ \big\|\mathfrak{D}\big\|_{X([0,\infty))}=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\big\|\mathcal{T}^{i}\phi\big\|_{H^{k+1-i}([0,\infty))}. $$

We note that the space of asymptotically AdS characteristic data sets is not a vector space, since the compatibility conditions in Definition 2.6 are nonlinear, so $X([0,\infty))$ is not a norm. In the asymptotically flat case, the solution to this issue is to consider the linear space of seed data consisting of $\phi$ instead (see for example [16]). However, as explained in Remark A.3, for asymptotically AdS characteristic data equation (2.18) imposes nonlinear constraints on $\phi$ already. Nevertheless, we use $X([0,\infty))$ to define a distance function as follows:

#### Definition 2.8.

For any two $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data sets $\mathfrak{D}$ and $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime},$ we define the distance function:

$$ d_{X([0,\infty))}(\mathfrak{D},\mathfrak{D}^{\prime})=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\Big\|\mathcal{T}^{i}\phi-\big(\mathcal{T}^{i}\phi\big)^{\prime}\Big\|_{H^{k+1-i}([0,\infty))}. $$

We note that any two asymptotically AdS characteristic data sets satisfying $d_{X([0,\infty))}(\mathfrak{D},\mathfrak{D}^{\prime})=0$ are related by a change of double null coordinates $U\rightarrow\tilde{U}(U),V\rightarrow\tilde{V}(V)$ . If this holds, we denote $\mathfrak{D}\sim\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ , and we notice that $\sim$ defines an equivalence relation on the space of $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data sets.

We can finally use the distance function (2.26) to define a topology on the set of initial data. More specifically, we define the moduli space of $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data as follows:

#### Definition 2.9.

We define the moduli space of $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data as the metric space $\big(\mathfrak{M},d_{X([0,\infty))}\big),$ where $\mathfrak{M}$ is given by:

$$ \mathfrak{M}=\big\{\mathfrak{D}:\ \mathfrak{D}\text{ is a }C^{k}\text{ asymptotically AdS characteristic data set}\big\}/_{\sim}. $$

### 2.3 Local well-posedness theory

We state the main local well-posedness result, which applies to asymptotically AdS characteristic data as in Definition 2.6:

#### Proposition 2.1.

Let $k\geq 2$ be an integer. For any $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}=\big(r,\ldots,\partial_{U}^{k+1}r,\Omega,\ldots,\partial_{U}^{k}\Omega,m,\ldots,\partial_{U}^{k}m,\phi,\ldots,\partial_{U}^{k}\phi,\mathcal{T}\phi,\ldots,\mathcal{T}^{k}\phi\big)$ on the outgoing null cone $C_{0}^{+}=\big\{V_{\mathcal{I}}\big\}\times\big[V_{\Gamma},V_{\mathcal{I}}\big)$ , there exists $\delta>0$ and a unique solution $\big(r,\Omega,\phi\big)$ of the equations (2.2)-(2.6) with reflective boundary conditions at infinity $m_{\mathcal{I}}=M,$ which is defined in the domain:

$$ \mathcal{Q}=\Big\{(U,V):\ U\in\big[V_{\mathcal{I}},V_{\mathcal{I}}+\delta\big],\ V\in\big[V_{\Gamma}(U),U\big)\Big\}, $$

where we have that the center $\Gamma$ and null infinity $\mathcal{I}$ given by:

$$ \Gamma=\Big\{\big(U,V_{\Gamma}(U)\big):\ U\in\big[V_{\mathcal{I}},V_{\mathcal{I}}+\delta\big]\Big\},\ \mathcal{I}=\Big\{\big(U,U\big):\ U\in\big[V_{\mathcal{I}},V_{\mathcal{I}}+\delta\big]\Big\} $$

represent timelike curves. Moreover, the corresponding circularly symmetric spacetime $\big(\mathcal{M},g\big)$ is asymptotically AdS as in Definition 2.3, and for each $U\in\big[V_{\mathcal{I}},V_{\mathcal{I}}+\delta\big]$ it induces $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data on $\big\{U\big\}\times\big[V_{\Gamma}(U),U\big]$ as in Definition 2.6.

The proof of Proposition 2.1 uses standard methods and follows in detail the steps of [30], so we do not repeat it here. We remark that one can also establish further standard properties, such as persistence of regularity and Cauchy stability. To illustrate how the methods of [30] are adapted to our setting, we prove a priori estimates for $C^{2}$ solutions (in the sense of Definition 2.6) of the linear wave equation on asymptotically AdS spacetimes in a neighborhood of $\mathcal{I}$ . It is clear that using the methods of [30] and a propagation of regularity argument, one can turn this proof into the local well-posedness result.

#### Proposition 2.2.

Let $\big(\mathcal{M},g\big)$ be a circularly symmetric asymptotically AdS spacetime. We consider a coordinate system $(U,V)$ and the domain:

$$ \mathcal{D}=\Big\{(U,V):\ U\in\big[V_{\mathcal{I}},V_{\mathcal{I}}+\delta\big],\ V\in\big[V_{0},U\big),\ \ V_{0}<V_{\mathcal{I}}\Big\}, $$

such that the asymptotics in Definition 2.3 hold in $\mathcal{D}$ , and similar rates hold for higher order derivatives of $\Omega^{2}$ and $r.$

Let $\psi:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be a $C^{2}$ solution of the wave equation with reflective boundary conditions:

$$ \begin{cases}\square_{g}\psi=0,\\
\psi=0,\ \text{ on }\mathcal{I},\end{cases} $$

which satisfies the bound on $\mathcal{D}\cap\big\{U=V_{\mathcal{I}}\big\}$ and $\mathcal{D}\cap\big\{V=V_{0}\big\}$ :

$$ \sum_{i=0}^{2}\big\|\mathcal{T}^{i}\psi\big\|_{H^{3-i}\big(\{V_{\mathcal{I}}\}\times[V_{0},V_{\mathcal{I}})\big)}+\sum_{i=0}^{2}\big\|\mathcal{T}^{i}\psi\big\|_{H^{3-i}\big([V_{\mathcal{I}},V_{\mathcal{I}}+\delta)\times\{V_{0}\}\big)}<C_{0}. $$

Then, we have that $\psi$ satisfies the following estimates for any $\big(U,V\big)\in\mathcal{D}:$

$$ \sum_{i=0}^{2}\big\|\mathcal{T}^{i}\psi\big\|_{H^{3-i}\big(\{U\}\times[V_{0},V]\big)}+\sum_{i=0}^{2}\big\|\mathcal{T}^{i}\psi\big\|_{H^{3-i}\big([\max(V,V_{\mathcal{I}}),U]\times\{V\}\big)}<C, $$

$$ r^{3/2}|\psi|+r^{1/2}|\partial_{V}\psi|+r^{1/2}|\partial_{U}\psi|+r^{-1/2}|\partial_{V}^{2}\psi|+r^{-1/2}|\partial_{U}^{2}\psi|<C, $$

where the constant $C$ depends on $C_{0}$ and the background $g.$

#### Proof.

We follow the same steps as [31] and [30, Proposition 6.4]. The starting point is the following approximate conservation law derived from (2.2):

$$ \partial_{U}\Big(r(\partial_{V}\psi)^{2}\Big)+\partial_{V}\Big(r(\partial_{U}\psi)^{2}\Big)=-\partial_{U}\psi\partial_{V}\psi\cdot Tr, $$

where $T=\partial_{U}+\partial_{V}.$ We integrate this equation in the domain $\mathcal{D}\cap\big\{U^{\prime}\leq U,\ V^{\prime}\leq V\big\}$ using the reflective boundary conditions, which imply that the flux terms on $\mathcal{I}$ vanish. The decay of $Tr$ in Definition 2.3 implies that the terms on the RHS are lower order, so we obtain the estimate:

$$ \int_{V_{0}}^{V}r\big(\partial_{V}\psi\big)^{2}\big(U,V^{\prime}\big)dV^{\prime}+\int_{\max(V,V_{\mathcal{I}})}^{U}r\big(\partial_{U}\psi\big)^{2}\big(U^{\prime},V\big)dU^{\prime}<C. $$

Next, we commute (2.2) by $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{T}^{2}$ . Repeating the same proof, we obtain that (2.31) also holds for $\mathcal{T}\psi$ and $\mathcal{T}^{2}\psi.$

The estimate (2.31) for $\psi,\mathcal{T}\psi,\mathcal{T}^{2}\psi,$ and the reflective boundary conditions also imply the pointwise estimate $r|\psi|+r|\mathcal{T}\psi|+r|\mathcal{T}^{2}\psi|\leq C.$ Furthermore, we have the following Hardy inequality for any function $f$ such that the RHS of (2.32) is finite:

$$ r^{2}f^{2}+\int_{r}^{\infty}\tilde{r}f^{2}d\tilde{r}\leq\lim_{\tilde{r}\rightarrow\infty}\tilde{r}^{2}f^{2}+\int_{r}^{\infty}\tilde{r}^{3}\big(\partial_{r}f\big)^{2}d\tilde{r}. $$

Using (2.32) for $\psi,\mathcal{T}\psi,$ and $\mathcal{T}^{2}\psi$ , we control the $H^{1}$ norms in (2.29). Using (2.2) as well, the $H^{1}$ bounds further imply that (2.29) holds. Moreover, we then get the pointwise estimates $|\partial_{U}\psi|+|\partial_{V}\psi|+|\partial_{U}\mathcal{T}\psi|+|\partial_{V}\mathcal{T}\psi|\leq C$ and $|\partial_{U}^{2}\psi|+|\partial_{U}\partial_{V}\psi|+|\partial_{V}^{2}\psi|\leq Cr.$

For the rest of the proof we show the improved pointwise estimate (2.30). We define the quantity:

$$ \zeta=\sqrt{r}\frac{\partial_{U}\psi}{\partial_{U}r}. $$

We compute that:

$$ \partial_{V}\zeta=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{r}}\partial_{V}\psi-2|\Lambda|r\cdot\frac{\partial_{V}r}{|\Lambda|r^{2}-m+1}\cdot\zeta=-\frac{T\psi}{2\sqrt{r}}+\bigg(\frac{\partial_{U}r}{2r^{2}}-\frac{2|\Lambda|\partial_{V}r}{|\Lambda|r^{2}-m+1}\bigg)r\zeta. $$

We define $A=r^{n}\zeta,$ which satisfies the equation:

$$ \partial_{V}A=|\Lambda|rA\bigg(\frac{n\partial_{V}r}{|\Lambda|r^{2}}+\frac{\partial_{U}r}{2|\Lambda|r^{2}}-\frac{2\partial_{V}r}{|\Lambda|r^{2}-m+1}\bigg)-r^{n}\frac{T\psi}{2\sqrt{r}}. $$

We take $n=2,$ which results in having a bounded integrating factor. The remaining term on the RHS is lower order and can be controlled using the previous pointwise estimates. Therefore, $A$ is bounded, so we obtain the improved estimate $r^{1/2}|\partial_{U}\psi|\leq C.$ The pointwise bound for $\mathcal{T}\psi$ also implies that $r^{1/2}|\partial_{V}\psi|\leq C$ and $r^{3/2}|\psi|\leq C.$ Using the wave equation (2.2), we also have that $r^{-1/2}|\partial_{U}\partial_{V}\psi|\leq C$ . The bound $|\partial_{V}\mathcal{T}\psi|+|\partial_{U}\mathcal{T}\psi|\leq C$ then implies $|\partial_{U}^{2}\psi|+|\partial_{V}^{2}\psi|\leq Cr^{1/2}.$ ∎

### 2.4 Global structure of spacetimes

In this section, we state some general properties of circularly symmetric solutions of (1.1), including: monotonicity properties, a description of first singularities, the existence of maximal globally hyperbolic developments, properties of black hole spacetimes, a description of the general structure of the boundary of spacetimes arising in gravitational collapse, and the decomposition of the moduli space of initial data. The results of this section are analogous to the $(3+1)$ -dimensional setting, see for example [23, 24, 30, 36]. Adapting the proofs to the $(2+1)$ -dimensional setting is straightforward, so we simply record the results needed for the rest of the paper.

#### Monotonicity properties.

We first state some important monotonicity properties, which follow directly from (2.3), (2.9), (2.8), and the boundary conditions at $\Gamma:$

#### Lemma 2.1.

In $\mathcal{Q}$ we have that:

$$ \partial_{u}r<0,\ \partial_{u}\partial_{v}r\leq 0,\ m\geq 0,\ \partial_{v}m\geq 0. $$

Moreover, $\partial_{v}r$ and $\partial_{u}m$ have opposite signs. Additionally, $\partial_{u}\partial_{v}r<0$ on $\mathcal{Q}\backslash\Gamma$ . Finally, in the causal past of $\Gamma$ we have $\partial_{v}r>0.$

Depending on the behavior of $r,$ we divide the spacetime $\mathcal{Q}$ into the following regions:

#### Definition 2.10.

We define the regular, trapped and marginally trapped regions of $\mathcal{Q}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R} \displaystyle=\Big\{p\in\mathcal{Q}:\ \partial_{v}r(p)>0\Big\}, \displaystyle\mathcal{T} \displaystyle=\Big\{p\in\mathcal{Q}:\ \partial_{v}r(p)<0\Big\}, \displaystyle\mathcal{A} \displaystyle=\Big\{p\in\mathcal{Q}:\ \partial_{v}r(p)=0\Big\}. $$

We record some simple properties of the trapped region, which follow directly from (2.6),(2.7), and the monotonicity properties in (2.33):

#### Lemma 2.2.

We have an equivalent characterization of the trapped region in terms of the Hawking mass:

$$ p\in\mathcal{T}\Longleftrightarrow m(p)>1-\Lambda r^{2}(p). $$

Moreover, the trapped region is a future set: if $p\in\mathcal{T}$ , then $J^{+}(p)\cap\mathcal{Q}\subset\mathcal{T}.$ Similarly, if $p\in\mathcal{T}\cup\mathcal{A}$ , then $J^{+}(p)\cap\mathcal{Q}\subset\mathcal{T}\cup\mathcal{A}$ and $J^{+}(p)\cap\mathcal{Q}\cap\{u>u(p)\}\subset\mathcal{T}.$

#### First singularities.

We state the description of first singularities away from the center of [36, Theorem 1.8] (see also [30, Proposition A.1]), adapted to our setting:

#### Proposition 2.3.

Let $p\in\overline{\mathcal{Q}}\backslash\mathcal{Q}$ be a first singularity away from the center, i.e. $p\notin\overline{\Gamma}\backslash\Gamma.$ For any $q\in\big(I^{-}(p)\cap\mathcal{Q}\big)\backslash\{p\}$ such that $\mathcal{D}=\big(J^{+}(q)\cap J^{-}(p)\big)\backslash\{p\}\subset\mathcal{Q}$ we have that $\inf_{r\in\mathcal{D}}=0.$

The proof of this result follows the same steps as [36, Theorem 1.8], but is greatly simplified in our case due to the structure of equation (2.3). In particular, Proposition 2.3 also implies that every first singularity away from the center must be preceded by trapped surfaces, which is analogous to the result of [23]. As a consequence, every first singularity in the regular region must occur at the center:

#### Corollary 2.1.

Let $p\in\overline{\mathcal{Q}}\backslash\mathcal{Q}$ be a first singularity such that $J^{-}(p)\backslash\{p\}\subset\mathcal{R}.$ Then $p\in\overline{\Gamma}\backslash\Gamma.$

#### Existence of maximal globally hyperbolic developments.

In view of the timelike boundary at infinity, we modify the usual definition of global hyperbolicity as follows, similarly to [30, Definition 8.1]:

#### Definition 2.11.

An asymptotically AdS spacetime $\big(\mathcal{M},g\big)$ is globally hyperbolic if there exists an outgoing null cone $C_{0}^{+}$ such that $C_{0}^{+}\cap\Gamma\neq\emptyset,\ \overline{C_{0}^{+}}\cap\mathcal{I}\neq\emptyset$ and all past directed inextendible causal curves in $\mathcal{M}$ either intersect $C_{0}^{+}$ or have a limit endpoint on $\mathcal{I}$ .

It is standard to use the local well-posedness result in Proposition 2.1 to prove the existence of a unique maximal globally hyperbolic development of initial data. We refer the reader to [30, Section 4] and the references therein.

#### Proposition 2.4.

For any $k\geq 2$ and $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}$ , there exists a maximal globally hyperbolic development $\big(\mathcal{M},g,\phi\big)$ of the initial data, which is unique up to isometry.

#### Black hole spacetimes.

As a consequence of the monotonicity properties established so far, we have that $J^{-}(\mathcal{I})\cap\mathcal{Q}\subset\mathcal{R}.$ Thus, the black hole region $\mathcal{BH}=\mathcal{Q}\backslash J^{-}(\mathcal{I})$ satisfies $\mathcal{T}\cup\mathcal{A}\subset\mathcal{BH}.$ In particular, if $\mathcal{T}\neq\emptyset$ then $\mathcal{BH}\neq\emptyset.$ In the case when $\mathcal{BH}\neq\emptyset,$ we define the event horizon $\mathcal{H}^{+}$ as the future boundary of $J^{-}(\mathcal{I})\cap\mathcal{Q}$ in $\mathcal{Q}.$

We state the following result for black hole spacetimes, similarly to [24]. For the proof one adapts the arguments of [22, Section 5] and [30, Section 8.2] to the $(2+1)$ -dimensional setting, once again using the good monotonicity properties in our system.

#### Proposition 2.5.

Let $\big(\mathcal{M},g,\phi\big)$ be the maximal globally hyperbolic development of a $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data set with $k\geq 2$ , and denote $M=m|_{\mathcal{I}}.$ If $\mathcal{BH}\neq\emptyset,$ then $\mathcal{H}^{+}$ is future complete and satisfies the Penrose inequality $|\Lambda|r^{2}+1\leq M$ . Moreover, in this case we also have that $\mathcal{I}$ is future complete.

#### Global structure of spacetimes.

We explain the general structure of the boundary of spacetimes. We first define the other possible components of the boundary, as in [15, 36].

#### Definition 2.12.

We denote $b_{\Gamma}=\overline{\Gamma}\backslash\Gamma.$ If $b_{\Gamma}\neq i^{+}$ , we say that $b_{\Gamma}$ is a first singularity at the center. In this case, we define the central component of the singular boundary:

$$ \mathcal{B}_{0}=\Big\{(u_{b_{\Gamma}},v)\in\overline{\mathcal{Q}}\Big\}. $$

Finally, we define the singular component of the boundary:

$$ \mathcal{B}=\Big\{(u,v)\in\overline{\mathcal{Q}}\backslash\mathcal{Q}:\ u_{i^{+}}<u<u_{b_{\Gamma}}\Big\}. $$

Using the description of first singularities in Proposition 2.3 and the monotonicity properties (2.33), it is straightforward to show that $\mathcal{B}$ is spacelike and $r=0$ on $\mathcal{B}$ . Similarly to the $(3+1)$ -dimensional case (see [36, Section 1.4.1] and the references therein), one can prove that there is no incoming null component of the boundary arising from $i^{+}.$ Thus, the boundary of the quotient spacetime is given by:

$$ \partial\mathcal{Q}=C_{0}^{+}\cup\mathcal{I}\cup i^{+}\cup\mathcal{B}\cup\mathcal{B}_{0}\cup b_{\Gamma}\cup\Gamma, $$

and we point out that some of the boundary components might be empty.

#### The decomposition of the moduli space $\mathfrak{M}$ .

We note that $\big(\mathcal{M},g\big)$ is a black hole spacetime if and only if $\mathcal{B}\neq\emptyset$ . We define66 6 In defining the subsets of $\mathfrak{M}$ , we follow the notation convention of [2]. the corresponding subset of the moduli space by:

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}=\big\{\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}:\ \mathcal{B}\neq\emptyset\big\}. $$

Equivalently, $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}$ if and only if $\mathcal{T}\neq\emptyset.$ The latter is an open condition, so $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}$ is open.

We can classify black hole spacetimes depending on the nature of the singularity inside the black hole region. In the case when $\mathcal{B}\neq\emptyset$ and $\mathcal{B}_{0}=\emptyset$ , the singularity is spacelike-only and the spacetime has the Penrose diagram in Figure 1a). We denote the corresponding subset of the moduli space by:

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}=\big\{\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}:\ \mathcal{B}\neq\emptyset,\ \mathcal{B}_{0}=\emptyset\big\}. $$

We also have the case when $\mathcal{B}\neq\emptyset$ and $\mathcal{B}_{0}\neq\emptyset,$ so the spacetime has the Penrose diagram in Figure 1b). We denote the corresponding subset of the moduli space by:

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{loc.naked}}=\big\{\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}:\ \mathcal{B}\neq\emptyset,\ \mathcal{B}_{0}\neq\emptyset\big\}. $$

The superscript stands for locally naked, which we define below in (2.41). Our discussion shows that $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}$ can be written as the disjoint union77 7 We note that the results of Section 6 and [19] can be used to show that $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{loc.naked}}\neq\emptyset$ and $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}\neq\emptyset$ . $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}=\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{loc.naked}}.$

Next, we have the case $\mathcal{B}=\emptyset$ and $\mathcal{B}_{0}=\emptyset$ . As a result, we must have $b_{\Gamma}=i^{+}$ and the spacetime has the Penrose diagram in Figure 1c). We say that such solutions are non-collapsing, and we define the corresponding subset of the moduli space as:

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}=\big\{\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}:\ \mathcal{B}=\emptyset,\ \mathcal{B}_{0}=\emptyset\big\}. $$

We note that Corollary 1.2 implies that $\mathrm{int}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\big)\neq\emptyset.$ Using the monotonicity properties of the system and a "zig-zag" argument as in [32, Section 3], one can prove that $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}$ implies $\mathcal{I}$ is future complete and that $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}$ if and only if $\Gamma$ is future complete.

In the case when $\mathcal{B}=\emptyset$ and $\mathcal{B}_{0}\neq\emptyset$ , the spacetime has the Penrose diagram as in Figure 1d). We say that such solutions are naked singularities and we define the corresponding subset of the moduli space as:

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}=\big\{\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}:\ \mathcal{B}=\emptyset,\ \mathcal{B}_{0}\neq\emptyset\big\}. $$

Finally, we say that a spacetime is a locally naked singularity spacetime if it satisfies $\mathcal{B}_{0}\neq\emptyset.$ We denote the corresponding subset of the moduli space as:

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}=\big\{\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}:\ \mathcal{B}_{0}\neq\emptyset\big\}. $$

Equivalently, these are spacetimes with no trapped surfaces in a neighborhood of $b_{\Gamma}$ (this follows from Lemma 2.1 and Proposition 2.3). We note that the results of [19] imply that $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}\neq\emptyset.$ Moreover, we can write $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}$ as the disjoint union:

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}=\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{loc.naked}}. $$

In conclusion, our discussion shows that the moduli space of initial data can be written as the following disjoint unions:

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{M} \displaystyle=\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}=\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}} \displaystyle=\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{loc.naked}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\sqcup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}. $$

#### Remark 2.3.

We recall that [27, 15] define naked singularity spacetimes as having a future incomplete $\mathcal{I}$ . We claim that this is a more restrictive notion than our definition of naked singularities. We define the following subset of the moduli space:

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{incomplete}}=\big\{\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}:\ \mathcal{I}\text{ is future incomplete}\big\}. $$

As explained above, the maximal developments of data in $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}$ have a future complete $\mathcal{I}$ . Moreover, according to Proposition 2.5, black hole spacetimes have a future complete $\mathcal{I}$ . Therefore, (2.43) implies that $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{incomplete}}\subset\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}$ , so all spacetimes with a future incomplete $\mathcal{I}$ are naked singularities. We point out that, in principle, this inclusion could be strict. For example, a similar argument to [24] implies that any naked singularity spacetime with $r$ uniformly bounded on $\mathcal{B}_{0}$ has a future complete $\mathcal{I}$ .

## 3 The mass gap

The goal of this section is to establish the mass gap property. More concretely, we prove that no singularities can form in the domain of dependence of a disk bounded by a circle with Hawking mass strictly less than 1. We recall the statement of Theorem 1.2: See 1.2

We first claim that $m\leq 1-\delta$ in the domain of dependence of $C_{0}^{+}\cap\{v\leq v_{0}\}.$ We suppose there exists $p\in\mathcal{Q}$ in the domain of dependence of $C_{0}^{+}\cap\{v\leq v_{0}\},$ which satisfies $p\in\mathcal{A}$ and $J^{-}(p)\backslash\{p\}\subset\mathcal{R}$ . Lemma 2.1 implies $m(p)\leq 1-\delta$ , so Lemma 2.2 implies that $p\in\mathcal{R},$ a contradiction. As a consequence, the domain of dependence of $C_{0}^{+}\cap\{v\leq v_{0}\}$ is contained in the regular region $\mathcal{R}$ and $m\leq 1-\delta$ .

The proof of Theorem 1.2 is by contradiction. According to Corollary 2.1, any first singularities in the boundary of the domain of dependence of $C_{0}^{+}\cap\{v\leq v_{0}\}$ must occur at the center. For the rest of the section, we work under the following assumption:

#### Assumption 3.1.

We assume that for some $v_{\Gamma}<v_{*}\leq v_{0},$ the future ingoing null cone:

$$ C_{*}^{-}=\Big\{(u,v_{*}):\ u_{0}\leq u<u_{*},\ r(u_{*},v_{*})=0\Big\} $$

starting at $(u_{0},v_{*})$ ends in a first singularity at the center at $(u_{*},v_{*})\in\overline{\Gamma}\backslash\Gamma.$ Also, we denote $r_{*}=r(u_{0},v_{*}).$

The idea of the proof is to establish uniform $C^{k}$ estimates in the domain:

$$ \mathcal{D}=\Big\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{Q}:\ u_{0}\leq u<u_{*},\ v\leq v_{*}\Big\}, $$

which will contradict Assumption 3.1 by Proposition 2.1. We follow the strategy outlined in Section 1.3.1.

Since the domain of dependence of $C_{0}^{+}\cap\{v\leq v_{0}\}$ is contained in $\mathcal{R},$ the Bondi coordinates $(u,r)$ are defined globally in $\mathcal{D}.$ It is convenient for the purpose of this section to change coordinates from the double null coordinates $(u,v)$ to the Bondi coordinates $(u,r)$ , which we introduce in detail in Section 3.1.

We outline the structure of the section. In Section 3.1, we introduce Bondi coordinates. In Section 3.2, we prove bounds on certain geometric quantities. In Section 3.3, we prove preliminary estimates for the scalar field. In Section 3.4, we establish improved estimates for the scalar field. Finally, in Section 3.5, we complete the proof of Theorem 1.2.

### 3.1 Bondi coordinates

We make the change of coordinates $(u,v)\rightarrow\big(u,r(u,v)\big)$ from double null coordinates to Bondi coordinates. In Bondi coordinates $(u,r)$ , the metric (2.1) takes the form:

$$ g=-e^{2\nu}du^{2}-2e^{\nu+\lambda}dudr+r^{2}d\theta^{2}. $$

The unknowns in Bondi coordinates are given by the functions $\big(\nu,\lambda,\phi\big).$ We also define the quantity $\overline{\gamma}=e^{\nu-\lambda}.$ The relation between the double null unknowns $\big(r,\Omega,\phi\big)$ and the Bondi unknowns is:

$$ \gamma=2e^{\nu+\lambda},\ -2\partial_{u}r=\overline{\gamma}=e^{\nu-\lambda}, $$

where we recall that $\gamma$ was defined in (2.11) as $\gamma^{-1}=\Omega^{-2}\partial_{v}r.$ Therefore, we can regard $\big(\gamma,\overline{\gamma},\phi\big)$ as the unknowns in Bondi coordinates.

In Bondi coordinates, the Hawking mass (1.10) takes the following form:

$$ m=1-2\cdot\frac{\overline{\gamma}}{\gamma}-\Lambda r^{2}=1-e^{-2\lambda}-\Lambda r^{2}. $$

We fix the freedom to rescale the $u$ coordinate by setting $\nu=0$ on $\Gamma.$ Since $m=0$ on $\Gamma,$ we also have that $\lambda=0$ on $\Gamma,$ so we also get $\gamma=2,\ \overline{\gamma}=1$ on $\Gamma.$

We notice that $\partial_{r}$ is a future directed outgoing null vector. We then define the future directed ingoing null vector:

$$ n=\partial_{u}-\frac{1}{2}\overline{\gamma}\partial_{r}. $$

The system of equations (2.2)-(2.6) is equivalent to:

$$ \displaystyle 2\partial_{u}\partial_{r}\phi+\frac{1}{r}\partial_{u}\phi-\frac{1}{r}\partial_{r}\big(r\overline{\gamma}\partial_{r}\phi\big)=0 \displaystyle\partial_{r}\log\gamma=r\big(\partial_{r}\phi\big)^{2} \displaystyle\partial_{r}\log\overline{\gamma}=-2r\Lambda e^{2\lambda} \displaystyle nm=-4r\gamma^{-1}\big(n\phi\big)^{2} \displaystyle\partial_{r}m=re^{-2\lambda}\big(\partial_{r}\phi\big)^{2}. $$
