$$ |u|^{-1}e^{-2\mathbf{b}(u)}\big|\widetilde{r\gamma}\big|^{2}(u,v)\lesssim\lambda^{2}v^{2n+1}+\lambda^{2}v^{2n+\frac{3}{2}}|u|^{2}\gamma(u,0). $$

We integrate (6.41), using (5.4) and (6.2). We plug this bound into (6.39), together with (6.40), to conclude that $III$ is bounded by the RHS of (6.37). This completes the proof of (6.37). ∎

### 6.2 Proof of Proposition 6.1

In this section, we complete the proof of Proposition 6.1. The main role is played by the curve $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}$ :

$$ \mathcal{C}_{\lambda}=\Big\{\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big):\ u\in[u_{0},0),\ v_{\sharp}(u)>0,\ |\lambda|\big[v_{\sharp}(u)\big]^{n}=e^{-\mathbf{b}(u)}|u|^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{10n}}\sqrt{\gamma(u,0)}\Big\}, $$

represented schematically in Figure 3. Below, we shall see that the blueshift instability drives the growth of certain quantities and allows us to apply the formation of trapped surfaces criterion in Theorem 1.3 for points on $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}.$

We first show that the curve $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}$ is indeed contained in the domain $\mathcal{P}_{\lambda},$ for which we proved quantitative estimates in Proposition 6.2.

#### Lemma 6.3.

The curve $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}$ converges to $b_{\Gamma}=(0,0)$ as $u\rightarrow 0$ . Moreover, for all $|u|$ small enough, $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}$ is contained in the region $\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}$ defined in Proposition 6.2.

#### Proof.

The curve $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}$ converges to $b_{\Gamma}=(0,0)$ as $u\rightarrow 0$ since:

$$ |\lambda|\big[v_{\sharp}(u)\big]^{n}=e^{-\mathbf{b}(u)}|u|^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{10n}}\sqrt{\gamma(u,0)}\leq 2\Omega(u_{0},0)\cdot e^{-\mathbf{b}(u)/2}|u|^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{10n}}\leq 2\Omega(u_{0},0)\cdot|u|^{\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{10n}}|u_{0}|^{-1}. $$

The same bound also implies that for $|u|$ small enough we get $v_{\sharp}(u)\leq\min\big(v_{0}^{\prime},\lambda^{4},|u|^{\frac{1}{n}}\big).$ In order to check the next condition in the definition of $\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}$ in (6.2), we notice that for all $|u|$ small enough:

$$ \displaystyle|\lambda|\big[v_{\sharp}(u)\big]^{n+\frac{1}{4}} \displaystyle=\big[v_{\sharp}(u)\big]^{\frac{1}{4}}\cdot e^{-\mathbf{b}(u)}|u|^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{10n}}\sqrt{\gamma(u,0)} \displaystyle\leq e^{-\mathbf{b}(u)}|u|^{\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4n}-\frac{1}{10n}}\sqrt{\gamma(u,0)}\leq e^{-\mathbf{b}(u)}|u|^{\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{10n}}\sqrt{\gamma(u,0)}, $$

so the second condition in (6.2) holds as well. Finally, for the third condition in (6.2), we compute that:

$$ \displaystyle\big[v_{\sharp}(u)\big]^{\frac{1}{10n}}\cdot\mathbf{s}(u) \displaystyle=|\lambda|^{-\frac{1}{10n^{2}}}e^{-\frac{\mathbf{b}(u)}{10n^{2}}}|u|^{\frac{1}{20n^{2}}-\frac{1}{100n^{3}}}\big[\gamma(u,0)\big]^{\frac{1}{20n^{2}}}\cdot\mathbf{s}(u) \displaystyle\lesssim|\lambda|^{-\frac{1}{10n^{2}}}|u_{0}|\cdot\big[\Omega^{2}(u_{0},0)\big]^{\frac{1}{20n^{2}}}\cdot e^{-\frac{\mathbf{b}(u)}{20n^{2}}}\mathbf{b}(u)\cdot|u|^{\frac{1}{20n^{2}}-\frac{1}{100n^{3}}}\rightarrow 0\text{ as }u\rightarrow 0, $$

where we used the fact that $\mathbf{s}(u)\leq|u_{0}|\mathbf{b}(u)$ and $\mathbf{b}(u)\rightarrow\infty$ as $u\rightarrow 0.$ This implies that $\big[v_{\sharp}(u)\big]^{\frac{1}{10n}}\cdot\mathbf{s}(u)\lesssim\epsilon^{\prime}$ for all $|u|$ sufficiently small, so the curve $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}$ is contained in the region $\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}$ for $|u|$ small enough. ∎

We now have all the necessary ingredients to complete the proof of Proposition 6.1, establishing the instability of locally naked singularity spacetimes to trapped surface formation arbitrarily close to $b_{\Gamma}$ :

#### Proof of Proposition 6.1.

According to Lemma 6.3, the curve $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}$ is contained in the region $\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}$ for all $|u|$ small enough. Thus, we fix $u_{\mathcal{C}}\in(u_{0},0)$ such that $\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)\in\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}$ for all $u\in[u_{\mathcal{C}},0).$

Our goal is to use Theorem 1.3. Firstly, we have by (6.3) that for any $u\in[u_{\mathcal{C}},0):$

$$ \delta_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)=\frac{r_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)}{r_{\lambda}(u,0)}-1\lesssim v_{\sharp}(u)|u|^{-1}e^{-\mathbf{b}(u)}. $$

Next, we want to obtain a lower bound for $\eta_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big).$ We use (6.1), (6.12), (6.6), and (5.11) to get that for $u\in[u_{\mathcal{C}},0):$

$$ \displaystyle\lambda^{2}\big[v_{\sharp}(u)\big]^{2n+1}e^{2\mathbf{b}(u)} \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{0}^{v_{\sharp}(u)}\Big|e^{\mathbf{b}_{\lambda}(u,v^{\prime})}\widetilde{\theta}(u_{0},v^{\prime})\Big|^{2}dv^{\prime} \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{0}^{v_{\sharp}(u)}\big|\widetilde{\theta}(u,v^{\prime})\big|^{2}dv^{\prime}+\int_{0}^{v_{\sharp}(u)}\Big|\widetilde{\theta}(u,v^{\prime})-e^{\mathbf{b}_{\lambda}(u,v^{\prime})}\widetilde{\theta}(u_{0},v^{\prime})\Big|^{2}dv^{\prime} \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{0}^{v_{\sharp}(u)}\big|\theta_{\lambda}(u,v^{\prime})\big|^{2}dv^{\prime}+\int_{0}^{v_{\sharp}(u)}\big|\theta(u,v^{\prime})\big|^{2}dv^{\prime}+\lambda^{2}v^{2n+\frac{4}{3}}e^{2\mathbf{b}(u)} \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{0}^{v_{\sharp}(u)}\big|\theta_{\lambda}(u,v^{\prime})\big|^{2}dv^{\prime}+v_{\sharp}(u)\cdot|u|\gamma(u,0)+\lambda^{2}\big[v_{\sharp}(u)\big]^{2n+\frac{4}{3}}e^{2\mathbf{b}(u)}. $$

By the construction of $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda},$ we have that $v_{\sharp}(u)\cdot|u|\gamma(u,0)=\lambda^{2}\big[v_{\sharp}(u)\big]^{2n+1}e^{2\mathbf{b}(u)}\cdot|u|^{\frac{1}{5n}}$ . As a result, there exists $u_{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime}\in[u_{\mathcal{C}},0)$ such that for all $u\in[u_{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime},0):$

$$ \int_{0}^{v_{\sharp}(u)}\big|\theta_{\lambda}(u,v^{\prime})\big|^{2}dv^{\prime}\gtrsim\lambda^{2}\big[v_{\sharp}(u)\big]^{2n+1}e^{2\mathbf{b}(u)}. $$

This lower bound confirms our expectation that the leading order term in $\theta_{\lambda}$ comes from the amplification of the initial data perturbation $\lambda v^{n}$ by the blueshift $e^{\mathbf{b}(u)}.$

We use (2.8) and (6.44) to derive a lower bound for $\eta_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)$ for any $u\in[u_{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime},0):$

$$ \displaystyle\eta_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big) \displaystyle=\frac{m_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)-m_{\lambda}(u,0)}{|\Lambda|r_{\lambda}^{2}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)}\gtrsim|u|^{-2}\int_{0}^{v_{\sharp}(u)}\gamma_{\lambda}^{-1}|\partial_{u}r_{\lambda}|\theta_{\lambda}^{2}\partial_{v}r_{\lambda}(u,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime} \displaystyle\gtrsim|u|^{-2}e^{-\mathbf{b}(u)}\gamma^{-1}(u,0)\int_{0}^{v_{\sharp}(u)}\big|\theta_{\lambda}(u,v^{\prime})\big|^{2}dv^{\prime}\gtrsim\lambda^{2}\big[v_{\sharp}(u)\big]^{2n+1}|u|^{-2}e^{\mathbf{b}(u)}\gamma^{-1}(u,0). $$

According to the definition of $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}$ we further have that for all $u\in[u_{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime},0):$

$$ \eta_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)\gtrsim v_{\sharp}(u)|u|^{-1-\frac{1}{5n}}e^{-\mathbf{b}(u)}. $$

Combining (6.43) and (6.45), we get that there exists $u_{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime\prime}\in[u_{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime},0)$ such that for all $u\in[u_{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime\prime},0)$ we have $\eta_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)>\delta_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)$ and $\delta_{\lambda}\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big)>0$ is sufficiently small as required in Theorem 1.3. Thus, the trapped surface formation criterion in Theorem 1.3 implies that for all $u\in[u_{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime\prime},0)$ a trapped surface forms on the ingoing cone $\big\{v=v_{\sharp}(u)\big\}$ to the future of $\big(u,v_{\sharp}(u)\big).$ ∎

## 7 Proof of Theorem 1.1

We combine the results in Section 2, Section 6, and Appendix A, to complete the proof of Theorem 1.1, establishing the weak cosmic censorship conjecture for circularly symmetric solutions of (1.1):

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1.

The most important part of the proof is showing (1.9):

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}\subset\mathrm{cl}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}\big)\backslash\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}, $$

establishing the fact that all locally naked singularities are unstable to the formation of spacelike-only singularities.

In order to prove (7.1), we consider any $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}.$ For any $\epsilon>0,$ we prove that there exists $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}$ such that:

$$ d_{X([0,\infty))}\big(\mathfrak{D},\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}\big)<\epsilon. $$

We denote by $\big(\mathcal{M},g,\phi\big)$ the maximal globally hyperbolic development of the asymptotically AdS characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}$ on the initial outgoing null cone $C_{0}^{+}.$ Since $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}},$ we have by definition that the solution has a first singularity $b_{\Gamma}$ at the center $\Gamma.$ We denote by $C_{0}^{-}$ the ingoing null cone that ends at $b_{\Gamma}$ . By global hyperbolicity, we have that either $C_{0}^{-}\cap C_{0}^{+}\neq\emptyset$ or $C_{0}^{-}$ has a limit endpoint on $\mathcal{I}.$ If the latter holds, we fix an outgoing null cone $C_{1}^{+}$ such that $C_{0}^{-}\cap C_{1}^{+}\neq\emptyset$ and $\overline{C_{1}^{+}}\cap\mathcal{I}\neq\emptyset$ . On the other hand, if we already have $C_{0}^{-}\cap C_{0}^{+}\neq\emptyset$ , we simply apply the argument below for $C_{1}^{+}=C_{0}^{+}.$

We denote by $\mathfrak{D}_{*}$ the asymptotically AdS characteristic data set induced by $\big(\mathcal{M},g,\phi\big)$ on $C_{1}^{+}$ . We note that we can also apply the results in Section 2.3 and Section 2.4 towards the past. By Cauchy stability, there exists $\delta>0$ such that for any asymptotically AdS characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}_{*}^{\prime}$ on $C_{1}^{+}$ which satisfies:

$$ d_{X([0,\infty))}\big(\mathfrak{D}_{*},\mathfrak{D}_{*}^{\prime}\big)<\delta, $$

the maximal globally hyperbolic (past) development of $\mathfrak{D}_{*}^{\prime}$ induces an asymptotically AdS characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ on $C_{0}^{+}$ which satisfies $d_{X([0,\infty))}\big(\mathfrak{D},\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}\big)<\epsilon.$

In view of the above argument, to prove (7.2) it suffices to show that for any $\delta>0$ there exists $\mathfrak{D}_{*}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}$ satisfying (7.3). The strategy is to use the results in Section 6 to construct locally a perturbation of $\mathfrak{D}_{*}$ which in evolution forms trapped surfaces arbitrarily close to $b_{\Gamma}$ , and then extend this to a global perturbation of $\mathfrak{D}_{*}$ using the results in Appendix A.

In order to use the results in Section 6, we choose double null coordinates $(u,v)$ on $\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{M}/U(1),$ such that:

$$ b_{\Gamma}=(0,0),\ C_{0}^{-}=\big\{v=0,\ 2r=-u\big\},\ C_{1}^{+}=\big\{u=u_{1},\ 2r=v-u_{1}\big\}. $$

Let $n>k+1$ be an integer. We fix $R_{0}>0$ large enough depending on $\mathfrak{D}_{*}$ and $k$ , as required in Proposition A.1, and we set $v_{1}=2R_{0}+u_{1}.$ We carry out the construction in Section 6. For any $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\backslash\{0\},$ we define characteristic data as in (6.1), which determines uniquely on $\big\{u=u_{1},\ v\in[u_{1},v_{1}]\big\}$ a $C^{k}$ characteristic partial data set $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}$ , as in Definition A.1, which coincides with $\mathfrak{D}_{*}$ for $\big\{u=u_{1},\ v\in[u_{1},0]\big\}.$

We want to apply Proposition A.1 to extend $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}$ to $C_{1}^{+}$ as a small perturbation of $\mathfrak{D}_{*}.$ We point out that this is a nontrivial difficulty that is not present in the asymptotically flat setting. We denote by $C_{0}>0$ the constant in Proposition A.1, which depends only on $\mathfrak{D}_{*},R_{0}$ and $k.$ We choose $\varepsilon>0$ to be small enough in terms of $\mathfrak{D}_{*},R_{0},$ and $k,$ as required in Proposition A.1, and to satisfy $C_{0}\varepsilon<\delta.$

By uniform continuity in $\lambda$ on $[0,R_{0}],$ there exists $\lambda\neq 0$ sufficiently small, such that:

$$ d_{X([0,R_{0}])}\big(\mathfrak{D}_{*},\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}\big)<\varepsilon. $$

We apply Proposition A.1 with $r_{0}=R_{0}.$ We get that $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}$ can be extended as a $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data set on $C_{1}^{+}$ such that:

$$ d_{X([0,\infty))}\big(\mathfrak{D}_{*},\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}\big)<C_{0}\varepsilon<\delta. $$

We relabel the extended characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}_{\lambda}$ by $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}_{*},$ so $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}_{*}$ satisfies (7.3). According to our construction, Proposition 6.1 implies that the maximal globally hyperbolic development of $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}_{*}$ contains trapped surfaces arbitrarily close to $b_{\Gamma}$ , so $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}_{*}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}.$ This completes the proof of (7.1).

We define $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{generic}}=\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}\sqcup\mathrm{int}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\big).$ According to (2.42), (2.43), and (7.1), we have that (1.8) holds. To complete the proof of Theorem 1.1, we show that $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{generic}}$ is open and dense in $\mathfrak{M}$ . According to Section 2.4, $\mathfrak{D}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}$ if and only if $\mathcal{T}\neq\emptyset.$ By Cauchy stability, having trapped surfaces is an open condition, so $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}$ is open. Since $\mathrm{int}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\big)$ is open by definition, we get that $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{generic}}$ is open in $\mathfrak{M}.$ Finally, we prove that $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{generic}}$ is dense in $\mathfrak{M}$ by showing that $\mathrm{cl}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{generic}}\big)=\mathfrak{M}.$ By the definition of $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{generic}}$ , we have that $\mathrm{cl}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{generic}}\big)=\mathrm{cl}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}\big)\cup\mathrm{cl}\big(\mathrm{int}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\big)\big).$ Then, (1.8) implies that:

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}\cup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}\cup\mathrm{int}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\big)\subset\mathrm{cl}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{generic}}\big). $$

This equation and (2.43) also imply that:

$$ \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\backslash\mathrm{int}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\big)\subset\mathrm{cl}\big(\mathfrak{M}\backslash\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{non}}\big)=\mathrm{cl}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{naked}}\cup\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}\big)\subset\mathrm{cl}\big(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{generic}}\big), $$

so we conclude that $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{generic}}$ is dense in $\mathfrak{M}$ , completing the proof of Theorem 1.1. ∎

#### Remark 7.1.

Since (1.9) shows that locally naked singularities are unstable to the formation of spacelike-only singularities, one might wonder whether $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{loc.naked}}$ is non-generic as well. However, it is not clear if $\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{black}}^{\mathrm{spacelike}}$ is open or if it even has a nonempty interior.

## Appendix A Appendix

The goal of this section is to prove that local perturbations at the level of initial data can be extended to global perturbations. While this is straightforward for asymptotically flat characteristic data, the proof in the case of asymptotically AdS characteristic data is more involved due to the timelike asymptotic boundary $\mathcal{I}.$

We first define the notion of a characteristic partial data set:

#### Definition A.1.

Let $k\geq 2$ . For any $r_{0}>0,$ we say that the tuple of functions on $[0,r_{0}]$ :

$$ \mathfrak{D}=\big(r,\ldots,\partial_{U}^{k+1}r,\Omega,\ldots,\partial_{U}^{k}\Omega,m,\ldots,\partial_{U}^{k}m,\phi,\ldots,\partial_{U}^{k}\phi,\mathcal{T}\phi,\ldots,\mathcal{T}^{k}\phi\big) $$

represents a $C^{k}$ characteristic partial data set if it satisfies conditions $1.$ to $4.$ in Definition 2.6 on the interval $\{r\in[0,r_{0}]\}$ .

In this section, we establish the following extension result for characteristic partial data sets, which plays a key role in the proof of Theorem 1.1 in Section 7.

#### Proposition A.1.

Let $k\geq 2$ and let $\mathfrak{D}$ be a $C^{k}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data set. There exists $R_{0}>0$ large enough (depending on $\mathfrak{D},\Lambda,$ and $k$ ), such that for any $r_{0}\geq R_{0}$ and any $\varepsilon>0$ sufficiently small in terms of $\mathfrak{D},r_{0},\Lambda,$ and $k$ , the following holds: any $C^{k}$ characteristic partial data set on $[0,r_{0}]$ :

$$ \underline{\mathfrak{D}}=\big(\underline{r},\ldots,\underline{\partial_{U}^{k+1}r},\underline{\Omega},\ldots,\underline{\partial_{U}^{k}\Omega},\underline{m},\ldots,\underline{\partial_{U}^{k}m},\underline{\phi},\ldots,\underline{\partial_{U}^{k}\phi},\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi},\ldots,\underline{\mathcal{T}^{k}\phi}\big), $$

which satisfies:

$$ d_{X([0,r_{0}])}\big(\mathfrak{D},\underline{\mathfrak{D}}\big)<\varepsilon, $$

can be extended to an asymptotically AdS characteristic data set on $[0,\infty)$ such that:

$$ d_{X([0,\infty))}\big(\mathfrak{D},\underline{\mathfrak{D}}\big)<C_{0}\varepsilon, $$

where the constant $C_{0}>0$ depends only on $\mathfrak{D},r_{0},\Lambda,$ and $k$ .

#### Remark A.1.

We briefly explain the connection of Proposition A.1 to the characteristic gluing literature. The problem of characteristic gluing consists of constructing characteristic data on a truncated null hypersurface connecting prescribed data on two codimension-2 spheres. This was initiated in the series of works [3, 4, 5] for the Einstein vacuum equations in a perturbative regime around Minkowski space, up to linear obstructions (see also [17] for the non-vanishing cosmological constant case). These results were later extended to the obstruction-free case in [20]. More recently, the works [35, 34] proved non-perturbative characteristic gluing results. Proposition A.1 can be interpreted as a characteristic gluing result, in the sense that we glue a characteristic partial data set $\underline{\mathfrak{D}}$ to an asymptotic BTZ sphere at $\mathcal{I}.$ We note that our result is perturbative around any given asymptotically AdS characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}$ . Moreover, we expect that our methods can also be used to prove that $\underline{\mathfrak{D}}$ can be glued to a finite BTZ sphere. We also note that in contrast to the characteristic gluing results referenced above, which prescribe seed data at zeroth-order, we prescribe data at the level of the top-order transversal derivative of $\phi.$

We prove this result for the rest of the section. For the sake of exposition, we restrict to the case $k=2$ for the proof, as it is clear that our methods can be adapted to the general case as explained in Remark A.4. We briefly outline the idea of the proof and the structure of the Appendix.

The main obstructions to extending $\underline{\mathfrak{D}}$ are given by the compatibility conditions in Definition 2.6 and the global regularity requirements (2.18). In order to enforce the needed compatibility conditions, we want to extend $\underline{\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi}$ to $(r_{0},\infty),$ then compute the remaining components of $\underline{\mathfrak{D}}$ uniquely by solving transport equations with initial data at $r_{0}$ . We set up the system of null constraint equations in Section A.1. We point out that except for the lapse and its derivatives, the elements of $\underline{\mathfrak{D}}$ are independent of the choice of a $V$ coordinate, so we carry out most of the argument using the coordinate $r$ . However, it is clear that not every choice of $\underline{\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi}\in H^{1}((r_{0},\infty))$ will lead to $\underline{\phi}\in H^{3}([0,\infty))$ and $\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}\in H^{2}([0,\infty)).$ For this to hold, we need certain vanishing conditions which guarantee the suitable decay of $\underline{\phi}$ and $\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi},$ which we prove in Section A.2. The idea is that the vanishing conditions hold for $\mathfrak{D},$ so we prove the existence of a suitable $\underline{\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi}$ as a perturbation of $\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi$ using the Implicit Function Theorem. Finally, we prove in Section A.3 that under the vanishing conditions of Section A.2, the smallness bound (A.2) holds.

### A.1 Null constraint equations

In this section, we derive the system of null constraint equations (A.3)-(A.10) satisfied by the elements of a characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}$ and we set up these equations as a system of ODEs (A.11)-(A.20).

We define the renormalized outgoing derivative:

$$ \partial_{r}=\frac{\partial_{V}}{\partial_{V}r}, $$

which is independent of the choice of the outgoing coordinate $V.$ We recall the definition of $\gamma$ in (2.11) and we express the Kodama vector field $\mathcal{T}$ defined in (2.20) as:

$$ \mathcal{T}=\Omega^{-2}\partial_{V}r\partial_{U}-\Omega^{-2}\partial_{U}r\partial_{V}=\frac{1}{\gamma}\partial_{U}-\frac{1}{\gamma}\partial_{U}r\partial_{r}. $$

Firstly, we notice that equations (2.2), (2.6), and (2.3) are equivalent to:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{r}\theta+\bigg(\frac{1}{2r}+\frac{\Lambda\gamma r}{2\partial_{U}r}\bigg)\theta= \displaystyle\frac{\partial_{r}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T\phi}\big)}{-\partial_{U}r} \displaystyle\partial_{r}\log\gamma= \displaystyle\theta^{2} \displaystyle\partial_{r}\partial_{U}r= \displaystyle\frac{\Lambda}{2}\gamma r. $$

In order to derive the higher order equations, we compute the following commutation relation:

$$ \big[\mathcal{T},\partial_{r}\big]=\bigg[\mathcal{T},\frac{\partial_{V}}{\partial_{V}r}\bigg]=\theta^{2}\mathcal{T}. $$

Commuting equations (A.3)-(A.5) with $\mathcal{T},$ we obtain the equations:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}\theta+\bigg(\frac{1}{2r}+\frac{\Lambda\gamma r}{2\partial_{U}r}+\theta^{2}\bigg)\mathcal{T}\theta= \displaystyle\frac{\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi\big)}{-\partial_{U}r}+\frac{\theta^{2}\mathcal{T}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi\big)}{-\partial_{U}r}+\frac{\mathcal{T}\partial_{U}r\cdot\partial_{r}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T\phi}\big)}{(\partial_{U}r)^{2}} \displaystyle+\frac{\Lambda}{2}r\theta\frac{\mathcal{T}\gamma}{-\partial_{U}r}+\frac{\Lambda}{2}r\theta\frac{\gamma\mathcal{T}\partial_{U}r}{(\partial_{U}r)^{2}}, \displaystyle\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}\gamma= \displaystyle 2\gamma\theta\mathcal{T}\theta, \displaystyle\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}\partial_{U}r= \displaystyle-\theta^{2}\mathcal{T}\partial_{U}r+\frac{\Lambda}{2}r\mathcal{T}\gamma. $$

Moreover, we also compute that:

$$ \partial_{r}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T\phi}\big)=\gamma\mathcal{T}\theta+\frac{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}{2\sqrt{r}},\ \partial_{r}\big(\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi\big)=\frac{\gamma\mathcal{T}\theta}{\sqrt{r}}. $$

We refer to equations (A.3)-(A.10) as the null constraint equations. We note that one can derive equations with similar structure for any order $k\geq 2,$ see Remark A.4.

#### Remark A.2.

Given a tuple $\mathfrak{D}$ at $r_{0},$ solutions of the null constraint equations on $[r_{0},\infty)$ determine the tuple $\mathfrak{D}$ uniquely on $[r_{0},\infty)$ (up to the choice of a coordinate $V$ ); moreover, the elements of $\mathfrak{D}$ satisfy the compatibility conditions in Definition 2.6. To see this, we note that equations (A.3)-(A.5) imply (2.2), (2.3), and (2.6). Also, equations (A.3)-(A.5), (A.8), and (A.10) imply (2.4), while using (A.9) as well we obtain (2.5). At higher order, we notice that (A.7) implies the equation obtained by taking a $\partial_{U}$ derivative of (2.2). Finally, the quantities $\partial_{U}^{2}\Omega$ and $\partial_{U}^{3}r$ are not computed directly from the solutions of the null constraints, so we define them using the equations obtained by taking a $\partial_{U}$ derivative of (2.4) and (2.5).

In view of Remark A.2, the goal in Proposition A.1 is to construct solutions of the null constraint equations (A.3)-(A.10) on $(r_{0},\infty).$ We notice that all the quantities are determined at $r_{0}$ by the partial data set on $[0,r_{0}]$ . Moreover, the only quantity that appears on the RHS in (A.3)-(A.10) but does not satisfy a $\partial_{r}$ equation itself is the top order quantity $\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi\big).$ Thus, in order to construct solutions of the null constraint equations, we prescribe $\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi\big)$ on $(r_{0},\infty)$ and solve equations (A.3)-(A.10) as a system of ODEs with initial data at $r_{0}.$

Our discussion motivates us to study separately the following system of ODEs:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{r}A_{1}+\bigg(\frac{1}{2r}+\frac{\Lambda B_{0}r}{2D_{0}}+A_{0}^{2}\bigg)A_{1}= \displaystyle\frac{F_{1}}{-D_{0}}+\frac{A_{0}^{2}P_{2}}{-D_{0}}+\frac{D_{1}F_{0}}{D_{0}^{2}} \displaystyle+\frac{\Lambda}{2}r\frac{A_{0}B_{1}}{-D_{0}}+\frac{\Lambda}{2}r\frac{A_{0}B_{0}D_{1}}{D_{0}^{2}}, \displaystyle\partial_{r}B_{1}= \displaystyle 2B_{0}A_{0}A_{1}, \displaystyle\partial_{r}D_{1}= \displaystyle-A_{0}^{2}D_{1}+\frac{\Lambda}{2}rB_{1}, \displaystyle\partial_{r}P_{2}= \displaystyle F_{1}, \displaystyle\partial_{r}A_{0}+\bigg(\frac{1}{2r}+\frac{\Lambda B_{0}r}{2D_{0}}\bigg)A_{0}= \displaystyle\frac{F_{0}}{-D_{0}}, \displaystyle F_{0}= \displaystyle B_{0}A_{1}+\frac{P_{1}}{2\sqrt{r}}, \displaystyle\partial_{r}B_{0}= \displaystyle A_{0}^{2}B_{0}, \displaystyle\partial_{r}D_{0}= \displaystyle\frac{\Lambda}{2}B_{0}r, \displaystyle\partial_{r}P_{1}= \displaystyle\frac{B_{0}A_{1}}{\sqrt{r}}, \displaystyle A_{i}(r_{0})=a_{i},\ B_{i}(r_{0})=b_{i},\ D_{i}(r_{0})= \displaystyle d_{i},\ P_{i+1}(r_{0})=p_{i+1},\ i=0,1. $$

We study the system (A.11)-(A.20) in detail in Section A.2. We also point out that the null constraint equations (A.3)-(A.10) are equivalent to the system (A.11)-(A.20) for:

$$ A_{0}=\theta,A_{1}=\mathcal{T}\theta,B_{0}=\gamma,B_{1}=\mathcal{T}\gamma,D_{0}=\partial_{U}r,D_{1}=\mathcal{T}\partial_{U}r, $$

$$ P_{1}=\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi,P_{2}=\mathcal{T}(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T\phi}),\ F_{0}=\partial_{r}(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T\phi}),\ F_{1}=\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T\phi}). $$

### A.2 Vanishing conditions

According to Section A.1, the strategy to construct characteristic data sets is to prescribe $\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi\big)$ on $(r_{0},\infty)$ and treat the null constraint equations as a system of ODEs. However, prescribing $\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi\big)$ freely on $(r_{0},\infty)$ will not lead in general to $\phi,\mathcal{T}\phi,$ and $\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi$ decaying sufficiently fast, unless additional vanishing conditions hold. We know these hold for the elements of an asymptotically AdS characteristic data set $\mathfrak{D}.$ More specifically, we have that Definition 2.6 (more specifically, equation (2.18)) and equations (A.3)-(A.10) imply:

$$ \sqrt{r}\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T\phi}\big)\in L^{2}([r_{0},\infty)), $$

$$ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T\phi}\big)dr=-\mathcal{T}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T\phi}\big)(r_{0}),\ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{\gamma\mathcal{T}\theta}{\sqrt{r}}dr=-\gamma\mathcal{T\phi}(r_{0}),\ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{\theta}{\sqrt{r}}dr=-\phi(r_{0}), $$

where we also used the fact that $\mathcal{T}\gamma$ is uniformly bounded due to (A.8) and (2.18).

#### Remark A.3.

One could take an alternative approach and prescribe instead the seed data $\phi$ on $(r_{0},\infty)$ , similarly to the asymptotically flat case of [16], see also Remark 2.1. Using the null constraint equations (A.3)-(A.10), one recovers all the other quantities in the system in terms of $\phi$ . However, the vanishing conditions (A.22) represent nonlinear and non-local constraints for $\phi,$ so we do not expect to be able to express the space of seed data as a vector space. We choose not to pursue this approach, and instead prescribe $\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi\big)$ on $(r_{0},\infty)$ as outlined in our above strategy.

Given an asymptotically AdS data set $\mathfrak{D},$ our goal is to prove that there exists $\partial_{r}\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)$ such that:

$$ \sqrt{r}\partial_{r}\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)\in L^{2}([r_{0},\infty)),\ \big\|\sqrt{r}\partial_{r}\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)-\sqrt{r}\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T\phi}\big)\big\|_{L^{2}([r_{0},\infty))}<C_{0}\varepsilon, $$

$$ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\partial_{r}\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)dr=-\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma}\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)(r_{0}),\ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\theta}}{\sqrt{r}}dr=-\underline{\gamma}\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}(r_{0}),\ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{\underline{\theta}}{\sqrt{r}}dr=-\underline{\phi}(r_{0}), $$

where the constant $C_{0}>0$ is independent of $\varepsilon$ and $\partial_{r}\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)$ .

We prove for the rest of the section the existence of $\partial_{r}\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)$ satisfying (A.23)-(A.24). This requires proving a series of results for the ODE system (A.11)-(A.20). We show that the system (A.11)-(A.20) has global solutions in Lemma A.1, and that the solution map is $C^{1}$ in Lemma A.2. We then prove a non-degeneracy condition in Lemma A.3, which allow us to use the Implicit Function Theorem in Corollary A.1 and conclude the existence of a suitable $\partial_{r}\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)$ in Proposition A.2.

We first define the suitable weighted spaces used in our argument. We fix a constant $M>0$ and a large constant $R_{0}>0$ (to be determined in the course of the proof). For any $r_{0}\geq R_{0},$ we define:

#### Lemma A.2.

The solution map of the system (A.30)-(A.39) given by $\dot{\mathcal{S}}_{(w,F_{1})}:\mathbb{R}^{8}\times TY\rightarrow Z$ :

$$ (\dot{a}_{0},\dot{a}_{1},\dot{b}_{0},\dot{b}_{1},\dot{d}_{0},\dot{d}_{1},\dot{p}_{1},\dot{p}_{2},\dot{F}_{1})\mapsto(\dot{A}_{0},\dot{A}_{1},\dot{B}_{0},\dot{B}_{1},\dot{D}_{0},\dot{D}_{1},\dot{P}_{1},\dot{P}_{2}) $$

We make the notation convention for the purpose of this proof that we write $x\lesssim y$ for any quantities $x,y>0$ if there is a constant $C(\Lambda,M)>0$ such that $x\leq Cy.$ We first have that (A.33) implies the bound:

$$ |\dot{P}_{2}|\leq|\dot{p}_{2}|+r_{0}^{-1/2}\|\dot{F}_{1}\|_{TY}. $$

Similarly to the derivation of (A.27), we integrate the equation (A.34) for $\dot{A}_{0}$ :

$$ \dot{A}_{0}(r)=\frac{\dot{a}_{0}d_{0}\sqrt{r_{0}}}{D_{0}\sqrt{r}}+\frac{1}{-D_{0}\sqrt{r}}\int_{r_{0}}^{r}\sqrt{r^{\prime}}\bigg(\dot{F}_{0}+F_{0}\frac{\dot{D}_{0}}{-D_{0}}+\frac{\Lambda A_{0}\dot{B}_{0}r^{\prime}}{2}+\frac{\Lambda A_{0}B_{0}\dot{D}_{0}r^{\prime}}{-2D_{0}}\bigg)dr^{\prime}. $$

We do not write the estimates in detail here, but we notice that integrating (A.34) and (A.30) implies:

$$ \big|\dot{A}_{0}\big|(r)\lesssim r^{-5/2}\int_{r_{1}}^{r}\sqrt{\tilde{r}}\big|\dot{F_{0}}\big|+\big|\dot{B_{0}}\big|+\tilde{r}^{-2}\big|\dot{D_{0}}\big|d\tilde{r}, $$

$$ \big|\dot{A}_{1}\big|(r)\lesssim r^{-5/2}\int_{r_{1}}^{r}\sum_{i=0}^{1}\bigg[\sqrt{\tilde{r}}\big|\dot{F_{i}}\big|+\big|\dot{B_{i}}\big|+\tilde{r}^{-2}\big|\dot{D_{i}}\big|\bigg]+\tilde{r}^{-5/2}\big|\dot{P_{2}}\big|+\tilde{r}^{3/2}\big|\dot{A_{0}}\big|+\tilde{r}^{-3/2}\big|\dot{D_{0}}F_{1}\big|d\tilde{r}. $$

After the first iteration, we obtain the improved preliminary bounds:

$$ \dot{A}_{0},\dot{A}_{1}\lesssim r^{-3/2},\ \dot{B}_{0},\dot{B}_{1}\lesssim r_{1}^{-2},\ \dot{D}_{0},\dot{D}_{1}\lesssim r_{1}^{-2}r^{2},\ \dot{P}_{1}\lesssim r_{1}^{-1},\ \dot{P}_{2}\lesssim 1,\ \dot{F}_{0}\lesssim r_{1}^{-1}r^{-1/2}. $$

Repeating our argument by starting with (A.45), we further improve to:

$$ \dot{A}_{0}\lesssim r_{1}^{-1}r^{-3/2},\ \dot{A}_{1}\lesssim r_{1}^{-1}r^{-3/2}+\sqrt{r_{1}}r^{-5/2},\ \dot{B}_{0}\lesssim r_{1}^{-3},\ \dot{B}_{1}\lesssim r_{1}^{-5/2}, $$

$$ \dot{D}_{0}\lesssim r_{1}^{-3}r^{2},\ \dot{D}_{1}\lesssim r_{1}^{-5/2}r^{2},\ \dot{P}_{1}\lesssim r_{1}^{-3/2},\ \dot{P}_{2}\lesssim 1,\ \dot{F}_{0}\lesssim r_{1}^{-3/2}r^{-1/2}. $$

Finally, we iterate our argument one last time to obtain the sharp pointwise bounds:

$$ \displaystyle\dot{A}_{0}\lesssim r_{1}^{-3/2}r^{-3/2},\ \dot{A}_{1}\lesssim r_{1}^{-3/2}r^{-3/2}+\sqrt{r_{1}}r^{-5/2},\ \dot{B}_{0}\lesssim r_{1}^{-7/2},\ \dot{B}_{1}\lesssim r_{1}^{-5/2}, \displaystyle\dot{D}_{0}\lesssim r_{1}^{-7/2}r^{2},\ \dot{D}_{1}\lesssim r_{1}^{-5/2}r^{2},\ \dot{P}_{1}\lesssim r_{1}^{-3/2},\ \dot{P}_{2}\lesssim 1,\ \dot{F}_{0}\lesssim r_{1}^{-3/2}r^{-1/2}. $$

We use (A.46)-(A.47) to bound the terms in (A.42) as follows:

$$ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{\big|B_{0}\dot{A}_{1}\big|}{\sqrt{r}}dr\lesssim r_{1}^{-3/2},\ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{\big|\dot{B}_{0}A_{1}\big|}{\sqrt{r}}dr\lesssim r_{1}^{-7/2},\ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{\big|\dot{A}_{0}\big|}{\sqrt{r}}dr\lesssim r_{1}^{-5/2}. $$

We notice that equations (A.42), (A.43), and (A.48) imply that $|\eta_{1}|\lesssim|\eta_{2}|r_{1}^{-3/2}+|\eta_{3}|r_{1}^{-5/2}$ . Since $r_{1}$ can be arbitrarily large, we obtain that $\eta_{1}=0.$

Integrating equation (A.30), we have that:

$$ \dot{A}_{1}(r)=\frac{1}{-D_{0}\sqrt{r}}\int_{r_{1}}^{r}\sqrt{\tilde{r}}\dot{F}_{1}(\tilde{r})d\tilde{r}+O\big(r_{1}^{-3/2}r^{-3/2}\big). $$

We note that the first term on the RHS is non-negative. Using (A.26) and (A.43), we obtain that for $r>r_{1}+1$ :

$$ \dot{A}_{1}(r)\sim\sqrt{r_{1}}r^{-5/2}+O\big(r_{1}^{-3/2}r^{-3/2}\big). $$

Therefore, equations (A.26), (A.48), and (A.49) imply that:

$$ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{B_{0}\dot{A}_{1}+\dot{B}_{0}A_{1}}{\sqrt{r}}dr>\int_{r_{1}+1}^{\infty}\frac{B_{0}\dot{A}_{1}}{\sqrt{r}}dr+O\big(r_{1}^{-5/2}\big)\gtrsim r_{1}^{-3/2}+O\big(r_{1}^{-5/2}\big). $$

We use this estimate in equation (A.42), in order to get that $|\eta_{2}|r_{1}^{-3/2}\lesssim|\eta_{3}|r_{1}^{-5/2}$ . Since $r_{1}$ can be arbitrarily large, we obtain that $\eta_{2}=0.$

Integrating equation (A.38), we have that:

$$ \dot{P}_{1}(r)=\int_{r_{1}}^{r}\frac{B_{0}}{\sqrt{r^{\prime}}}\bigg(\frac{1}{-D_{0}\sqrt{r^{\prime}}}\int_{r_{1}}^{r^{\prime}}\sqrt{\tilde{r}}\dot{F}_{1}(\tilde{r})d\tilde{r}\bigg)dr^{\prime}+O\big(r_{1}^{-5/2}\big). $$

The first term on the RHS is non-negative, and we get that for all $r>2r_{1}:$

$$ \dot{P}_{1}(r)\sim r_{1}^{-3/2}+O\big(r_{1}^{-5/2}\big). $$

According to (A.35), we also get the equation:

$$ \dot{F}_{0}(r)=\frac{B_{0}}{-D_{0}\sqrt{r}}\int_{r_{1}}^{r}\sqrt{\tilde{r}}\dot{F}_{1}(\tilde{r})d\tilde{r}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{r}}\int_{r_{1}}^{r}\frac{B_{0}}{\sqrt{r^{\prime}}}\bigg(\frac{1}{-D_{0}\sqrt{r^{\prime}}}\int_{r_{1}}^{r^{\prime}}\sqrt{\tilde{r}}\dot{F}_{1}(\tilde{r})d\tilde{r}\bigg)dr^{\prime}+O\big(r_{1}^{-5/2}r^{-1/2}\big), $$

where the first two terms are non-negative. Thus, for all $r>2r_{1}:$

$$ \dot{F}_{0}(r)\gtrsim r_{1}^{-3/2}r^{-1/2}+O\big(r_{1}^{-5/2}r^{-1/2}\big). $$

Next, we integrate equation (A.34):

$$ \displaystyle\dot{A}_{0}(r) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{-D_{0}\sqrt{r}}\int_{r_{1}}^{r}\sqrt{r^{\prime}}\dot{F}_{0}(r^{\prime})dr^{\prime}+O\big(r_{1}^{-5/2}r^{-3/2}\big) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{-2D_{0}\sqrt{r}}\int_{r_{1}}^{r}\bigg[\int_{r_{1}}^{r^{\prime}}\frac{B_{0}}{\sqrt{r^{\prime\prime}}}\bigg(\frac{1}{-D_{0}\sqrt{r^{\prime\prime}}}\int_{r_{1}}^{r^{\prime\prime}}\sqrt{\tilde{r}}\dot{F}_{1}(\tilde{r})d\tilde{r}\bigg)dr^{\prime\prime}\bigg]dr^{\prime} \displaystyle\ +\frac{1}{-D_{0}\sqrt{r}}\int_{r_{1}}^{r}\bigg(\frac{B_{0}}{-D_{0}}\int_{r_{1}}^{r^{\prime}}\sqrt{\tilde{r}}\dot{F}_{1}(\tilde{r})d\tilde{r}\bigg)dr^{\prime}+O\big(r_{1}^{-5/2}r^{-3/2}\big). $$

We notice that the first two terms are non-negative and for any $r>3r_{1}$ , we have:

$$ \dot{A}_{0}(r)\gtrsim r_{1}^{-3/2}r^{-3/2}+O\big(r_{1}^{-5/2}r^{-3/2}\big). $$

As a result, we also have:

$$ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{\dot{A}_{0}}{\sqrt{r}}dr>\int_{3r_{1}}^{\infty}\frac{\dot{A}_{0}}{\sqrt{r}}dr+O\big(r_{1}^{-7/2}\big)\gtrsim r_{1}^{-5/2}. $$

Thus, equation (A.42) implies that $\eta_{3}=0$ as well, which contradicts $(\eta_{1},\eta_{2},\eta_{3})\neq(0,0,0).$ ∎

According to Lemma A.1, Lemma A.2, and Lemma A.3, the map $\mathcal{C}$ satisfies the required conditions to apply the Implicit Function Theorem. We obtain the following result:

#### Corollary A.1.

Let $(w,p_{0},F_{1})\in W\times\mathbb{R}\times Y$ such that $\mathcal{C}(w,p_{0},F_{1})=0$ and $r_{0}\geq R_{0}$ is large enough, as required in Lemmas A.1, A.2, and A.3. There exist neighborhoods $(w,p_{0})\in U\subset W\times\mathbb{R}$ , $F_{1}\in V\subset Y,$ and a $C^{1}$ function $\mathcal{F}:U\rightarrow V$ such that $F_{1}=\mathcal{F}(w,p_{0})$ and $\mathcal{C}\big(\underline{w},\underline{p_{0}},\mathcal{F}(\underline{w},\underline{p_{0}})\big)=0$ for any $(\underline{w},\underline{p_{0}})\in U.$

We conclude this section by proving that in the set-up of Proposition A.1, we can extend $\partial_{r}\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)$ to $[r_{0},\infty),$ while satisfying the vanishing conditions (A.23)-(A.24):

#### Proposition A.2.

Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be a $C^{2}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data set. We fix $R_{0}>0$ large enough depending on $\mathfrak{D}$ and $\Lambda$ , so that Lemmas A.1, A.2, A.3, and Corollary A.1 apply for any $r_{0}\geq R_{0}$ with:

$$ w=\big(\theta(r_{0}),\mathcal{T}\theta(r_{0}),\ldots,\mathcal{T}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi\big)(r_{0})\big),\ p_{0}=\phi(r_{0}),\ F_{1}=\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T\phi}\big). $$

There exists a constant $C_{1}>0,$ such that the following holds: for all $\varepsilon>0$ small enough in terms of $\mathfrak{D},\Lambda,$ and $r_{0}$ , and any partial data set $\underline{\mathfrak{D}}$ on $[0,r_{0}]$ which satisfies (A.1) and $\underline{\partial_{U}^{i}r}(0)=\partial_{U}^{i}r(0)$ for $i\in\{1,2\}$ , we denote:

$$ \underline{w}=\big(\underline{\theta}(r_{0}),\underline{\mathcal{T}\theta}(r_{0}),\ldots,\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma}\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)(r_{0})\big),\ \underline{p_{0}}=\underline{\phi}(r_{0}). $$

Then, there exists $\underline{F_{1}}:[r_{0},\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ such that $\underline{F_{1}}\in Y,\ \|\underline{F_{1}}-F_{1}\|_{Y}<C_{1}\varepsilon,$ and:

$$ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\partial_{r}\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)dr=-\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)(r_{0}),\ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\theta}}{\sqrt{r}}dr=-\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}(r_{0}),\ \int_{r_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{\underline{\theta}}{\sqrt{r}}dr=-\underline{\phi}(r_{0}), $$

where $\big(\underline{\theta},\underline{\mathcal{T}\theta},\ldots,\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma}\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)\big)=\mathcal{S}\big(\underline{w},\underline{F_{1}}\big).$

#### Proof.

We note that Definition 2.6, the null constraint equations (A.3)-(A.10), and (A.21)-(A.22) imply that there exists $M>0$ depending on $\mathfrak{D}$ such that $w,p_{0},$ and $F_{1}$ defined in (A.50) satisfy $w\in W,\ F_{1}\in Y,$ and $\mathcal{C}(w,p_{0},F_{1})=0,$ for all $r_{0}$ sufficiently large in terms of $\mathfrak{D}$ and $\Lambda$ . Given this value of $M,$ we fix $R_{0}$ such that Lemmas A.1, A.2, A.3, and Corollary A.1 apply for any $r_{0}\geq R_{0}$ .

According to Corollary A.1, we get neighborhoods $(w,p_{0})\in U\subset W\times\mathbb{R}$ , $F_{1}\in V\subset Y,$ and a $C^{1}$ function $\mathcal{F}:U\rightarrow V$ such that $F_{1}=\mathcal{F}(w,p_{0})$ and $\mathcal{C}\big(\underline{w^{\prime}},\underline{p_{0}^{\prime}},\mathcal{F}(\underline{w^{\prime}},\underline{p_{0}^{\prime}})\big)=0$ for any $(\underline{w^{\prime}},\underline{p_{0}^{\prime}})\in U.$

The smallness condition (A.1) and the boundary conditions at $\Gamma$ imply that there exists a constant $C_{1}^{\prime}>0$ independent of $\varepsilon$ and $r_{0},$ such that the following estimates hold at $r_{0}:$

$$ \displaystyle\big|\underline{\gamma}-\gamma\big|(r_{0})<C_{1}^{\prime}\varepsilon,\  \displaystyle\big|\underline{\partial_{U}r}-\partial_{U}r\big|(r_{0})<C_{1}^{\prime}\varepsilon r_{0}^{2},\ \big|\underline{\phi}-\phi\big|(r_{0})<C_{1}^{\prime}\varepsilon r_{0}^{-1}, \displaystyle\big|\underline{\theta}-\theta\big|(r_{0})<C_{1}^{\prime}\varepsilon r_{0}^{-3/2},\  \displaystyle\big|\underline{\mathcal{T}\gamma}-\mathcal{T}\gamma\big|(r_{0})<C_{1}^{\prime}\varepsilon,\ \big|\underline{\mathcal{T}\partial_{U}r}-\mathcal{T}\partial_{U}r\big|(r_{0})<C_{1}^{\prime}\varepsilon r_{0}^{2}, \displaystyle\big|\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}-\mathcal{T}\phi\big|(r_{0})<C_{1}^{\prime}\varepsilon r_{0}^{-1},\  \displaystyle\big|\underline{\mathcal{T}\theta}-\mathcal{T}\theta\big|(r_{0})<C_{1}^{\prime}\varepsilon r_{0}^{-3/2},\ \big|\underline{\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi}-\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi\big|(r_{0})<C_{1}^{\prime}\varepsilon r_{0}^{-1}. $$

Therefore, for all $\varepsilon>0$ sufficiently small in terms of $\mathfrak{D},\Lambda,$ and $r_{0},$ we have that $(\underline{w},\underline{p_{0}})\in U$ . We define $\underline{F_{1}}=\mathcal{F}(\underline{w},\underline{p_{0}}),$ which satisfies $\underline{F_{1}}\in V$ and $\mathcal{C}(\underline{w},\underline{p_{0}},\underline{F_{1}})=0,$ so (A.51) holds. Since $\mathcal{F}\in C^{1}$ , there exists a constant $C_{1}>0$ depending on $\mathfrak{D},\Lambda,$ and $r_{0},$ such that $\|\underline{F_{1}}-F_{1}\|_{Y}\leq C_{1}\varepsilon.$ ∎

### A.3 Proof of Proposition A.1

#### Proof of Proposition A.1.

We prove the result for $k=2,$ and we refer the reader to Remark A.4 for the general case. Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be a $C^{2}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data set. We fix $r_{0}>0$ large enough in terms of $\mathfrak{D}$ and $\Lambda$ , as in the proof of Proposition A.2. We make the notation convention for the purpose of this proof that we write $x\lesssim y$ for any quantities $x,y>0$ if there is a constant $C(\Lambda,\mathfrak{D},r_{0})>0$ such that $x\leq Cy.$

For any $\varepsilon>0$ sufficiently small in terms of $\mathfrak{D},\Lambda,$ and $r_{0}$ , let $\underline{\mathfrak{D}}$ be a $C^{2}$ characteristic partial data set satisfying (A.1). At first, we use double null coordinates adapted to $\mathfrak{D}.$ We choose an ingoing coordinate for $\underline{\mathfrak{D}}$ such that $\underline{\partial_{U}^{i}r}(0)=\partial_{U}^{i}r(0),\ i\in\{1,2\}$ , and we use the asymptotically Eddington-Finkelstein coordinate $V$ of $\mathfrak{D}$ for $\underline{\mathfrak{D}}$ as well.

According to Proposition A.2, there exists $\underline{F_{1}}\in Y$ such that $\|\underline{F_{1}}-F_{1}\|_{Y}<C_{1}\varepsilon$ and the vanishing conditions (A.51) hold, where $\big(\underline{\theta},\underline{\mathcal{T}\theta},\ldots,\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma}\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)\big)=\mathcal{S}\big(\underline{w},\underline{F_{1}}\big).$ As a consequence, we get that:

$$ \underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}(r)=-\int_{r}^{\infty}\frac{\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\theta}}{\sqrt{r^{\prime}}}dr^{\prime}. $$

In particular, we improve the pointwise bounds in Lemma A.1 as follows:

$$ \big|\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}\big|\lesssim r^{-1},\ \big|\partial_{r}(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi})\big|\lesssim r^{-3/2}. $$

Integrating equations (A.15) and (A.11) as in the proof of Lemma A.1, we improve the pointwise bounds (A.28), (A.29):

$$ |\underline{\theta}|\lesssim r^{-5/2}\log r,\ |\partial_{r}\underline{\theta}|\lesssim r^{-7/2}\log r,\ |\underline{\mathcal{T}\theta}|\lesssim r^{-5/2}(\log r)^{2}. $$

Using (A.51), we can extend $\underline{\phi}$ as a $C^{2}$ function to $[r_{0},\infty)$ by:

$$ \underline{\phi}(r)=-\int_{r}^{\infty}\frac{\underline{\theta}}{\sqrt{r^{\prime}}}dr^{\prime}, $$

which satisfies $\underline{\phi}\in L^{2}([r_{0},\infty)).$ The pointwise bounds in (A.56) further imply that $\underline{\phi}\in H^{2}([r_{0},\infty)).$ Differentiating equation (A.3), we also obtain that:

$$ |\partial_{r}^{3}\underline{\phi}|\lesssim r^{-5}(\log r)^{2}+r^{-9/2}|\underline{F_{1}}|, $$

which implies that $\underline{\phi}\in H^{3}([r_{0},\infty)).$

We use the improved pointwise bounds (A.56) in (A.55) to get:

$$ |\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}|\lesssim r^{-2}(\log r)^{3},\ |\partial_{r}\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}|\lesssim r^{-3}(\log r)^{2}, $$

so we get that $\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}\in H^{1}([r_{0},\infty)).$ Equation (A.7) also implies that:

$$ |\partial_{r}^{2}\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}|\lesssim r^{-4}(\log r)^{2}+r^{-5/2}|\underline{F_{1}}|, $$

so we further get that $\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}\in H^{2}([r_{0},\infty)).$

Additionally, using (A.51) we can extend $\underline{\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi}$ as a $C^{0}$ function to $[r_{0},\infty)$ :

$$ \underline{\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi}(r)=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma}(r)}\int_{r}^{\infty}\underline{F_{1}}(r^{\prime})dr^{\prime}-\frac{\underline{\mathcal{T}\gamma}}{\underline{\gamma}}\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}, $$

which also implies that $\underline{F_{1}}=\partial_{r}\underline{\mathcal{T}}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi}\big).$ We also notice that:

$$ \lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}r^{2}\big(\underline{\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi}\big)^{2}\leq\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}r\bigg(\int_{r}^{\infty}\underline{F_{1}}(r^{\prime})dr^{\prime}\bigg)^{2}\leq\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}\int_{r}^{\infty}\big(r^{\prime}\underline{F_{1}}\big)^{2}dr^{\prime}=0, $$

$$ \int_{r}^{\infty}\tilde{r}^{2}\Big[\partial_{r}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma}\underline{\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi}\big)\Big]^{2}d\tilde{r}\lesssim\big\|\underline{F_{1}}\big\|_{Y}^{2}+\int_{r}^{\infty}\tilde{r}^{2}\Big[\partial_{r}\big(\sqrt{r}\underline{\mathcal{T}\gamma}\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}\big)\Big]^{2}d\tilde{r}\lesssim\big\|\underline{F_{1}}\big\|_{Y}^{2}+\big\|\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}\big\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\lesssim 1. $$

Similarly to (2.32), we have the following Hardy inequality for any function $f$ such that the RHS of (A.59) is finite:

$$ rf^{2}+\int_{r}^{\infty}f^{2}d\tilde{r}\leq 2\lim_{\tilde{r}\rightarrow\infty}\tilde{r}f^{2}+8\int_{r}^{\infty}\tilde{r}^{2}\big(\partial_{r}f\big)^{2}d\tilde{r}. $$

Using (A.59) for $\sqrt{r}\underline{\gamma}\cdot\underline{\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi},$ together with (A.57)-(A.58), we obtain that $\underline{\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi}\in H^{1}([r_{0},\infty)).$

So far, we proved that $\underline{\phi}\in H^{3}([r_{0},\infty)),\ \underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}\in H^{2}([r_{0},\infty)),\ \underline{\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi}\in H^{1}([r_{0},\infty)).$ Using a similar argument for differences of solutions, it is straightforward to obtain that:

$$ \big\|\underline{\phi}-\phi\big\|_{H^{3}[r_{0},\infty)}+\big\|\underline{\mathcal{T}\phi}-\mathcal{T}\phi\big\|_{H^{2}[r_{0},\infty)}+\big\|\underline{\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi}-\mathcal{T}^{2}\phi\big\|_{H^{1}[r_{0},\infty)}\lesssim\varepsilon. $$

According to Remark A.2, the tuple $\underline{\mathfrak{D}}$ is determined uniquely on $[r_{0},\infty)$ by the solution to the null constraint equations (A.3)-(A.10) that we constructed, and it satisfies the compatibility conditions in Definition 2.6. In view of (A.60), we have that the extended $\underline{\mathfrak{D}}$ satisfies (A.2) as desired. Next, we choose coordinates $(\underline{U},\underline{V})$ that are asymptotically Eddington-Finkelstein with respect to $\underline{\mathfrak{D}}$ . We define $\underline{M}=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}\underline{m}(r)$ , then choose an asymptotically Eddington-Finkelstein coordinate $\underline{V}$ satisfying (2.14) and (2.21). We rescale the ingoing coordinate $\underline{U}=U\cdot(1+O(\varepsilon))$ such that $\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}\underline{\gamma}(r)=2,$ which implies that (2.22)-(2.23) hold at zero order. Furthermore, using the already established pointwise estimates, it is straightforward to prove the asymptotic rates (2.22)-(2.24), concluding that $\underline{\mathfrak{D}}$ is a $C^{2}$ asymptotically AdS characteristic data set. ∎

#### Remark A.4.

In the general case $k\geq 2$ , we have the commuted system for all $0\leq n\leq k-1:$

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}^{n}\theta+\bigg(\frac{1}{2r}+\frac{\Lambda\gamma r}{2\partial_{U}r}\bigg)\mathcal{T}^{n}\theta= \displaystyle\frac{\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}^{n}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi\big)}{-\partial_{U}r}+Err_{1}^{n}, \displaystyle\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}^{n}\gamma= \displaystyle Err_{2}^{n}, \displaystyle\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}^{n}\partial_{U}r= \displaystyle\frac{\Lambda}{2}r\mathcal{T}^{n}\gamma+Err_{3}^{n}, $$

where we have the schematic error terms:

$$ \displaystyle Err_{1}^{n}= \displaystyle\sum_{i+j+l=n,\ l\geq 1}\mathcal{T}^{i}\theta\mathcal{T}^{j}\theta\mathcal{T}^{l}\theta+\sum_{h+i+j+l=n,\ l\geq 1}\mathcal{T}^{h}\bigg(\frac{\sqrt{r}}{-\partial_{U}r}\bigg)\mathcal{T}^{i}\theta\mathcal{T}^{j}\theta\mathcal{T}^{l}\big(\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi\big)+ \displaystyle+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{T}^{i}\bigg(\frac{1}{-\partial_{U}r}\bigg)\partial_{r}\mathcal{T}^{n-i}\big(\sqrt{r}\gamma\mathcal{T}\phi\big)+\frac{\Lambda r}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{T}^{i}\bigg(\frac{\gamma}{\partial_{U}r}\bigg)\mathcal{T}^{n-i}\theta, \displaystyle Err_{2}^{n}= \displaystyle\sum_{i+j+l=n}\mathcal{T}^{i}\theta\mathcal{T}^{j}\theta\mathcal{T}^{l}\gamma, \displaystyle Err_{3}^{n}= \displaystyle\sum_{i+j+l=n,\ l\geq 1}\mathcal{T}^{i}\theta\mathcal{T}^{j}\theta\mathcal{T}^{l}\partial_{U}r. $$

This system has the same structure as the null constraint equations (A.3)-(A.10), so it is clear that the argument in the proof of Proposition A.1 can be adapted to the general case $k\geq 2$ using an induction argument.
